chapters.title: Water — The Essence of Life
chapters.summary: In this chapter: water on earth and freshwater; water has different forms; water cycle; groundwater.

lessons.title: Water on Earth and Freshwater

activities.prompt: If Earth is full of water, why can't we drink most of it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water All Around Us
activities.body: Look at a globe. Most of the Earth's surface is covered with water. But most of that water is salty, like the sea. The water we can use is called freshwater. All living beings need freshwater to live. We drink it, cook with it and grow our crops with it. If all the Earth's water were in one big glass, freshwater would fill only a teaspoon!
keyPoints: Most of the Earth's surface is covered with water.
Most of the water on Earth is salty.
All living beings need freshwater to live.
Freshwater is only a tiny part of all the water on Earth.
activities.explanation: Water is everywhere, but the freshwater we can use is very little, so we must use it carefully.

activities.prompt: Asha is very thirsty near the sea. She thinks sea water can be her drinking water. Is she right?
steps: Drinking water must be freshwater, because all living beings need freshwater to live.
Sea water is salty, and most water on Earth is salty like this.
Salty water is not freshwater, so it cannot be drinking water.
So Asha is wrong. She needs freshwater, not sea water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What covers most of the Earth?
activities.prompt: Most of the Earth's surface is covered by which of these?
options: Water
Sand
Grass
Rocks
activities.explanation: Well done! Most of the Earth's surface is covered with water.

activities.title: Why do we need freshwater?
activities.prompt: Why do we need freshwater every day?
options: For drinking and growing crops
For making the sea salty
For filling the oceans
For drying seawater
activities.explanation: Right! We need freshwater for drinking, for growing crops and for our daily activities.

activities.title: Fill the missing word
activities.prompt: Most of the water on Earth is ______, so we cannot drink it.
activities.hint: Think about the taste of sea water.
activities.explanation: That's it! Most of the water on Earth is salty, like the water in the sea.

activities.title: Salt from the sea
activities.prompt: In Gujarat, how do people collect salt from the sea?
options: By letting the seawater dry in the sun
By boiling the seawater with freshwater
By digging the sand near the sea
By catching fish from the sea
activities.explanation: Yes! In Gujarat, seawater is dried to collect salt. Gujarat is one of the largest salt producing areas in India.

activities.title: How a johad helps
activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order, from big to small, like the lesson describes them.
items: All the water on Earth
The freshwater in the world
A johad collecting rainwater in Rajasthan
A teaspoon of freshwater in a glass
activities.explanation: Super thinking! You went from all the water on Earth down to a tiny teaspoon, with a johad catching rainwater along the way.

activities.prompt: Ravi is at the beach. He played for a long time. Now he is very thirsty. He has a bottle of sea water. What will happen if he drinks it?
options: His thirst will go away, because sea water is water.
His thirst will not go away, because sea water is salty.
His thirst will not go away, because sea water is too cold.
His thirst will go away, because the sea is very big.

why.His thirst will go away, because sea wat: Thinks any water can be drinking water, but sea water is salty.
why.His thirst will not go away, because sea: Thinks coldness matters, but the real problem is the salt.
why.His thirst will go away, because the sea: Thinks a big sea means good water, but size does not remove salt.

activities.explanation: Right. Drinking water must be freshwater, and sea water is salty.

activities.prompt: In Gujarat, people dry sea water to collect salt. Gujarat makes a lot of salt this way. Meena says she can dry pond water the same way and get lots of salt. What is wrong with Meena's idea?
options: Pond water is too dirty to make salt from it.
Ponds are too small, so salt needs a big pond.
Pond water is freshwater, so it has very little salt.
Salt can only be made in winter, not in summer.

why.Pond water is too dirty to make salt fro: Thinks dirt makes salt, but salt comes from salty water.
why.Ponds are too small, so salt needs a big: Thinks size is the problem, but the real problem is the water.
why.Salt can only be made in winter, not in: Thinks season matters, but the salt in the water is what matters.

activities.explanation: Right. Freshwater has almost no salt, so drying it gives no salt.

activities.prompt: Many plants and animals live in freshwater. A fish lives in a freshwater pond. Someone moves it to the sea. What will happen to the fish and why?
options: It will be happy, because the sea has more water.
It will be happy, because fish like to swim far.
It will not live well, because it needs freshwater to live.
It will not live well, because the sea has too many fish.

why.It will be happy, because the sea has mo: Thinks more water is always better, but the fish needs freshwater.
why.It will be happy, because fish like to s: Thinks swimming space matters, but the water kind matters more.
why.It will not live well, because the sea h: Thinks crowding is the problem, but the salty water is the problem.

activities.explanation: Right. Living beings need freshwater, and sea water is salty.

activities.prompt: Freshwater is needed for growing crops. A farmer gets a new field. A pipe brings only salty sea water to this field. What will happen to the crops?
options: They will grow very well, because sea water never ends.
They will not grow well, because crops need freshwater.
They will grow very well, because salt helps crops grow.
They will not grow well, because the field is too far away.

why.They will grow very well, because sea wa: Thinks lots of water is enough, but crops need freshwater.
why.They will grow very well, because salt h: Thinks salt is good for crops, but crops need freshwater.
why.They will not grow well, because the fie: Thinks distance matters, but the kind of water is the problem.

activities.explanation: Right. Crops need freshwater, and sea water is salty.

lessons.title: Water has Different Forms

activities.prompt: How can the same water be ice, rain, and steam?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Wears Three Costumes
activities.body: Water is amazing! It can wear three different costumes. As a liquid, it flows — like rain. As a solid, it is hard — like ice. As a vapour, it floats in the air — like steam. Water can change from one form to another and then change back again. Watch a glass of ice cubes and you will see it happen!
keyPoints: Water has three forms: liquid, solid, and vapour.
Rain is liquid, ice is solid, and steam is vapour.
Water can change into ice and steam, and back to liquid.
activities.explanation: Same water, three different looks!

activities.prompt: Priya takes a cold glass of water outside on a hot day. Soon she sees tiny drops on the outside of the glass. Where did the drops come from?
steps: The water inside is cold, so the glass is cold too.
The air around has water vapour in it, which we cannot see.
When the vapour touches the cold glass, it cools down and turns into small droplets.
So the drops came from the air, not from inside the glass.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Water Changes in the Sky
activities.body: The Sun's heat causes water to turn into water vapour. When this vapour cools high up, it forms small droplets. Soon, these droplets fall back down as rain. So water travels up as vapour and comes back down as droplets!
keyPoints: The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour.
Cooling vapour forms small droplets.
The droplets fall back down.
activities.explanation: Water goes up as vapour and comes back down as droplets.

activities.title: Which Form is Rain?
activities.prompt: Rain is falling outside your window. Which form of water is rain?
options: Solid
Liquid
Vapour
It is not water
activities.explanation: Rain is a liquid form of water. Well spotted!

activities.title: Ice and Steam
activities.prompt: Which form of water is ice?
options: Vapour
Liquid
Solid
Gas
activities.explanation: Ice is the solid form of water. Steam is the vapour form.

activities.title: The Melting Ice Cube
activities.prompt: Ice cubes left in a glass slowly ______ after some time.
activities.hint: Think about what happens to ice in your drink.
activities.explanation: Ice cubes left in a glass melt after some time. The solid turns to liquid!

activities.title: Match the Form
activities.prompt: Match each thing to its form of water.
activities.explanation: Rain is liquid, ice is solid, and steam is vapour. Three forms, all water!

activities.title: What Does the Sun's Heat Do?
activities.prompt: On a hot day, water in a puddle slowly disappears. What does the Sun's heat cause the water to become?
options: Ice
Water vapour
Steam from a kettle
Small stones
activities.explanation: The Sun's heat causes water to turn into water vapour.

activities.title: Put the Water Journey in Order
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order, from first to last.
items: The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour
The water vapour cools
Small droplets form
The droplets fall back down
activities.explanation: Heat makes vapour, cooling makes droplets, and the droplets fall back down. Great ordering!

activities.prompt: A cold bottle of water sits on a table. Small drops appear on the outside of the bottle. Why do the drops form?
options: Water leaked out through tiny holes in the bottle.
Water vapour in the air cooled and formed droplets.
The bottle melted a little and made the drops.
The drops came from rain that fell on the table.

why.Water leaked out through tiny holes in t: This child thinks water can pass through the bottle, but the bottle holds water in.
why.The bottle melted a little and made the: This child thinks the bottle itself changed, but glass does not melt on a table.
why.The drops came from rain that fell on th: This child brings in rain, but there is no rain inside a room.

activities.explanation: Right. When water vapour cools, it forms small droplets.

activities.prompt: Ravi wants to find out if the Sun's heat turns water into vapour. He puts one bowl of water in the sun. What should he do to make it a fair test?
options: Put another bowl with the same water in a shady place.
Put ice cubes into the bowl that is in the sun.
Use a much bigger bowl of water in the shade.
Boil the water in a pot before putting it in the sun.

why.Put ice cubes into the bowl that is in t: This child changed the water too, so the test would not be fair.
why.Use a much bigger bowl of water in the s: This child made the bowls different, so the test would not be fair.
why.Boil the water in a pot before putting i: This child changed the water before the test, so the test would not be fair.

activities.explanation: Right. Two same bowls, one in sun and one in shade, show what the Sun's heat does.

activities.prompt: Meena says rain is brand new water that clouds make. She says it was never water on Earth before. What is wrong with her claim?
options: Rain is droplets that cooled from vapour and fell back down.
Rain is ice that falls down from very cold clouds.
Rain is steam that comes out of boiling pots.
Rain is liquid that leaks out of the clouds.

why.Rain is ice that falls down from very co: This child mixes up rain and ice, but rain is the liquid form of water.
why.Rain is steam that comes out of boiling: This child mixes up rain and steam, but steam is the vapour form of water.
why.Rain is liquid that leaks out of the clo: This child thinks clouds leak, but the drops form when vapour cools.

activities.explanation: Right. Vapour cools into droplets, and the droplets fall back down as rain.

lessons.sceneCaption: Heating water makes it boil, and steam escapes from the kettle spout.

lessons.title: Water Cycle

activities.prompt: Where does rain come from, and where does it go after falling?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Goes Round and Round
activities.body: Have you ever seen a puddle shrink on a sunny day? The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour. This vapour rises and forms clouds. When the vapour cools, it makes tiny droplets. These droplets fall back down as rain, snow, or hail. The water flows back into rivers, lakes, and oceans. Then the Sun starts the journey again. This constant circular movement of water is called the water cycle.
keyPoints: The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour.
Water vapour forms clouds, and clouds come down as rain, snow, and hail.
The constant circular movement of water in nature is called the water cycle.
activities.explanation: Water keeps travelling through air, land, and sky, changing form as it goes.

activities.title: Follow a drop

tasks.say: Follow the water until it falls as rain.
tasks.then: Drops in the clouds grow heavy and fall.
Rivers carry the water back to the sea, ready to start again.

activities.takeaway: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as rain and flows back: the water cycle.
activities.explanation: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as rain and flows back: the water cycle.

activities.prompt: You leave a wet towel on a chair near a sunny window. After some hours, the towel is dry. Where did the water go?
steps: The Sun shines through the window, so the towel gets warm.
Heat makes water turn into water vapour, so the water leaves the towel and mixes with the air.
The towel is dry because all its water became vapour and went into the air.
That vapour can later cool and become part of a cloud, so the water is still travelling in the water cycle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What makes water from rivers and oceans turn into water vapour?
options: The wind blowing over it
The Sun's heat
The clouds above it
The fish swimming in it
activities.explanation: The Sun's heat gives water the energy to become water vapour. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: The Sun's ______ causes water to turn into water vapour.
activities.hint: Think of what you feel on your skin on a hot, sunny day.
activities.explanation: Heat is what makes water change into vapour. Great job!

activities.prompt: Match each part of the water cycle with what happens next.
pairs: The water then goes back into
activities.explanation: Each step leads to the next, and the journey starts all over again.

activities.prompt: What happens when water vapour cools down high in the sky?
options: It turns into small droplets
It turns into salt
It disappears forever
It sinks into the ground
activities.explanation: Cooling vapour forms small droplets. Later, these droplets fall back down to the earth.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the water cycle in the right order, starting with the Sun.
items: The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour
The water vapour forms clouds
The clouds come down as rain, snow, and hail
The water goes back into rivers, lakes, and oceans
activities.explanation: Heat makes vapour, vapour makes clouds, clouds give us rain, and the water flows back home. Then it all begins again!

activities.prompt: Why do we call it the water 'cycle'?
options: Because water moves in a constant circle in nature
Because water can only be seen in summer
Because water stays in one place forever
Because water is only found in oceans
activities.explanation: Water keeps going round and round, from sky to land and back again. That endless loop is the cycle!

activities.prompt: A bowl of water sits in the hot Sun all day. The water level goes down. What happened to the water?
options: It turned into water vapour and went into the air.
It sank to the bottom of the bowl and stayed there.
It became a cloud inside the bowl.
It turned into ice because the Sun was bright.

why.It sank to the bottom of the bowl and st: This child thinks water just hides in the bowl instead of changing form.
This child thinks clouds form right where water sits, not high in the sky.
why.It turned into ice because the Sun was b: This child mixes up heat and cold; heat does not make ice.

activities.explanation: Right. Heat makes water become water vapour, so it leaves the bowl.

activities.prompt: Water vapour rises high in the sky. The air up there is cold. What will the vapour do?
options: It will get hotter and stay as vapour forever.
It will cool and form small droplets.
It will turn into salt and sink into the ocean.
It will disappear and never come back.

why.It will get hotter and stay as vapour fo: This child thinks cold air makes things hotter, which is backwards.
why.It will turn into salt and sink into the: This child thinks vapour changes into a new material instead of water.
This child thinks water can leave the water cycle, but it keeps moving.

activities.explanation: Right. When water vapour cools, it forms small droplets.

activities.prompt: A child says: 'Rain falls, so the water cycle stops after one rain.' What is wrong with this claim?
options: Rain is not really made of water at all.
The cycle stops at night and starts again in the day.
The rain water goes back to rivers, lakes and oceans, so it keeps moving.
The Sun stops the cycle by drying up all the rain at once.

This child forgot that rain, snow and hail are forms of water from clouds.
why.The cycle stops at night and starts agai: This child thinks the cycle needs daylight only, but it is constant.
why.The Sun stops the cycle by drying up all: This child thinks drying ends the cycle, but it is part of the movement.

activities.explanation: Right. The water goes back into rivers, lakes and oceans, so the circular movement continues.

activities.prompt: Rain falls on a town. The water flows into a big lake. What can happen to that lake water next in the water cycle?
options: The Sun's heat can turn it into vapour, and it can form clouds again.
It stays in the lake forever and never moves again.
It turns into hail inside the lake water.
It becomes new water that is not part of the cycle.

why.It stays in the lake forever and never m: This child thinks water stops moving, but the cycle is constant.
why.It turns into hail inside the lake water: This child thinks hail forms in lakes, but hail comes down from clouds.
why.It becomes new water that is not part of: This child thinks rain water leaves the cycle, but water keeps changing form as it travels.

activities.explanation: Right. Heat turns water into vapour, and vapour forms clouds, so the cycle continues.

lessons.title: Groundwater

activities.prompt: Where does rainwater go after it disappears into the ground?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where does rainwater go?
activities.body: When it rains, some water is soaked up by the soil. It sinks down through layers of soil and rocks. Water stored deep underground is called groundwater. We dig wells, borewells, tube wells and handpumps to draw it up for our use. Open areas let water seep back into the ground to recharge it.
keyPoints: Rainwater soaks into the soil and sinks through soil and rocks.
Water stored deep underground is called groundwater.
We draw groundwater using wells, borewells, tube wells and handpumps.
activities.explanation: Rain does not just flow away — some of it travels down to become groundwater.

activities.prompt: After a big rain, Meena sees water pools on the new cement road near her house. But in the mud field next to it, there is no pool. Where did the field water go?
steps: The mud field is open, so rainwater can sink into the soil.
Water sinks down through soil and rocks when the ground is open.
The cement road is hard, so rainwater cannot sink into it there.
So the field water went underground, but the road water stayed on top.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is groundwater?
options: Water floating in the clouds
Water stored deep underground
Water flowing in rivers only
Water frozen on mountain tops
activities.explanation: Water that sinks into the soil and rocks is stored deep underground as groundwater. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Water stored deep ______ is called groundwater.
activities.hint: Think about where the water has travelled to.
activities.explanation: Groundwater sits deep underground, below layers of soil and rocks.

activities.prompt: Your family wants to draw groundwater. Which of these could you use?
options: A bucket left in the rain
A handpump or a well
A kite on a long string
A mirror facing the sky
activities.explanation: We dig wells, borewells, tube wells and handpumps to draw groundwater up.

activities.prompt: Why do planting trees and keeping open areas help groundwater?
options: They make rain fall as ice
They let water seep into the ground
They push water up the handpump
They make the soil dry faster
activities.explanation: Open, uncovered areas and tree roots let water seep into the ground and recharge groundwater.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of a raindrop in order, from first to last.
items: Rain falls from the sky
The water soaks into the soil
It sinks through layers of soil and rocks
It is stored deep underground as groundwater
We draw it up from a well
activities.explanation: A raindrop soaks in, sinks deep down, joins the groundwater, and later comes up through a well.

activities.prompt: A school covers its whole playground with cement. Now it rains hard. The rainwater cannot sink into the ground there. What will happen to the groundwater under the school over time?
options: It will get less because rain cannot refill it.
It will grow fast because cement holds water well.
It will stay the same because rain always fills it.
It will turn into a pond on top of the cement.

why.It will grow fast because cement holds w: Thinks cement helps water go in, but cement blocks the water.
why.It will stay the same because rain alway: Thinks rain fills groundwater no matter what covers the ground.
why.It will turn into a pond on top of the c: Thinks water piles up underground like a pond, but it just cannot sink in.

activities.explanation: Right. Cement stops water from sinking, so the groundwater is not refilled.

activities.prompt: Two houses get the same rain. House A has a big open garden with mud. House B has cement all around it. Both use wells. After many dry days, which well will have more water?
options: House B, because cement keeps the water safe below.
House A, because open mud lets rain sink down and refill it.
Both the same, because rain falls equally on both houses.
Neither, because wells never change when the weather changes.

why.House B, because cement keeps the water: Thinks cement protects water, but cement actually blocks rain from sinking in.
why.Both the same, because rain falls equall: Thinks equal rain means equal groundwater, but the ground cover matters.
why.Neither, because wells never change when: Thinks wells never change, but wells show what is under the ground.

activities.explanation: Right. Open mud lets rain seep down and refill the groundwater.

activities.prompt: Ravi does a test. He fills two pots with the same soil. He pours one full cup of water on each pot. Pot A is open mud. Pot B has a plastic sheet on top. Which pot lets the water sink into the soil?
options: Pot B, because the sheet stops water from running away.
Both pots, because water always finds a way into soil.
Pot A, because open soil lets water sink through it.
Neither pot, because poured water always stays on top.

why.Pot B, because the sheet stops water fro: Thinks covering soil helps, but the sheet blocks the water.
why.Both pots, because water always finds a: Thinks water always gets in, but a cover stops it from sinking.
why.Neither pot, because poured water always: Thinks water never sinks, but open soil soaks water up.

activities.explanation: Right. Open soil lets water seep down through it.

activities.prompt: A village well is getting dry. Dev says, 'Dig a deeper well. Then the groundwater will refill itself.' What is wrong with Dev's claim?
options: Nothing is wrong; deeper wells always make more water.
A deeper well draws more water, but it does not refill the groundwater.
Deeper wells are wrong because wells must always be shallow.
The well is dry because handpumps cannot draw groundwater.

why.Nothing is wrong; deeper wells always ma: Thinks digging deeper creates water, but digging only reaches water.
why.Deeper wells are wrong because wells mus: Thinks the problem is well depth rules, but the problem is refilling.
why.The well is dry because handpumps cannot: Thinks handpumps cannot draw groundwater, but they are made to do that.

activities.explanation: Right. A well draws water out; only seeping rain can refill it.

activities.prompt: A village digs a new pond and keeps the land around it open. Rain falls into the pond and on the open land. What will happen to the groundwater under the village?
options: It will get less, because ponds dry up the ground.
It will stay the same, because ponds only hold water on top.
It will refill, because pond water and rain can seep underground.
It will disappear, because ponds push water far away.

why.It will get less, because ponds dry up t: Thinks ponds take water away, but ponds help water go down.
why.It will stay the same, because ponds onl: Thinks ponds only sit on top, but their water can seep down.
why.It will disappear, because ponds push wa: Thinks ponds push water away, but ponds let it sink nearby.

activities.explanation: Right. Ponds and open land let rainwater seep down and refill groundwater.

activities.prompt: Near a well, people cut down all the trees and leave bare, hard ground. Years pass with normal rain. What will happen to the well?
options: It will give more water, because trees used to drink the water.
It will give less water, because fewer trees means less rain sinks in.
It will not change, because trees and wells are not connected.
It will fill up, because cutting trees makes more rain fall in.

why.It will give more water, because trees u: Thinks trees steal water, but trees actually help water sink into the ground.
why.It will not change, because trees and we: Thinks trees and wells are separate, but trees help refill the water wells use.
why.It will fill up, because cutting trees m: Thinks cutting trees makes more rain, but rain amount is not the problem here.

activities.explanation: Right. Trees help rainwater seep down, so fewer trees means less refilling.

lessons.title: Surface Water and Rivers

activities.prompt: Where does a river's journey begin, and where does it end?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where Rivers Begin
activities.body: Rivers, ponds and lakes give us freshwater. A river often starts its journey high up in the mountains. Then it flows down across the land. The shape of the land tells the water when to flow, stop or curve. And the flowing water can change the shape of the land too. In this lesson, you will follow a river on its journey.
keyPoints: Rivers, ponds and lakes are natural sources of freshwater.
A river often begins up in the mountains and flows down across the land.
The shape of the land guides the water, and water can reshape the land.
activities.explanation: Water and land are partners: the land guides the river, and the river slowly reshapes the land.

activities.prompt: A boy drops a paper boat in a small stream near his village. The stream goes around a big rock and then turns left. Why did the boat not go straight?
steps: The land under the stream is not flat, so the water must bend around the rock.
Water always follows the shape of the land it flows over.
So the boat turned left because the land made the water turn.
Over many years, the flowing water can also wear the land and change its shape.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where does a river often begin its journey?
options: Beside the sea
In a big city
Up in the mountains
Inside a school
activities.explanation: A river often starts high up in the mountains, then flows down across the land.

activities.prompt: After starting in the mountains, a river flows ______ across the land.
activities.hint: Think of a slide: which way do you go?
activities.explanation: A river flows down across the land, from the mountains towards lower ground.

activities.prompt: What decides whether water flows, stops or curves?
options: The time of day
The shape of the land
The colour of the sky
The name of the river
activities.explanation: Water follows the land. Hills, dips and bends make it flow, stop or curve.

activities.prompt: Match each river fact to its partner.
pairs: the marshy lands of the Rann
activities.explanation: Rivers can take different paths. Some reach a sea, and the Luni ends in the Rann.

activities.prompt: Put the story of a river's journey in the correct order.
items: A river begins its journey up in the mountains.
It flows down across the land.
The shape of the land makes the water flow, stop or curve.
The flowing water can change the shape of the land.
activities.explanation: First the river starts high, then it flows down, the land guides it, and slowly the water reshapes the land.

activities.prompt: Hiware Bazar in Maharashtra is a water-positive village. How did local people help make this happen?
options: They stopped using water at home
They moved the village to the mountains
They waited for the government to dig a canal
They practised rainwater harvesting and watershed management
activities.explanation: Local communities worked together on watershed management and rainwater harvesting. Teamwork made the village water-positive!

activities.prompt: A river meets a flat plain and then a hill of hard rock. What will the river do at the hill?
options: It will curve or stop because of the land shape.
It will climb over the top of the hill.
It will flow in a straight line through the rock.
It will dry up at once and disappear.

This child thinks water can move uphill, but it cannot.
why.It will flow in a straight line through: This child thinks land never changes the path of a river.
This child thinks rivers always end when land blocks them.

activities.explanation: Right. Water flows, stops, or curves according to the shape of land.

activities.prompt: A river flows fast over soft soil for many years. What will happen to the soil?
options: The flowing water will slowly change the shape of the land.
The soil will become as hard as a mountain rock.
The soil will rise up and make the river stop.
The soil will stay exactly the same forever.

why.The soil will become as hard as a mounta: This child thinks water makes soil harder, but flowing water wears it.
why.The soil will rise up and make the river: This child thinks soil grows on its own and blocks rivers.
why.The soil will stay exactly the same fore: This child thinks land never changes, but water shapes it.

activities.explanation: Right. The flow of water can change the shape of land.

activities.prompt: Two villages get the same rain. Village A saves rainwater with its people's help. Village B does nothing. What will happen?
options: Village A will have more water because people managed the water.
Village B will have more water because it used none.
Both villages will have the same water no matter what.
Village A will have less water because saving uses water up.

why.Village B will have more water because i: This child thinks doing nothing saves water, but stored rain is what helps.
why.Both villages will have the same water n: This child thinks people's work makes no difference to water.
why.Village A will have less water because s: This child confuses saving water with losing water.

activities.explanation: Right. Communities helping with watershed work and rainwater harvesting add water.

activities.prompt: A girl says every river must end in a sea. Her friend remembers one river that does not. Which river is she thinking of?
options: The Luni, which ends in the marshy lands of the Rann.
The Luni, which ends in the Arabian Sea.
The Luni, which ends in the Bay of Bengal.
The Luni, which ends on a high mountain top.

This child assumes all rivers reach the Arabian Sea.
why.The Luni, which ends in the Bay of Benga: This child assumes all rivers reach the Bay of Bengal.
why.The Luni, which ends on a high mountain: This child thinks rivers end where they begin, up high.

activities.explanation: Right. The Luni does not drain into a sea; it ends in the Rann.

activities.prompt: A boy says the Luni starts in a desert and flows uphill. What is wrong with his claim?
options: The Luni starts in the Aravalli Range and flows down.
The Luni starts in the Rann and flows uphill.
The Luni starts in the Arabian Sea and flows inland.
The Luni starts in Hiware Bazar and flows uphill.

why.The Luni starts in the Rann and flows up: This child mixes up where the river starts with where it ends.
why.The Luni starts in the Arabian Sea and f: This child thinks rivers begin at the sea and flow backwards.
why.The Luni starts in Hiware Bazar and flow: This child mixes up a water-positive village with a river's start.

activities.explanation: Right. The Luni begins in the Aravalli Range and rivers flow down.

lessons.title: Life in Water

activities.prompt: Who lives in the pond near our school, and how do they breathe there?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Pond is a Busy Home
activities.body: Rain filled the pond near the school ground. Now many plants and animals live there. Water hyacinth floats and spreads fast. Lotus flowers float too. Fish swim with fins. A water scorpion breathes through a tail tube. A pond heron stands still on its long legs to catch fish. Aquatic plants and animals have special features that help them survive in water.
keyPoints: Many kinds of plants and animals live in water.
Water animals have special features, like fins, to survive.
Freshwater is essential for supporting life on Earth.
activities.explanation: A small pond can be a busy home for many living things.

activities.prompt: A fish swims easily in the pond. But a cow that walks into deep water starts to struggle. Why can the fish swim well but the cow cannot?
steps: The fish lives in water, so its body has special parts for water life.
It has fins, and fins help it swim smoothly in the pond.
The cow lives on land, so its body was made for walking, not swimming.
So animals get the body parts that match the place where they live.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Water animals use which body part to swim?
options: Fins
Wings
Long legs
Tail tubes
activities.explanation: Animals in water have fins to swim. Well done!

activities.prompt: Reeds grow along the edges of ponds.
activities.explanation: Yes, reeds like to grow right at the pond's edge.

activities.prompt: A dragonfly lays its eggs near ______.
activities.hint: Think about where the dragonfly likes to fly.
activities.explanation: The dragonfly lays eggs near water, and it eats mosquitoes too.

activities.prompt: Match each pond living thing to its special feature.
activities.explanation: Every pond animal has its own clever way of living in water.

activities.prompt: The water scorpion lives underwater. How does it breathe?
options: With a tail tube
With big fins
With long legs
With floating flowers
activities.explanation: The water scorpion uses a tail tube to breathe underwater. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Lotus and water lily flowers sink to the bottom of the pond.
activities.explanation: Not quite! These lovely flowers float on the water.

activities.prompt: Why does the pond heron stand still in the water?
options: To catch fish
To lay eggs
To breathe underwater
To spread on water
activities.explanation: Standing still on its long legs helps the heron catch fish.

activities.prompt: Water hyacinth grows very fast. What happens in the pond?
options: It spreads on the water
It sinks to the bottom
It turns into fins
It flies like a dragonfly
activities.explanation: Water hyacinth floats and spreads quickly on the water.

activities.prompt: Ravi puts a goldfish in a bucket of rainwater. The fish swims around happily. Now Ravi wonders why the fish can live in this water. What does the water give the fish?
options: It gives the fish a home where it can live and swim
It gives the fish long legs for standing still
It gives the fish wings to fly away fast
It gives the fish a tail tube for breathing air

why.It gives the fish long legs for standing: This mixes up fish with a bird like the pond heron.
why.It gives the fish wings to fly away fast: This mixes up fish with a fast flyer like the dragonfly.
why.It gives the fish a tail tube for breath: This mixes up fish with the water scorpion's breathing tube.

activities.explanation: Right. Freshwater supports life, so the fish can live and swim in it.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'Any animal can live in water if it just tries hard.' His friend puts a small land animal into a pond of rainwater to check this. What will the friend most likely see?
options: The animal will swim fast using new fins it grows
The animal will catch mosquitoes near the water
The animal will not breathe well and will need help
The animal will float like a lotus flower on top

why.The animal will swim fast using new fins: Animals cannot grow new fins quickly, so this prediction is wrong.
why.The animal will catch mosquitoes near th: Catching mosquitoes is a dragonfly's job, not a land animal's.
why.The animal will float like a lotus flowe: Floating like a lotus is a plant feature, not an animal one.

activities.explanation: Right. Land animals cannot breathe in water, so it will struggle.

activities.context: Meena lives in a village in Rajasthan where rainwater flows away quickly after every rain. Her grandfather suggests building a johad, a traditional small earthen dam, to collect the rainwater. Far away in Gujarat, her uncle works by the sea, where seawater is dried to collect salt. Meena wonders why the seawater near her uncle cannot be used for drinking or for growing crops.
activities.prompt: Why can Meena's uncle NOT use the seawater at his workplace for drinking or for growing crops?
options: Because seawater is salty
Because seawater is too deep to carry
Because seawater is muddy and dirty
Because seawater is too cold to use

why.Because seawater is too deep to carry: Depth does not stop water from being used; deep water can still be pumped or carried.
why.Because seawater is muddy and dirty: Muddy water can be cleaned by settling or filtering, so this is not the real reason.
why.Because seawater is too cold to use: Cold water can be warmed and used, so temperature is not the reason.

activities.explanation: Correct. Seawater is salty, so it cannot be used for drinking or growing crops.

activities.context: Meena lives in a village in Rajasthan where rainwater flows away quickly after every rain. Her grandfather suggests building a johad, a traditional small earthen dam, to collect the rainwater. Far away in Gujarat, her uncle works by the sea, where seawater is dried to collect salt. Meena wonders why the seawater near her uncle cannot be used for drinking or for growing crops.
activities.prompt: If the villagers decide NOT to build the johad, what will most likely happen to the rainwater in Meena's village?
options: It will flow away and the village will have less water stored for daily activities
It will slowly turn into seawater
It will change into salt on the ground
It will become salty like the water near Meena's uncle

why.It will slowly turn into seawater: Rainwater does not turn into seawater just by flowing on land.
why.It will change into salt on the ground: Salt is collected by drying seawater, not by leaving rainwater on the ground.
why.It will become salty like the water near: Rainwater is freshwater and does not become salty by itself.

activities.explanation: Correct. A johad collects rainwater; without it, the water flows away and cannot be stored for use.

activities.prompt: Explain why all living beings need freshwater even though most of the Earth's surface is covered with water.
activities.answer: Most of the water on Earth is salty, so living beings cannot drink it or use it to grow crops. All living beings need freshwater to live, for drinking, for growing crops and for daily activities. That is why freshwater is precious even though there is so much water around.
points: Says most of the water on Earth is salty
Says living beings cannot use salty water for drinking or crops
Mentions freshwater is needed for drinking, crops and daily activities
Concludes that freshwater is what all living beings need
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi fills a glass with water and drops in some ice cubes. He leaves the glass on a windowsill where the Sun is shining. After some time, he notices the ice cubes have become smaller, and tiny drops of water have appeared on the outside of the glass. Later, his mother boils water in a kettle, and Ravi sees steam rising from it.
activities.prompt: If Ravi leaves the glass on the windowsill for even longer, what will most likely happen to the ice cubes?
options: They will slowly turn back into water
They will turn into steam and float away
They will grow bigger and colder
They will turn into little pieces of rain

why.They will turn into steam and float away: Steam comes from heating water until it boils, not from ice sitting on a windowsill
why.They will grow bigger and colder: Ice cannot grow bigger on its own; the Sun's warmth is making things warmer, not colder
why.They will turn into little pieces of rai: Rain is not something that forms inside a glass; this confuses rain with melting ice

activities.explanation: Correct: ice is the solid form, and left in a glass it melts after some time back to liquid

activities.context: Ravi fills a glass with water and drops in some ice cubes. He leaves the glass on a windowsill where the Sun is shining. After some time, he notices the ice cubes have become smaller, and tiny drops of water have appeared on the outside of the glass. Later, his mother boils water in a kettle, and Ravi sees steam rising from it.
activities.prompt: Why did tiny drops of water appear on the outside of Ravi's glass?
options: Water vapour in the air touched the cold glass, cooled down, and turned into drops
The glass had small holes that let the water inside leak out
The ice cubes passed through the glass and gathered on the outside
The Sun pulled the water up and out through the sides of the glass

why.The glass had small holes that let the w: A glass does not leak; the drops come from the air, not from inside
why.The ice cubes passed through the glass a: Ice cannot move through glass; this is not how the solid form behaves
why.The Sun pulled the water up and out thro: The Sun's heat turns water into vapour, but it does not pull water through a glass

activities.explanation: Correct: when water vapour cools, it forms small droplets, which is what happened on the cold glass

activities.context: Ravi fills a glass with water and drops in some ice cubes. He leaves the glass on a windowsill where the Sun is shining. After some time, he notices the ice cubes have become smaller, and tiny drops of water have appeared on the outside of the glass. Later, his mother boils water in a kettle, and Ravi sees steam rising from it.
activities.prompt: Ravi wants to see water change into its vapour form quickly. What should he do?
options: Put the glass of water inside a refrigerator
Ask his mother to heat the water until it boils
Stir the water quickly with a spoon
Cover the glass with a tight lid

why.Put the glass of water inside a refriger: Cooling makes vapour turn into droplets, which is the opposite of what Ravi wants
why.Stir the water quickly with a spoon: Stirring only moves the water around; it does not change its form
why.Cover the glass with a tight lid: A lid would trap the water and stop any vapour from being seen

activities.explanation: Correct: heating water makes it boil, and that is how it changes into steam, the vapour form

activities.context: Meera lives near a large lake. On hot sunny days, she notices the water level of the lake slowly going down, even though no one is taking water out. Far away, she sees clouds gathering in the sky. A few days later, it rains heavily, and water flows back into the lake through a small stream. Meera wonders where the missing water went and how it came back.
activities.prompt: Why did the lake's water level go down on the hot sunny days?
options: The Sun's heat turned some lake water into vapour that rose into the air
The clouds pulled the lake water down into the ground
The fish in the lake drank up the water
The stream carried the lake water away to the ocean

why.The clouds pulled the lake water down in: Wrong: clouds form from vapour and bring water down, they do not pull lake water away
why.The fish in the lake drank up the water: Wrong: living things drinking water is not part of how water moves in nature
why.The stream carried the lake water away t: Wrong: the stream brings water in; nothing in the case says it carries water out

activities.explanation: Correct: heat from the Sun makes water from sources like lakes become vapour

activities.context: Meera lives near a large lake. On hot sunny days, she notices the water level of the lake slowly going down, even though no one is taking water out. Far away, she sees clouds gathering in the sky. A few days later, it rains heavily, and water flows back into the lake through a small stream. Meera wonders where the missing water went and how it came back.
activities.prompt: What most likely happened to the water vapour that rose from the lake before the rain came?
options: It cooled and formed tiny droplets that joined together as clouds
It froze into hail and stayed floating in the sky
It turned back into lake water while still in the air
It sank back into the lake without changing form

why.It froze into hail and stayed floating i: Wrong: hail falls from clouds; vapour does not freeze and float
why.It turned back into lake water while sti: Wrong: vapour cools into droplets first, it does not become liquid water directly in mid-air
why.It sank back into the lake without chang: Wrong: vapour travels upward and changes form; it does not simply sink back unchanged

activities.explanation: Correct: when vapour cools it forms small droplets, and droplets make clouds

activities.context: Meera lives near a large lake. On hot sunny days, she notices the water level of the lake slowly going down, even though no one is taking water out. Far away, she sees clouds gathering in the sky. A few days later, it rains heavily, and water flows back into the lake through a small stream. Meera wonders where the missing water went and how it came back.
activities.prompt: If the Sun stayed hidden behind thick clouds for many days, what would Meera most likely observe?
options: Less water leaving the lake as vapour, so the water level would drop more slowly
The lake would dry up completely because clouds take water away
The lake would freeze into snow because there is no sunshine
The lake water would turn into hail inside the water

why.The lake would dry up completely because: Wrong: clouds do not remove lake water; heat is what moves water out as vapour
why.The lake would freeze into snow because: Wrong: nothing in the lesson says lack of sunshine makes water freeze
why.The lake water would turn into hail insi: Wrong: hail falls from clouds in the sky, it does not form inside lake water

activities.explanation: Correct: with less heat, less water becomes vapour, so less water leaves the lake

activities.prompt: How does water change form as it travels through air, land, and sky in the water cycle?
activities.answer: Water travels through the sky as vapour when heat turns it into vapour. In the air, the cooling vapour changes into small droplets that form clouds. From the clouds it falls to the land as rain, snow, or hail, and then moves back into rivers, lakes, and oceans.
points: Heat turns water into vapour (in the sky/air)
Cooling vapour forms droplets and clouds
Water falls as rain, snow, or hail
Water returns to rivers, lakes, and oceans
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In Green Park colony, people drew water from a well for many years. Rain fell freely on the open ground around it, and water seeped into the soil below. Last year, the colony covered most of its open ground with cement to build a parking area. This year, the water in the well has become much lower than before.
activities.prompt: Why has the water in the well become much lower this year?
options: The cemented parking area stops rainwater from seeping into the ground, so less water goes underground to refill the well
The well became deeper last year, so the water sank to the bottom and cannot be drawn out easily
The rain this year was stored in the soil instead of the well, so the well level went down
The handpumps in the colony pushed the groundwater up to the surface, emptying the well

why.The well became deeper last year, so the: Wrong: nothing in the case says the well was made deeper; the change was the cemented surface
why.The rain this year was stored in the soi: Wrong: water stored underground is what fills the well; it does not move away from the well into the soil
why.The handpumps in the colony pushed the g: Wrong: handpumps draw water for our use, but the case does not say handpumps were installed or caused the drop

activities.explanation: Correct: cemented surfaces block rainwater from entering the ground, so the groundwater is not recharged and the well gets less water

activities.context: In Green Park colony, people drew water from a well for many years. Rain fell freely on the open ground around it, and water seeped into the soil below. Last year, the colony covered most of its open ground with cement to build a parking area. This year, the water in the well has become much lower than before.
activities.prompt: If the colony plants many trees in the remaining open ground, what is the most likely result?
options: The trees will soak up all the rainwater, so even less water will reach underground
More rainwater will seep into the ground through the open, unplanted soil, helping the well fill up again
The trees will block the rain completely, so the well will stay at the same low level forever
The tree roots will push the groundwater out of the ground, so the well will overflow

why.The trees will soak up all the rainwater: Wrong: trees help rainwater return underground; they do not stop water from reaching it
why.The trees will block the rain completely: Wrong: trees do not block rain; they help water soak into the soil below them
why.The tree roots will push the groundwater: Wrong: tree roots help water go into the ground, not push water out of it

activities.explanation: Correct: open, uncovered areas with trees let rainwater seep into the ground and recharge the groundwater that fills the well

activities.context: In Green Park colony, people drew water from a well for many years. Rain fell freely on the open ground around it, and water seeped into the soil below. Last year, the colony covered most of its open ground with cement to build a parking area. This year, the water in the well has become much lower than before.
activities.prompt: The colony wants to keep its parking area but also help the well. What should they do?
options: Cover the remaining open ground with more cement so rainwater runs quickly into the drain
Build a roof over the whole colony so no rainwater touches the ground at all
Make soak pits so rainwater from the area can return underground and recharge the groundwater
Dig a new, deeper well in the middle of the cemented parking area to find more water

why.Cover the remaining open ground with mor: Wrong: more cement means less water can seep into the ground, which makes the problem worse
why.Build a roof over the whole colony so no: Wrong: a roof stops rainwater from reaching the ground, so groundwater gets no recharge
why.Dig a new, deeper well in the middle of: Wrong: drawing more groundwater without letting rainwater seep in will lower the water further

activities.explanation: Correct: soak pits help rainwater return underground, so the groundwater that feeds the well can be recharged

activities.prompt: Explain why a well in a colony with cemented surfaces may give less water than a well near open, uncovered ground.
activities.answer: Rainwater recharges groundwater by seeping through layers of soil and rocks. In a cemented colony, rainwater cannot go into the ground easily, so the groundwater is not recharged. Near open, uncovered ground, rainwater seeps in and refills the groundwater, so the well there gets more water.
points: Rainwater seeps through soil and rocks to recharge groundwater
Cemented surfaces stop rainwater from entering the ground
Open, uncovered ground lets water seep in
So the well near open ground gets more water
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The people of a village in Maharashtra watched rainwater rush down the nearby hills and flow away quickly. Inspired by Hiware Bazar, a water-positive village, every family joined in watershed management and rainwater harvesting. Nearby, a river that begins high up in the mountains flows down across the land, curving wherever the land bends, and slowly changing the shape of the land as it moves.
activities.prompt: If the villagers slow down the rainwater rushing down the hills, what will most likely happen to the shape of the land there?
options: The water will change the shape of the land more slowly than before
The water will begin flowing towards the Bay of Bengal
The river will start its journey from the mountains all over again
The water will stop flowing anywhere in the district forever

why.The water will begin flowing towards the: Wrong - which sea a river reaches depends on its course, not on slowing rainwater in this village
why.The river will start its journey from th: Wrong - a river's beginning in the mountains does not change because of harvesting rainwater
why.The water will stop flowing anywhere in: Wrong - slowing water is not the same as water stopping completely everywhere

activities.explanation: Correct - flowing water changes the shape of land, so slower flow changes it more slowly

activities.context: The people of a village in Maharashtra watched rainwater rush down the nearby hills and flow away quickly. Inspired by Hiware Bazar, a water-positive village, every family joined in watershed management and rainwater harvesting. Nearby, a river that begins high up in the mountains flows down across the land, curving wherever the land bends, and slowly changing the shape of the land as it moves.
activities.prompt: A student says that any river starting in a range like the Aravalli Range must end in a sea. What should the class conclude?
options: He is right, because every river flows towards the Arabian Sea
He is right, because every river flows towards the Bay of Bengal
He is wrong, because some rivers end in marshy lands instead of a sea
He is wrong, because rivers that start in mountains never flow down across the land

why.He is right, because every river flows t: Wrong - only some rivers flow towards the Arabian Sea, not all of them
Wrong - only some rivers flow towards the Bay of Bengal, not all of them
why.He is wrong, because rivers that start i: Wrong - rivers beginning in mountains do flow down across the land; that is not the mistake here

activities.explanation: Correct - the Luni begins in the Aravalli Range but ends in the marshy lands of the Rann, not in a sea

activities.prompt: Explain why the Luni river does not reach the sea even though it begins its journey the way many rivers do.
activities.answer: The Luni begins in the Aravalli Range in Rajasthan and flows down across the land like other rivers. But it does not drain into a sea. Instead, it ends in the marshy lands of the Rann, so its journey finishes on land, not in the sea.
points: Mentions the Luni originates in the Aravalli Range in Rajasthan
States the Luni does not drain into a sea
Says it ends in the marshy lands of the Rann
Compares it with rivers that do reach a sea
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between how a water scorpion and a land animal breathe?
activities.answer: A water scorpion lives underwater and breathes using a tail tube, so it can stay in the pond. A land animal cannot breathe in water at all. This shows that water animals have special features, while land animals are made for breathing outside water.
points: Water scorpion breathes underwater using a tail tube
Land animals cannot breathe in water
Water animals have special features to survive in water
Land animals breathe outside water
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Water — The Essence of Life

activities.prompt: Most of the water on Earth is salty. So what do living beings need to stay alive?
options: Salty seawater
Freshwater
Steam from clouds
Ice from mountains
activities.explanation: All living beings need freshwater to live. Most of Earth's water is salty, so freshwater is very precious.

activities.prompt: If all the water on Earth were in one glass, the freshwater part would be only a teaspoon.
activities.explanation: That is how little freshwater there is. It shows why we must use water carefully.

activities.prompt: Match each form of water with its example.
activities.explanation: Water has three forms: liquid, solid, and vapour. Ice, rain, and steam are examples of each.

activities.prompt: The Sun's heat causes water to turn into water ______.
activities.hint: Think of the gas form of water that rises into the air.
activities.explanation: Heat makes water change into vapour. This is the first step of the water cycle.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the water cycle in the correct order.
items: The Sun's heat turns water into water vapour
Water vapour forms clouds
Water vapour cools and forms small droplets
The droplets fall back down as rain, snow, and hail
The water goes back into rivers, lakes, and oceans
activities.explanation: Water travels in a circle: up as vapour, into clouds, down as rain, and back to rivers and oceans. This constant movement is the water cycle.

activities.prompt: When it rains, what happens to some of the water on the ground?
options: It all flows into the sea
It soaks into the soil and sinks down
It turns into steam at once
It freezes into ice
activities.explanation: Some rainwater is soaked up by the soil. It sinks through layers of soil and rocks to become groundwater.

activities.prompt: In cities with cemented surfaces, rainwater can easily go into the ground and recharge groundwater.
activities.explanation: Cemented surfaces stop rainwater from going into the ground. This stops groundwater from getting recharged.

activities.prompt: The Luni river starts in the Aravalli Range. How does its journey end?
options: It drains into the Arabian Sea
It drains into the Bay of Bengal
It ends in the marshy lands of the Rann
It ends in a big lake in the mountains
activities.explanation: The Luni begins in the Aravalli Range in Rajasthan. Unlike many rivers, it does not drain into a sea.

activities.prompt: Match each pond living thing with its special feature.
pairs: Long legs, stands still to catch fish
Fast-growing plant that floats and spreads
Grow along the edges of ponds
activities.explanation: Aquatic plants and animals have special features to survive in water. Each one is suited to pond life in its own way.

activities.prompt: In Gujarat, seawater is dried to collect ______.
activities.hint: This is why Gujarat is one of the largest producers of it in India.
activities.explanation: Drying seawater leaves salt behind. That is how Gujarat makes so much of it.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of a river in the correct order.
items: A river begins its journey up in the mountains
It flows down across the land
Its flow stops or curves according to the shape of the land
Its flow can also change the shape of the land
activities.explanation: A river starts high in the mountains and flows down across the land. Water and land shape each other as the river travels.

activities.prompt: Johads in Rajasthan are traditional small earthen dams built to collect rainwater.
activities.explanation: Johads collect rainwater so it does not run away. They are a clever old way of saving water.

chapters.title: Journey of a River
chapters.summary: In this chapter: where i begin, where i flow; the life i hold; the many ways i support lives; dams — storing my water, changing my flow.

lessons.title: Where I Begin, Where I Flow

activities.prompt: How does a tiny stream grow into a mighty river that travels so far?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the River Godavari
activities.body: The river has no feet, yet it travels far. It flows quietly from the mountain to the sea. This river is the Godavari. Its journey starts high in the Western Ghats at Trimbakeshwar in Maharashtra. It begins as a small stream. It travels 1,465 kilometres before it joins the Bay of Bengal.
keyPoints: The Godavari starts at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats.
It begins as a small stream and flows to the sea.
It travels 1,465 kilometres to reach the Bay of Bengal.
activities.explanation: Every big river starts small and grows on its long journey.

activities.prompt: A river has no feet, no legs and no wheels. Yet it travels from a mountain all the way to the sea. How can something travel so far without walking?
steps: A river is made of water, and water can flow.
Flowing water moves slowly downhill, from high places to low places.
The mountain is high and the sea is low, so the water keeps moving.
So the river travels without feet, because it flows from the mountain to the sea.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What the River Gives Us
activities.body: As the river travels, it passes through fields and forests, under the moon and stars. It quenches our thirst when we are thirsty. It also helps plants grow in the fields. The river gives and gives, all along its long journey to the sea.
keyPoints: The river flows through fields and forests.
It quenches thirst and helps plants grow.
It travels by day and night, under the moon and stars.
activities.explanation: The river is a quiet friend who helps people, plants and animals.

activities.prompt: Where does the journey of the Godavari begin?
options: At the Bay of Bengal
At Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats
In a big city in Maharashtra
At the end of a forest
activities.explanation: The Godavari starts high in the Western Ghats at Trimbakeshwar in Maharashtra.

activities.prompt: Small streams that join a big river are called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter t.
activities.explanation: Tributaries are the small streams that join a big river on its way.

activities.prompt: The river has feet, which help it travel far.
activities.explanation: The river has no feet, yet it travels far. Water moves all by itself!

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it means for the Godavari.
activities.explanation: Now you know the start, the end, the helpers and the length of the journey.

activities.prompt: Why does the Godavari become wider and stronger as it moves?
options: Because the sun shines on it
Because rainwater and other streams join it
Because people dig it wider
Because it slows down near the sea
activities.explanation: Rainwater and other streams join the river. The joining streams make it wider and stronger.

activities.prompt: Put the Godavari's journey in the correct order, from start to end.
items: It starts as a stream at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats.
Rainwater and other streams join it as it moves.
The joining streams make it wider and stronger.
It flows through fields and forests.
It joins the Bay of Bengal.
activities.explanation: A river grows step by step: a small start, helpers join in, then a grand end at the sea.

activities.prompt: A tiny stream starts on a hill. Rain falls. More small streams join it. What will the stream become?
options: Wider and stronger
Narrower and weaker
Still and frozen
Salty like the sea

why.Narrower and weaker: Thinks joining takes water away instead of adding water.
why.Still and frozen: Thinks joining streams stop the flow instead of feeding it.
why.Salty like the sea: Thinks mixing waters makes them salty, like the sea.

activities.explanation: Right: joining streams bring more water, so it grows wider and stronger.

activities.prompt: A raindrop falls at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats. It joins a small stream. It travels a very long way. Where will it end?
options: In the Bay of Bengal
Back on the mountain top
In a small puddle
Under the ground forever

why.Back on the mountain top: Thinks rivers loop back to where they started.
why.In a small puddle: Thinks the journey stops early instead of reaching the sea.
why.Under the ground forever: Thinks the water sinks down and never reaches the sea.

activities.explanation: Right: the river flows on and on until it joins the Bay of Bengal.

activities.prompt: A river starts as a small stream. Other streams join it. Meera says rivers are born big and strong. What is wrong with her claim?
options: Rivers start small and grow
Rivers start big and shrink
Rivers start inside the sea
Rivers start as heavy rain

why.Rivers start big and shrink: Thinks rivers shrink over time, the opposite of what happens.
why.Rivers start inside the sea: Thinks rivers begin at their end, not their start.
why.Rivers start as heavy rain: Thinks rain alone is the river, not the growing stream.

activities.explanation: Right: a river begins as a small stream and grows as streams join.

activities.prompt: Two same plants sit in the sun. One gets river water. One gets none. What will happen and why?
options: The watered one grows more
Both grow exactly the same
The dry one grows more
Both die on the first day

why.Both grow exactly the same: Thinks water makes no difference to how plants grow.
why.The dry one grows more: Thinks plants grow better dry, the opposite of the truth.
why.Both die on the first day: Thinks one day without water kills a plant at once.

activities.explanation: Right: river water quenches a plant's thirst and helps it grow.

lessons.title: The Life I Hold

activities.prompt: Where does a river's long journey finally come to an end?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Godavari
activities.body: The Godavari is a great river of southern India. It flows all year, so it is called a perennial river. Some rivers flow only when rain falls; those are seasonal rivers. The Godavari passes through rich forests full of wildlife. When it reaches the sea, it spreads into many small streams and forms a delta. People call it Dakshina Ganga because it flows through the south and is sacred.
keyPoints: A river that flows all year is a perennial river.
A river that flows only with rain is a seasonal river.
At the sea, the Godavari spreads into streams and forms a delta.
The Godavari is sacred, so it is called Dakshina Ganga.
activities.explanation: Rivers give life to forests, animals and people all along their journey.

activities.prompt: Ravi visits the Godavari in summer with his uncle. His friend says, 'The river will be dry, like the small stream near our school.' Should Ravi agree?
steps: The stream near school only flows when rain falls, so it is a seasonal river and dries up in summer.
The Godavari flows all year, so it is a perennial river, not a seasonal one.
So even in summer, when there is no rain, the Godavari will still have water.
Ravi should not agree, because a perennial river does not dry up like a seasonal stream.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The Godavari flows all year round. What kind of river is it?
options: A seasonal river
A perennial river
A rainy river
A small river
activities.explanation: A river that flows all year is called perennial. Well done!

activities.prompt: Near the sea, the Godavari spreads into many small streams and forms a ______.
activities.hint: This word names the fan of land a river builds at the sea.
activities.explanation: When a river reaches the sea, it splits into streams and forms a delta.

activities.prompt: Match each river word to what it means.
activities.explanation: These words help you describe a river's life from rain to the sea.

activities.prompt: Why is the Godavari called Dakshina Ganga?
options: It flows through southern India and is sacred
It is the longest river in the world
It flows only during the rains
It begins in the snowy mountains
activities.explanation: Dakshina means south. The river is sacred, so people honour it like the Ganga.

activities.prompt: Put the Godavari's journey in order, from start to end.
items: It flows all year as a perennial river
It passes through rich forests full of wildlife
It reaches the sea and spreads into many small streams
The streams form a delta at the Coringa Mangrove Forests
Its journey ends there
activities.explanation: A river travels from its flow, through forests, to the sea, where its journey ends.

activities.prompt: The Godavari passes through rich forests. Which of these lives there?
options: Indian golden gecko
Polar bear
Camel
Snow leopard
activities.explanation: The forests near the Godavari are home to the tiger, barking deer and Indian golden gecko.

activities.prompt: A river near Meena's village has water only in the rainy season. In summer it is dry. The Godavari flows all year. What will Meena see at the Godavari in summer?
options: It will be dry like her river.
It will still have water flowing.
It will flow only when it rains.
It will have more water than in rain.

This treats the Godavari like a seasonal river, but it is perennial.
This confuses the Godavari with a seasonal river that needs rain.
Summer has no rain, so the river cannot get extra water then.

activities.explanation: Right, because a perennial river flows all year, even without rain.

activities.prompt: A boy says, 'The Godavari must stop at the forest and end there.' He saw that forests come before the sea on the river's path. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Rivers cannot flow inside forests at all.
The river ends at the sea, not the forest.
Rivers always end inside a big forest.
The forest stops the river from moving on.

why.Rivers cannot flow inside forests at all: Rivers can pass through forests; the forest is not the problem.
Rivers do not always end in forests; this is a made-up rule.
why.The forest stops the river from moving o: The river flows through the forest, so the forest does not stop it.

activities.explanation: Right, the river passes through the forest and its journey ends at the sea.

activities.prompt: Some children say the tiger and the Indian golden gecko live near the Godavari because the river water is salty there. Why is their reason wrong?
options: The Godavari is freshwater, not salty water.
Tigers and geckos only live in the sea.
The animals live there only during Pushkaram.
The animals came there from the Ramayana stories.

Tigers and geckos are forest animals, not sea animals.
why.The animals live there only during Pushk: Pushkaram is a holy dip time, not when animals come to live.
why.The animals came there from the Ramayana: Stories tell about the river, but they do not bring the animals.

activities.explanation: Right, the Godavari is a freshwater source, so the salty-water reason cannot be true.

activities.prompt: Two children give reasons why the Godavari is called Dakshina Ganga. Anu says, 'It flows through southern India.' Dev says, 'It is a seasonal river.' Whose reason is right, and why?
options: Dev, because seasonal rivers are holy.
Dev, because the river flows only in rain.
Anu, because the river is sacred and in the south.
Anu, because the river ends in a delta.

Being seasonal does not make a river holy; Dev mixes up two ideas.
why.Dev, because the river flows only in rai: The Godavari is perennial, so Dev's reason is also wrong.
The delta is where the river ends; it does not explain the name.

activities.explanation: Right, Dakshina Ganga means the river is sacred and flows through southern India.

activities.prompt: A boy says, 'People take a holy dip in the Godavari during Pushkaram because the water there is freshwater.' What is the flaw in his claim?
options: People dip only in rivers that form a delta.
People dip because the water is holy, not just freshwater.
People dip only when the river flows through forests.
People dip in the sea, not in the river water.

why.People dip only in rivers that form a de: A delta is where the river ends; it is not the reason for the dip.
why.People dip only when the river flows thr: Forests with wildlife are on the river's path, not the reason for dipping.
why.People dip in the sea, not in the river: The holy dip is taken in the river's water during Pushkaram.

activities.explanation: Right, the dip is because the river is sacred, not because it is freshwater.
