chapters.title: How Things Work
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is energy?; energy in simple activities; sources of energy; electricity and safe use.

lessons.title: What is Energy?

activities.prompt: What invisible helper makes things move, glow, and warm up around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Energy is all around you
activities.body: Look around you. Things move, light up, make sounds, or get warmer or cooler. In a kitchen, food gets cooked. In nature, a Flying Snake can glide through the air by flattening its body. Something makes all this happen. We call it energy. Energy makes things move, light up, produce sound, do work and change temperature.
keyPoints: Around us, things move, light up, make sounds, or get warmer or cooler.
Something makes all this happen, and we call it energy.
Energy makes things move, light up, produce sound, do work and change temperature.
activities.explanation: Energy is the hidden helper behind everything that moves, glows, sounds or warms up.

activities.prompt: In the kitchen, the rice gets hot and starts bubbling. Nothing is touching the pot to push it. What is making all this happen?
steps: We watch the kitchen and see the rice bubbling and steam rising.
The pot is not being pushed by anyone, yet things still change.
Things that move, get warm, or make sounds need energy to happen.
So energy is making the rice cook, even though we cannot see it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Energy every day
activities.body: We use energy every day in many ways. Sometimes energy works so quietly that we do not even notice it. It can still move things, make sounds or do work. Watch a kitchen for some time and note what you see and wonder. You will spot energy busy at work all around you.
keyPoints: We use energy every day in many ways.
Energy can work sometimes without us noticing.
Watching a kitchen and noting what you see helps you spot energy at work.
activities.explanation: Energy is a quiet worker, busy even when you are not watching.

activities.prompt: Something makes things move, light up and make sounds. What do we call it?
options: Energy
Shadow
Rainbow
activities.explanation: Well done! Energy is the name we give to whatever makes all these things happen.

activities.prompt: The ______ gives us light and heat.
activities.hint: It shines bright in the sky in the day.
activities.explanation: Great! The Sun gives us both light and heat every day.

activities.prompt: Food gets cooked in the kitchen.
activities.explanation: Yes! Cooking food in the kitchen is one activity where energy is at work.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what energy makes it do.
activities.explanation: Super! Energy can move things, light them up, make sounds and change how warm they are.

activities.prompt: How does the Flying Snake glide through the air?
options: By flattening its body
By flapping its ears
By spinning its tail
activities.explanation: Correct! The Flying Snake flattens its body to glide through the air.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to explore a kitchen like a scientist.
items: Watch the kitchen for some time
Note what you see
Wonder about what is happening
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First watch, then note what you see, then wonder about it.

activities.prompt: A door slowly opens by itself when the wind blows. You hear a creak. What made the door move and the sound?
options: The door moved because energy made it move and sound.
The door moved because doors like to open on their own.
The door moved because the creak sound pushed it open.
The door moved because the wind was resting inside it.

why.The door moved because doors like to ope: Wrong: thinks doors can act by themselves with no cause.
why.The door moved because the creak sound p: Wrong: thinks sound is a push that moves objects.
why.The door moved because the wind was rest: Wrong: thinks wind stores energy instead of using it.

activities.explanation: Right: energy makes things move and produce sounds.

activities.prompt: A quiet room seems to have nothing happening. Then a clock ticks and the fan turns. What does this show about energy?
options: Energy works only when we can see it happening.
Energy can work without us noticing it at all.
Energy stops working when a room is very quiet.
Energy only makes loud sounds like ticking clocks.

why.Energy works only when we can see it hap: Wrong: thinks energy must always be seen to exist.
why.Energy stops working when a room is very: Wrong: thinks quiet rooms have no energy working.
why.Energy only makes loud sounds like ticki: Wrong: thinks energy only makes sounds, not movement.

activities.explanation: Right: energy can work sometimes without us noticing.

activities.prompt: A friend says a sleeping cat uses no energy because it does not move. Its body is warm and it purrs softly. What is the flaw in this claim?
options: The claim is wrong because purring and warmth show energy.
The claim is right because sleeping cats never use energy.
The claim is wrong because cats should move to use energy.
The claim is right because warmth is not a sign of energy.

why.The claim is right because sleeping cats: Wrong: thinks still things never use any energy.
why.The claim is wrong because cats should m: Wrong: thinks movement is the only sign of energy.
why.The claim is right because warmth is not: Wrong: thinks warmth has nothing to do with energy.

activities.explanation: Right: energy makes things warm and produce sounds.

activities.prompt: Two children watch a flying snake glide. One writes what the snake does. The other only guesses without watching. Whose notes will be better, and why?
options: The guesser, because guessing is faster than watching.
The guesser, because snakes glide without any watching.
The watcher, because watching for some time shows what happens.
The watcher, because notes must be written in the dark.

why.The guesser, because guessing is faster: Wrong: thinks speed matters more than careful watching.
why.The guesser, because snakes glide withou: Wrong: thinks watching adds nothing to what we know.
why.The watcher, because notes must be writt: Wrong: thinks notes need darkness instead of observation.

activities.explanation: Right: we can watch for some time and note what we see.

activities.prompt: A pot of water on the stove starts to bubble and hiss. Steam rises up. What will happen if the energy keeps working the same way?
options: The water will get cooler and stop making any sounds.
The water will keep getting hotter and keep making sounds.
The water will turn into ice and become very quiet.
The water will stay exactly the same and make no steam.

why.The water will get cooler and stop makin: Wrong: thinks energy makes things cooler instead of hotter.
why.The water will turn into ice and become: Wrong: thinks heating water makes it cold like ice.
why.The water will stay exactly the same and: Wrong: thinks energy working changes nothing at all.

activities.explanation: Right: energy changes temperature and produces sounds.

lessons.title: Energy in Simple Activities

activities.prompt: Where does the energy hiding in a balloon, a rubber band, and sunshine come from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Energy Is All Around You
activities.body: Energy hides in simple things you do every day. Blow up a balloon and let it go. The rushing air pushes it forward, and moving air makes energy. Pluck a rubber band and it vibrates to make sound energy. Leave water in sunlight and it grows warm, because sunlight gives heat energy.
keyPoints: Air rushing out of a balloon pushes it forward, and moving air makes energy.
Plucking a rubber band makes it vibrate and produce sound energy.
Sunlight heats water, so sunlight gives us heat energy.
activities.explanation: Even playing with a balloon or a rubber band shows energy at work.

activities.prompt: Meena blows up a balloon and lets it go. Why does it zoom forward?
steps: The blown balloon is full of air, so air is squeezed inside it.
When the mouth is released, the air rushes out fast, because air always escapes from an open mouth.
The rushing air pushes the balloon, because the movement of air makes energy.
So the balloon zooms forward, because the push comes from the air rushing out.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You release the mouth of a blown-up balloon. What pushes the balloon forward?
options: The air rushing out
Your hand letting go
The colour of the balloon
The wind outside
activities.explanation: When air rushes out, it pushes the balloon forward. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Water left in sunlight becomes ______ because the Sun heats it.
activities.hint: Think about how the water feels after sitting in the Sun.
activities.explanation: The Sun heats the water, so sunlight gives us heat energy.

activities.prompt: A plucked rubber band vibrates and makes a sound. What is this kind of energy called?
options: Heat energy
Sound energy
Air energy
Light energy
activities.explanation: The shaking rubber band produces sound energy. You remembered it!

activities.prompt: Match each thing to the energy it shows.
pairs: Air rushing out of a balloon
activities.explanation: Each simple activity shows a different kind of energy. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put the balloon activity steps in the right order.
items: Blow the balloon until it fills up
Hold the balloon tightly
Release the balloon's mouth
Air rushes out and pushes the balloon forward
activities.explanation: First you fill the balloon, then hold it, then let go, and the air pushes it forward.

activities.prompt: Why do families in cold hilly places keep cattle on the ground floor?
options: Heat from the animals warms the rooms above
The cattle can watch the door at night
It makes the house look bigger
The cattle like to climb stairs
activities.explanation: Heat from the animals keeps the family rooms warm in winter, with no extra firewood or electricity. A clever idea!

activities.prompt: Meera blows a big balloon until it fills up. She holds its mouth tightly. Then she lets the mouth go. Which way will the balloon move, and why?
options: It flies forward. The rushing air pushes it.
It flies backward. The air pulls it back.
It stays still. Rubber is too heavy to move.
It flies up. Warm air lifts balloons up.

why.It flies backward. The air pulls it back: Thinks air pulls things, but the air pushes the balloon forward.
why.It stays still. Rubber is too heavy to m: Thinks the rubber's weight stops it, and forgets the moving air inside.
Thinks balloons rise like hot air, but here the push comes from rushing air.

activities.explanation: Right: air rushes out of the mouth, and moving air makes energy that pushes the balloon forward.

activities.prompt: Ravi does not blow up his balloon at all. He just drops it from his hand. What happens, and why?
options: It flies forward. Air inside pushes it out fast.
It just drops. No air rushes out to push it.
It flies backward. Empty balloons always move that way.
It gets bigger. The rubber stretches by itself.

why.It flies forward. Air inside pushes it o: Thinks a flat balloon has air inside, but it was never blown up.
why.It flies backward. Empty balloons always: Thinks empty balloons move on their own, but nothing pushes them.
why.It gets bigger. The rubber stretches by: Thinks rubber stretches alone, but rubber needs a force to stretch.

activities.explanation: Right: with no air rushing out, there is no push, so it just drops.

activities.prompt: Two bowls of water stand outside. One bowl is in the Sun. One bowl is in the shade. After some time, what will Meena see, and why?
options: The shady bowl is warmer. Shade keeps heat inside water.
Both bowls stay the same. Water never changes in sunlight.
The sunny bowl is warmer. Sunlight gives heat energy to water.
The sunny bowl is colder. Sunlight blows cool air on water.

why.The shady bowl is warmer. Shade keeps he: Thinks shade holds heat in, but shade gives no heat to water.
why.Both bowls stay the same. Water never ch: Thinks sunlight does nothing to water, but the Sun heats it.
why.The sunny bowl is colder. Sunlight blows: Thinks sunlight cools things, but sunlight heats things instead.

activities.explanation: Right: sunlight gives heat energy, so water in the Sun becomes warmer.

activities.prompt: In Ladakh, winter is very cold. People keep cattle on the ground floor. The family lives on the floor above. Why does this keep the family warm?
options: The animals' heat rises. It warms the rooms above without firewood.
The animals block the wind. Wind cannot enter the house at all.
The animals eat the cold air. Cold air disappears downstairs.
The family's firewood burns below. Firewood heats every room.

why.The animals block the wind. Wind cannot: Thinks animals work like a wall, but their heat warms the rooms, not blocking.
why.The animals eat the cold air. Cold air d: Thinks animals eat air, but animals give heat, not eat cold.
why.The family's firewood burns below. Firew: Thinks firewood does the heating, but this way needs no extra firewood.

activities.explanation: Right: heat from the animals warms the rooms above, with no extra firewood or electricity.

lessons.title: Sources of Energy

activities.prompt: Where do you get the energy to run and play all day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where does energy come from?
activities.body: You can move, run and play because of energy. Food gives you the energy you need. When you eat, you feel active and ready to play. When you do not eat, you may feel tired. Animals get energy from food too. Cars and scooters need fuel like petrol and diesel. Cooking gas is a fuel as well.
keyPoints: Food is a source of energy for all living things.
Petrol and diesel are sources of energy for vehicles, like food for us.
Burning wood or coal creates smoke and pollution.
activities.explanation: Everything that moves needs energy, and energy comes from a source.

activities.prompt: Meena skips breakfast and feels tired at playtime. Her friend eats and feels ready to play. Why are they different?
steps: Meena did not eat, so her body got no food.
Without food, her body has no energy, so she feels tired.
Her friend ate food, so her body got energy and feels active.
So food is the source of energy that makes us ready to play.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What gives you the energy you need to move and play?
options: Food
Toys
Books
activities.explanation: Food gives us the energy we need. That is why eating makes you feel active.

activities.prompt: Food gives us the ______ we need.
activities.hint: It is what lets you run and play.
activities.explanation: Yes! Energy from food helps you move and play.

activities.prompt: Petrol and diesel are sources of energy for vehicles. They are like ______ for vehicles.
options: Water
Food
Air
activities.explanation: Just as food gives you energy, petrol and diesel give energy to vehicles.

activities.prompt: Put these in the right order to show how energy helps you play.
items: Eat your food
Get energy from the food
Feel active
Run and play
activities.explanation: First you eat, then food gives you energy, and then you feel active and ready to play.

activities.prompt: In some places, people burn wood or coal to cook food. What does burning them create?
options: Clean fresh air
Cool rain
Smoke and pollution
activities.explanation: Burning wood or coal creates smoke and pollution, so it is not kind to the air around us.

activities.prompt: Ravi did not eat his lunch. Now he feels tired at playtime. Why does he feel tired?
options: His body got no energy from food.
Games make every child feel tired.
His friends did not want to play.
The playground was too big for him.

This blames the game, but the real cause is no food.
Water is not the source of energy here.
Friends do not take away the energy from food.

activities.explanation: Right. No food means no energy, so the body feels tired.

activities.prompt: Papa's scooter has no petrol. Petrol is a source of energy for scooters. What will happen to the scooter?
options: It will stop running.
It will run faster than before.
It will run on food instead.
It will run without any energy.

Less fuel cannot give more energy to the scooter.
Food gives energy to us, not to scooters.
Scooters need fuel, just like we need food.

activities.explanation: Right. No fuel means no energy, so the scooter cannot run.

activities.prompt: A dog runs to catch a ball. Then it eats its food. After eating, it runs again. Why can it run again?
options: The food gave the dog new energy.
The ball gave the dog new energy.
The dog got energy from resting.
The dog got energy from the ground.

The ball is a toy, not a source of energy.
Rest helps a little, but food gives the energy.
The ground does not give energy to animals.

activities.explanation: Right. Animals get energy from food, so it can run again.

activities.prompt: Cooking gas burns with no smoke. Wood burns with smoke. Smoke makes the air dirty. Why do some families choose cooking gas?
options: Gas makes no smoke, so less pollution.
Gas makes more smoke, so more heat.
Wood makes no smoke, so it is clean.
Smoke is good for the food being cooked.

Gas makes no smoke, not more smoke.
Wood does make smoke, so it is not clean.
Smoke pollutes the air and is not good.

activities.explanation: Right. Gas burns without smoke, so the air stays cleaner.

lessons.title: Electricity and Safe Use

activities.prompt: Why should we never poke our finger into a socket?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Electricity: A Powerful Helper
activities.body: Electricity is a helper in your home. Many things you use every day need electricity to work. It can make things move, make sound, give light and give heat. Electricity is very useful, but it can be dangerous too. That is why we must always use it carefully and follow the safety rules in this lesson.
keyPoints: Things at home need electricity to work.
Electricity can be used for movement, sound, light and heat.
Electricity is useful but dangerous if not used carefully.
activities.explanation: Electricity helps us every day, but only when we treat it with care.

activities.prompt: Meena's room is very hot in summer. Her fan and light both need electricity. How can she stay cool and still save electricity?
steps: The fan and light need electricity to work, so she cannot switch them off and stay cool.
Electricity can make movement and light, so the fan and the bulb both use it.
An LED bulb gives the same light but uses less electricity, so changing the bulb saves energy.
Using less energy to do the same work is energy efficiency, so Meena stays cool and saves electricity too.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Safety Rules for Electricity
activities.body: Electricity can hurt you if you are not careful. Never touch wires or parts when they are plugged in. Never put your fingers or anything else into a socket. Stay away from broken wires and fallen poles. Do not play near electric boxes or transformers. If something looks unsafe, do not try to fix it yourself. Tell an adult instead.
keyPoints: Do not touch wires or parts when plugged in.
Stay away from broken wires and fallen poles, and tell an adult.
If unsafe, do not fix it yourself; tell an adult.
activities.explanation: Following these rules keeps you and your family safe around electricity.

activities.prompt: Why do things at home need electricity?
options: To make the walls thick
So that they can work
To make windows small
activities.explanation: Things at home need electricity to work. Well done!

activities.prompt: LED bulbs give the same light but use ______ electricity.
activities.hint: Think about saving energy.
activities.explanation: LED bulbs give the same light but use less electricity. That makes them a smart choice!

activities.prompt: You should never put your fingers into an electrical socket.
activities.explanation: That's right! Fingers or things must never go into a socket. It keeps you safe.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the right rule from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each rule keeps you safe or saves energy. Great matching!

activities.prompt: You see a fallen electric pole on the road. What should you do?
options: Go closer to look at it
Stay away and tell an adult
Play near it with friends
activities.explanation: Staying away and telling an adult is the safe thing to do. You made a wise choice!

activities.prompt: You spot a broken wire. Put these safe steps in the right order.
items: Stay away from the broken wire
Tell an adult about it
Do not touch or fix the wire yourself
activities.explanation: First keep your distance, then get help from an adult, and never fix it yourself. Perfect safety thinking!

activities.prompt: Ravi plugs in a radio. Then he wiggles the plug with wet fingers. His friend says stop. What should Ravi do and why?
options: Keep wiggling, because the radio is still playing music
Stop touching the plug, because it is plugged in and unsafe
Pull the plug out fast, because pulling is always safe
Wiggle more gently, because gentle touching cannot hurt

why.Keep wiggling, because the radio is stil: Wrong: he thinks a working machine means the plug is safe to touch.
why.Pull the plug out fast, because pulling: Wrong: he thinks pulling is safe, but touching a plug while it is plugged in is not.
why.Wiggle more gently, because gentle touch: Wrong: he thinks being gentle makes electricity safe, but it does not.

activities.explanation: Right: plugged-in parts can hurt you, so hands must stay off them.

activities.prompt: A toy falls behind the TV. The socket is right there. What is the safe thing to do?
options: Push the toy out with a long pencil
Put a finger in the socket to hook it out
Ask an adult to switch off and take the toy out
Push the toy deeper so the socket is free again

why.Push the toy out with a long pencil: Wrong: he thinks only fingers are dangerous, but metal or wood in a socket is unsafe too.
why.Put a finger in the socket to hook it ou: Wrong: he thinks a quick finger poke is safe, but fingers must never go into sockets.
why.Push the toy deeper so the socket is fre: Wrong: he thinks hiding the toy fixes it, but it leaves the danger there.

activities.explanation: Right: an adult can move the toy safely without touching the socket.

activities.prompt: After a storm, a wire hangs low over the path to school. The children are late. What should they do?
options: Jump over the wire quickly to save time
Walk far around it and tell an adult
Throw the wire off the path with a stick
Touch it lightly to check if it is live

why.Jump over the wire quickly to save time: Wrong: he thinks speed makes it safe, but even a quick jump near a wire is dangerous.
why.Throw the wire off the path with a stick: Wrong: he thinks a stick protects him, but moving the wire himself is not safe.
why.Touch it lightly to check if it is live: Wrong: he thinks a light touch is a safe test, but any touch can be dangerous.

activities.explanation: Right: staying away from a broken wire and telling an adult keeps everyone safe.

activities.prompt: Anita says her new bulb is best because it glows brighter than her old bulb. Her old bulb used more electricity for the same light. What is the flaw in her claim?
options: A better bulb gives the same light using less electricity
A better bulb must glow brighter than every other bulb
A better bulb uses more electricity to make more light
A better bulb needs a bigger room to work properly

why.A better bulb must glow brighter than ev: Wrong: she thinks brightness shows quality, but the same light with less electricity is the real test.
why.A better bulb uses more electricity to m: Wrong: she thinks more electricity means better, but good bulbs use less for the same light.
why.A better bulb needs a bigger room to wor: Wrong: she adds a room-size rule that has nothing to do with how bulbs work.

activities.explanation: Right: using less energy for the same work is what makes a bulb better.

activities.prompt: Two friends want to test which bulb saves more electricity. Bulb A and bulb B light the same desk equally. Which is a fair test?
options: Use the same desk and time, then compare the electricity each bulb uses
Use bulb A in the morning and bulb B at night
Use bulb A in a big room and bulb B in a small room
Use bulb A for one hour and bulb B for two hours

why.Use bulb A in the morning and bulb B at: Wrong: different times of day change the test, so the bulbs are not compared fairly.
why.Use bulb A in a big room and bulb B in a: Wrong: different rooms change the test, so the bulbs are not compared fairly.
why.Use bulb A for one hour and bulb B for t: Wrong: different times change the test, so the bulbs are not compared fairly.

activities.explanation: Right: keeping everything the same except the bulb makes the test fair.

lessons.title: Generating Energy from Sun, Wind and Water

activities.prompt: How can sunshine, wind, and water make electricity for our homes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Energy from Nature
activities.body: Everything that works needs energy. The Sun, wind and water are natural sources of energy. The Sun is the main source of energy for life on Earth. Solar panels catch sunlight and turn it into electricity. Windmills spin with the wind to make electricity. Fast-moving rivers and falling water can also make electricity. This clean energy makes no smoke or waste, so it keeps our air and world healthy.
keyPoints: The Sun is the main source of energy for life on Earth.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity; windmills turn wind into electricity.
Clean energy comes from natural sources and makes no smoke or waste.
activities.explanation: Nature gives us energy that can work without dirtying our air.

activities.prompt: A school wants electricity for its fans. One plan burns coal. Another plan uses solar panels on the roof. Which plan keeps the air clean, and why?
steps: Burning coal makes electricity, but burning it also makes smoke and harmful gases, so the air gets dirty.
Dirty air is not good for health and the environment, so the coal plan harms people and nature.
Solar panels capture sunlight and turn it into electricity without any smoke, so the air stays clean.
So the solar panel plan is better, because it makes electricity while keeping the air clean.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the main source of energy for life on Earth?
options: The wind
The Moon
The Sun
Flowing water
activities.explanation: Well done! The Sun is the main source of energy for all life on Earth.

activities.prompt: What do solar panels do?
options: They burn coal to make smoke
They capture sunlight and turn it into electricity
They spin with the wind
They grind grains in hilly areas
activities.explanation: Great thinking! Solar panels capture sunlight and turn it into electricity.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it gives us.
activities.explanation: Each source works in its own way. Coal makes smoke, but Sun, wind and water can make electricity cleanly.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a solar panel lights a bulb.
items: Sunlight shines on the solar panel
The solar panel captures the sunlight
The panel turns the sunlight into electricity
The electricity lights the bulb
activities.explanation: First the sunlight arrives, then the panel captures it and turns it into electricity, and finally the bulb lights up.

activities.prompt: A village has a fast river. People put a big water wheel in it. The wheel is joined to a grinder. What will happen?
options: The wheel will spin and grind the grains.
The wheel will melt because water is strong.
The wheel will stop and block the river.
The wheel will float away with the grains.

why.The wheel will melt because water is str: Thinks strong water destroys things, instead of making them work.
Thinks water only blocks things, forgetting it can give energy.
why.The wheel will float away with the grain: Thinks the wheel is light like a leaf, not fixed in place.

activities.explanation: Right. Fast-moving water can turn the wheel, so it can grind grains.

activities.prompt: A solar panel sits on a roof. A new tall building puts the panel in shadow all day. What happens to the electricity?
options: Less electricity, because the panel gets less sunlight.
More electricity, because shadow makes panels stronger.
The same electricity, because panels work in the dark.
The electricity changes into smoke in the shadow.

why.More electricity, because shadow makes p: Thinks shadow helps, not knowing sunlight is what panels need.
why.The same electricity, because panels wor: Thinks panels work without sunlight, mixing them with other sources.
why.The electricity changes into smoke in th: Thinks shadow creates smoke, confusing panels with burning fuels.

activities.explanation: Right. Panels capture sunlight, so less sunlight means less electricity.

activities.prompt: Riya wants to test if wind makes a windmill spin. She has two same windmills. Where should she put them for a fair test?
options: One in strong wind. One in still air.
Both in strong wind, to see them spin fast.
One in strong wind. One under deep water.
Both in a dark room, to see them spin.

why.Both in strong wind, to see them spin fa: Both get wind, so she cannot compare with a place with no wind.
why.One in strong wind. One under deep water: Water is a different test, so it does not show wind's effect.
A dark room has no wind, so neither will spin and nothing is compared.

activities.explanation: Right. Only the wind is different, so any spin difference shows wind's effect.

lessons.title: Energy All Around Us and Saving Energy

activities.prompt: Where does all the energy that moves our world come from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is Energy?
activities.body: Energy makes our world active and alive. It is at work everywhere! You use energy when you run, laugh or read. Energy can be heat, light, movement or sound. Humans and animals use food to move. Vehicles use fuel, and electricity lights our homes. Even batteries hold energy, ready to use.
keyPoints: Energy makes our world active and alive.
Types of energy include heat, light, movement and sound.
Food gives people and animals energy to move.
activities.explanation: Energy is the power that makes things happen all around you.

activities.prompt: Riya's toy car stops moving. Her friend says the battery is dead. Why does a dead battery stop the car?
steps: The toy car needs energy to move, so something inside must give it that energy.
The battery holds energy inside it, like a small store of power for the car.
When the battery is used up, the store is empty, so no energy can flow to the motor.
So the car stops because its stored energy in the battery is finished.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Clean Energy and Saving It
activities.body: Some energy is clean and kind to nature. We get clean energy from the Sun, wind and water. Energy should not be wasted. We should use and save energy wisely. Your body even stores energy for later, and batteries store energy too. Saving energy today means it is there when we need it.
keyPoints: Sun, wind and water give us clean energy.
We should use and save energy wisely.
Our body stores energy for future use.
activities.explanation: Wise use of energy keeps it ready for when we really need it.

activities.prompt: What do humans and animals use to move?
options: Water from rivers
Food they eat
Batteries they carry
activities.explanation: Food gives your body the energy it needs to run and play. Well done!

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the energy idea that goes with it.
activities.explanation: Each one shows energy doing a different job. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Vehicles can never run on electricity.
activities.explanation: Some vehicles can run on electricity, not only on fuel. Keep thinking!

activities.prompt: Batteries contain ______ energy inside them.
activities.hint: Think of a squirrel keeping nuts for later.
activities.explanation: Batteries hold energy until we need it. That is why a torch works even when switched off.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the Energy Flow Game in order.
items: Pick a slip with an energy source
Match it with a type of energy, like heat or light
Give an example, like a vehicle using fuel
activities.explanation: First you find a source, then its type of energy, then where it is used. You are an energy expert!

activities.prompt: What does Vaastu Shastra help people do?
options: Plan buildings in harmony with nature
Store energy inside batteries
Give food to animals
activities.explanation: Vaastu Shastra helps plan buildings so they fit well with nature. Lovely work!

activities.prompt: Meera's street has new buses that do not make smoke. They plug into a charger at night. What makes these buses move?
options: Electricity from the charger
Fuel burnt inside the bus
Food eaten by the driver
Wind pushing the bus along

why.Fuel burnt inside the bus: Wrong: this child thinks all vehicles must burn fuel like older buses.
why.Food eaten by the driver: Wrong: food gives energy to people and animals, not to buses.
why.Wind pushing the bus along: Wrong: wind is a clean energy source, but it does not push a plugged-in bus.

activities.explanation: Right: the bus is plugged in, so electricity is its energy to move.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'Energy is only in batteries and fuel.' At home he sees his dog running to catch a ball. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Dogs move without using any energy at all
The dog gets energy from food to move
The ball gives its energy to the dog
Running dogs use fuel like vehicles do

why.Dogs move without using any energy at al: Wrong: nothing moves without energy; energy is at work everywhere.
why.The ball gives its energy to the dog: Wrong: the ball does not give energy; the dog's food did.
why.Running dogs use fuel like vehicles do: Wrong: animals do not burn fuel; they use food for energy.

activities.explanation: Right: humans and animals use food to move, so energy is not only in batteries and fuel.

activities.prompt: A village wants clean energy for its new lights. It has strong sun, fast wind and a flowing river. Which plan uses only clean energy sources?
options: Sun panels, wind mills and water wheels
A big tank of fuel for a generator
Batteries filled at a fuel station
Burning wood to make heat for lights

why.A big tank of fuel for a generator: Wrong: fuel is not one of the clean sources named in the lesson.
why.Batteries filled at a fuel station: Wrong: batteries store energy, but filling them at a fuel station is not clean energy.
why.Burning wood to make heat for lights: Wrong: burning wood makes smoke and is not sun, wind or water energy.

activities.explanation: Right: sun, wind and water all give us clean energy.

activities.prompt: Anu eats a big lunch. In the evening she runs a race and feels strong. Where did the energy for running come from?
options: Her body saved energy from the food
The race track gave her energy
The sun shone on her while running
Her shoes stored energy for the race

why.The race track gave her energy: Wrong: a track is just ground; it does not give energy to runners.
why.The sun shone on her while running: Wrong: sunlight gives clean energy to the world, but Anu's running energy came from food.
why.Her shoes stored energy for the race: Wrong: shoes do not store energy for our bodies.

activities.explanation: Right: our body stores energy from food for future use, like running later.

activities.prompt: Two friends play the Energy Flow Game. One picks a slip that says 'torch'. The next slip must show a type of energy. Which slip matches best?
options: A slip that says light
A slip that says battery
A slip that says river
A slip that says food

why.A slip that says battery: Wrong: a battery stores energy; it is a source, not a type of energy.
why.A slip that says river: Wrong: a river is a source of energy, not a type like heat or light.
why.A slip that says food: Wrong: food is a source for our bodies, not a type of energy on the slips.

activities.explanation: Right: a torch gives us light, and light is a type of energy.

lessons.title: Test practice

activities.context: Riya sat in her kitchen for some time, watching and wondering. She saw food being cooked on the stove, the mixer making a loud sound, the bulb lighting up, and steam warming the room. Through the window, a flying snake glided past by flattening its body. She remembered that the Sun gives us light and heat, and wondered what made all these things happen.
activities.prompt: Why did Riya's mixer make a loud sound while it worked?
options: Because energy going into the mixer was changed into sound
Because the lid of the jar was not closed tightly
Because sound from outside the kitchen bounced off the walls
Because the mixer was standing on a cold floor

why.Because the lid of the jar was not close: A loose lid might rattle, but the mixer would make sound even with a tight lid.
why.Because sound from outside the kitchen b: The sound came from the mixer itself, not from outside sounds reflecting.
why.Because the mixer was standing on a cold: The floor being cold or warm does not cause the mixer's sound.

activities.explanation: Correct: energy makes things produce sound, so the working mixer turns energy into sound.

activities.context: Riya sat in her kitchen for some time, watching and wondering. She saw food being cooked on the stove, the mixer making a loud sound, the bulb lighting up, and steam warming the room. Through the window, a flying snake glided past by flattening its body. She remembered that the Sun gives us light and heat, and wondered what made all these things happen.
activities.prompt: The power supply suddenly goes off while Riya's food is cooking. What will most likely happen next, and why?
options: The food will cook faster because the stove gets a rest
The food will stop cooking because energy can no longer reach the stove
The kitchen will become brighter because the bulb needs less power
Nothing will change because cooking does not need energy

why.The food will cook faster because the st: Wrong: a rest does not make cooking faster; cooking needs a supply of energy.
why.The kitchen will become brighter because: Wrong: without energy the bulb cannot light up, so the kitchen gets darker.
why.Nothing will change because cooking does: Wrong: cooking food is an activity, and activities need energy to happen.

activities.explanation: Correct: cooking is work done by energy, so without energy the cooking stops.

activities.prompt: Explain why families in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Ladakh keep their cattle on the ground floor during winter.
activities.answer: Cattle give out heat from their bodies. When they stay on the ground floor, this heat rises and warms the rooms where the family lives above. In this clever way, people stay warm in winter without burning extra firewood or using electricity.
points: Animals give out heat from their bodies
Family lives on the floor above the cattle
Rooms above stay warm in winter
No extra firewood or electricity is needed
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: It was sports day at school. Meera had skipped breakfast and felt tired during the races. Her friend Aman, who had eaten, was active and ready to play. Later, Meera's family drove home in their car and filled it with petrol at the pump. At home, her grandmother cooked on the gas stove, while a neighbour cooked using wood.
activities.prompt: Why was Meera feeling tired during the races?
options: She had skipped breakfast, so her body had no energy from food
She was wearing the wrong shoes for running
The races were held on a hot afternoon
She was nervous about racing against Aman

why.She was wearing the wrong shoes for runn: Shoes are not part of the reason; tiredness here comes from missing food.
why.The races were held on a hot afternoon: The passage does not say the day was hot; this is a made-up reason.
why.She was nervous about racing against Ama: Nervousness is not linked to her tiredness; missing breakfast is.

activities.explanation: Correct. Food gives us energy, so without it she felt tired.

activities.context: It was sports day at school. Meera had skipped breakfast and felt tired during the races. Her friend Aman, who had eaten, was active and ready to play. Later, Meera's family drove home in their car and filled it with petrol at the pump. At home, her grandmother cooked on the gas stove, while a neighbour cooked using wood.
activities.prompt: What would happen to Meera's family car if its tank had no petrol at all?
options: It would not be able to keep running
It would begin to run faster on its own
It would start giving out thick smoke
It would need to be fed food like a person

why.It would begin to run faster on its own: A car cannot run without fuel; it certainly cannot go faster.
why.It would start giving out thick smoke: Smoke comes from burning wood or coal, not from an empty petrol tank.
why.It would need to be fed food like a pers: Cars take fuel, not food; food is the source of energy for living things.

activities.explanation: Correct. Vehicles need fuel like petrol to keep running, so without it the car stops.

activities.context: It was sports day at school. Meera had skipped breakfast and felt tired during the races. Her friend Aman, who had eaten, was active and ready to play. Later, Meera's family drove home in their car and filled it with petrol at the pump. At home, her grandmother cooked on the gas stove, while a neighbour cooked using wood.
activities.prompt: Why might the neighbour's cooking make the air around the houses smoky?
options: Because burning wood gives out smoke and pollution
Because the neighbour cooked a very large meal
Because cooking gas is a very strong fuel
Because the food itself makes smoke when it is ready

why.Because the neighbour cooked a very larg: The size of the meal is not the reason; the fuel used is.
why.Because cooking gas is a very strong fue: Cooking gas is a fuel, but the neighbour was using wood, not gas.
why.Because the food itself makes smoke when: Ready food does not cause the smoke; burning the wood does.

activities.explanation: Correct. Burning wood creates smoke and pollution, unlike a gas stove.

activities.prompt: Explain why vehicles and animals are similar in the way they get energy to move.
activities.answer: Both need a source of energy to move. Animals eat food to get energy to run, fly, swim and find food. Vehicles need fuel such as petrol or diesel to keep running. So petrol and diesel act like food for vehicles.
points: Both animals and vehicles need energy to move
Animals get their energy from food
Vehicles get their energy from fuel like petrol and diesel
Petrol and diesel are like food for vehicles
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera spends her summer holidays at her grandmother's old traditional house in an Indian village. The house has thick walls and small windows, yet inside it feels pleasant even at noon. One evening Meera plugs in a lamp and notices a broken wire. She wants to open the plug and fix it herself, but her cousin Ravi stops her. Later, grandmother fits LED bulbs in every room.
activities.prompt: Why does the house feel pleasant inside even at noon in summer?
options: The thick walls and small windows do not let heat come in quickly.
The small windows let cool wind rush in from outside.
The thick walls store electricity and turn it into coolness.
The LED bulbs inside the rooms give out cold air.

why.The small windows let cool wind rush in: Wrong. Small windows actually let in less air, not more.
why.The thick walls store electricity and tu: Wrong. Walls do not store or use electricity at all.
why.The LED bulbs inside the rooms give out: Wrong. Bulbs give light, not cold air.

activities.explanation: Correct. This is exactly how such traditional houses stayed cool in summer.

activities.context: Meera spends her summer holidays at her grandmother's old traditional house in an Indian village. The house has thick walls and small windows, yet inside it feels pleasant even at noon. One evening Meera plugs in a lamp and notices a broken wire. She wants to open the plug and fix it herself, but her cousin Ravi stops her. Later, grandmother fits LED bulbs in every room.
activities.prompt: After the LED bulbs are fitted, what change will grandmother notice in her rooms?
options: The rooms will be just as bright as before, but the bulbs will take less electricity.
The rooms will become much brighter, and the bulbs will take much more electricity.
The rooms will become dimmer, and the bulbs will take more electricity.
The rooms will stay bright only when the fan is also switched on.

why.The rooms will become much brighter, and: Wrong. LED bulbs do not use more electricity.
why.The rooms will become dimmer, and the bu: Wrong. LED bulbs do not give dimmer light or use more electricity.
why.The rooms will stay bright only when the: Wrong. Bulbs and fans work separately; a bulb does not need a fan.

activities.explanation: Correct. LED bulbs give the same light while using less electricity, so this is what she will see.

activities.prompt: Explain why electricity must be used carefully even though it is very useful.
activities.answer: Electricity is useful because it makes things at home work and gives us movement, sound, light and heat. But it is dangerous if not used carefully. Touching wires, sockets or plugged-in parts can harm us, so we should stay away from them and always ask an adult when something looks unsafe.
points: Electricity is useful for movement, sound, light and heat.
It is dangerous if not used carefully.
Never touch wires, sockets or plugged-in parts.
Tell an adult if something is unsafe.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi lives in a hilly village where a fast stream turns a gharaat to grind grain. The nearby town gets its electricity from a plant that burns coal, and on some days smoke hangs over the houses. The village panchayat wants electricity without dirtying the air. Ravi suggests using the stream, the strong hill winds, or the bright sunlight the village gets.
activities.prompt: Why does smoke appear over the town on some days?
options: Because the gharaat grinds too much grain
Because the town's electricity comes from burning coal
Because the stream flows too fast down the hill
Because the sunlight is too bright in the hills

why.Because the gharaat grinds too much grai: Grinding grain in a gharaat does not make smoke.
why.Because the stream flows too fast down t: Fast-flowing water is used to make electricity cleanly, not smoke.
why.Because the sunlight is too bright in th: Sunlight does not create smoke; it is a clean source.

activities.explanation: Correct: burning coal to make electricity creates smoke and harmful gases.

activities.context: Ravi lives in a hilly village where a fast stream turns a gharaat to grind grain. The nearby town gets its electricity from a plant that burns coal, and on some days smoke hangs over the houses. The village panchayat wants electricity without dirtying the air. Ravi suggests using the stream, the strong hill winds, or the bright sunlight the village gets.
activities.prompt: If the panchayat chooses Ravi's ideas instead of the coal plant, what will most likely happen to the village air?
options: It will stay clean because sunlight, wind and water make electricity without pollution
It will get more polluted because all electricity makes smoke
It will become polluted only during the grain-grinding season
It will not change, because electricity always dirties the air

why.It will get more polluted because all el: Not all electricity makes smoke; clean sources do not pollute.
why.It will become polluted only during the: Grain-grinding by gharaat is not linked to air pollution.
why.It will not change, because electricity: The air would change, because clean sources avoid smoke and harmful gases.

activities.explanation: Correct: sun, wind and water can produce electricity without polluting the air.

activities.prompt: Explain why polluted air is a problem, and how clean energy is different from energy made by burning coal.
activities.answer: Burning coal to make electricity creates smoke and harmful gases. This polluted air is not good for our health or the environment. Clean energy comes from natural sources like the Sun, wind and water, and it makes electricity without polluting the air with smoke or waste.
points: Burning coal makes smoke and harmful gases
Polluted air harms health and the environment
Clean energy comes from natural sources
Clean energy gives electricity without smoke or waste
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera's family is getting ready for a trip to her grandmother's village. Their new car does not need petrol because it runs on electricity. At home, the lights work because electricity reaches their house. Meera packs a torch whose batteries hold energy stored inside them. Her father reminds everyone to switch off the lights before leaving, saying energy should be used and saved wisely. On the way, they eat snacks so their bodies can keep moving.
activities.prompt: Why does Meera's family's car not need petrol for the trip?
options: It uses electricity instead of fuel to run
It has no engine, so it needs nothing at all
It stores energy the way Meera's body stores food
It was planned using Vaastu Shastra, so it never needs filling

why.It has no engine, so it needs nothing at: Wrong: every vehicle still needs some energy source; this car's source is electricity.
why.It stores energy the way Meera's body st: Wrong: storing energy in the body is about humans and animals, not about how cars run.
why.It was planned using Vaastu Shastra, so: Wrong: Vaastu Shastra is about planning buildings in harmony with nature, not about vehicles.

activities.explanation: Correct: the case says the car runs on electricity, so it does not need fuel like petrol.

activities.context: Meera's family is getting ready for a trip to her grandmother's village. Their new car does not need petrol because it runs on electricity. At home, the lights work because electricity reaches their house. Meera packs a torch whose batteries hold energy stored inside them. Her father reminds everyone to switch off the lights before leaving, saying energy should be used and saved wisely. On the way, they eat snacks so their bodies can keep moving.
activities.prompt: What would most likely happen if the family forgot to switch off the lights before leaving for the trip?
options: Energy would keep being used at home even though nobody was there
The lights would start giving out extra clean energy for the neighbours
The torch batteries would become charged while the house stayed empty
The house would become more active and alive with everyone away

why.The lights would start giving out extra: Wrong: lights use energy; they do not produce clean energy for anyone else.
why.The torch batteries would become charged: Wrong: batteries hold stored energy already; leaving lights on does not charge them.
why.The house would become more active and a: Wrong: an empty house uses energy without anyone there; it does not become more alive.

activities.explanation: Correct: lights left on keep using electricity, so energy is wasted when no one needs it.

activities.context: Meera's family is getting ready for a trip to her grandmother's village. Their new car does not need petrol because it runs on electricity. At home, the lights work because electricity reaches their house. Meera packs a torch whose batteries hold energy stored inside them. Her father reminds everyone to switch off the lights before leaving, saying energy should be used and saved wisely. On the way, they eat snacks so their bodies can keep moving.
activities.prompt: Why did Meera's family eat snacks on the way to the village?
options: Food is the fuel their bodies need so they can keep moving
The snacks would fill the torch batteries for the night
Eating snacks would help the electric car travel farther
Food gives the house electricity, so they ate before leaving

why.The snacks would fill the torch batterie: Wrong: batteries hold their own stored energy; eating food cannot fill them.
why.Eating snacks would help the electric ca: Wrong: the car runs on electricity, not on the food the family eats.
why.Food gives the house electricity, so the: Wrong: homes get electricity from the electricity supply, not from the food people eat.

activities.explanation: Correct: humans and animals use food to move, so snacks give their bodies energy for the journey.

activities.prompt: Explain why we should use and save energy wisely.
activities.answer: Energy is at work everywhere and makes our world active and alive. We need it for almost everything: food gives humans and animals energy to move, fuel runs vehicles and electricity lights our homes. Since so much depends on energy, we should use and save it wisely.
points: Energy is at work everywhere and keeps the world active and alive
Gives examples of uses: food for movement, fuel for vehicles, electricity for lights
Concludes that because energy is needed for so much, it must be used and saved wisely
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How Things Work

activities.prompt: A balloon zooms across the room when you let it go. What makes it move?
options: The air rushing out pushes it
The rubber gets heavier
The Sun pulls it forward
The balloon shrinks and lifts
activities.explanation: When air rushes out, it pushes the balloon forward. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Food is a source of energy for all living things.
activities.explanation: People and animals both get energy from food. That is why eating helps you play!

activities.prompt: When you pluck a rubber band on a box, it shakes quickly. This shaking is called ______, and it makes sound energy.
activities.hint: It means to shake quickly to and fro.
activities.explanation: Plucking rubber bands makes them vibrate and produce sounds.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the energy it gives us.
activities.explanation: Each source gives a different kind of energy. You matched them like a scientist!

activities.prompt: You see a broken electric wire on the road. What should you do?
options: Move it with a stick
Stay away and tell an adult
Hold it carefully with cloth
Step over it quickly
activities.explanation: Broken wires are dangerous. Stay away and tell an adult straight away.

activities.prompt: Traditional houses in India had big windows and thin walls to stay cool.
activities.explanation: They had small windows and thick walls. That kept houses cool in summer and warm in winter.

activities.prompt: Solar panels catch sunlight and turn it into ______.
activities.hint: It powers the lights and fans in your home.
activities.explanation: Solar panels capture sunlight and turn it into electricity. Clean and clever!

activities.prompt: Put the balloon experiment steps in the right order.
items: Blow the balloon until it fills up
Hold the balloon's mouth tightly
Release the balloon's mouth
Air rushes out and pushes the balloon forward
activities.explanation: First fill it, then hold, then release. The rushing air pushes it forward!

activities.prompt: Your family wants the same light at home but a smaller electricity bill. Which bulb is best?
options: A bulb that uses more electricity
A bulb that gives less light
An LED bulb that uses less electricity
A bulb that is switched on all day
activities.explanation: LED bulbs give the same light but use less electricity. That is energy efficiency!

activities.prompt: Match each clean energy source with what it does.
pairs: Spin with wind to make electricity
activities.explanation: Sun, wind and water give us clean energy that does not pollute. Great work!

chapters.title: Clothes — How Things are Made
chapters.summary: In this chapter: patterns with threads and nature's weavers; weaving and natural materials; traditions of weaving; thread and spinning.

lessons.title: Patterns with Threads and Nature's Weavers

activities.prompt: Which tiny artist was weaving beautiful nests long before humans learned to weave?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nature's Hidden Artists
activities.body: Nature is full of hidden artists. Animals, birds and insects weave, stitch, design and even glue things. One of these artists was weaving long before any human picked up a thread. In this lesson you will meet a bird that builds its home by weaving grass, just like a weaver at a loom.
keyPoints: Animals, birds and insects are nature's hidden artists.
They weave, stitch, design and glue things.
A hidden artist was weaving long before humans.
activities.explanation: Weaving is not only a human skill — nature had it first!

activities.prompt: A baya weaver builds a nest. A child says the bird must use glue like we use glue in class. Is the child right?
steps: The bird uses grass strands, so it works like a weaver, not like a gluer.
It puts each strand over and under other strands, so the strands hold each other.
Things that hold each other do not need glue, so the nest stays up without glue.
So the child is wrong: the baya weaver is a weaver, not a gluer.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who are the hidden artists all around us in nature?
options: Only people who paint pictures
Animals, birds and insects
Only birds that sing
Only insects that fly
activities.explanation: Nature is full of hidden artists like animals, birds and insects. Well done!

activities.prompt: What clever things do nature's hidden artists do?
options: They sing, dance and sleep
They weave, stitch, design and glue
They only hunt for food
They only build big nests
activities.explanation: These hidden artists weave, stitch, design and even glue things. Amazing, isn't it?

activities.prompt: The male baya weaver builds beautiful hanging nests from ______.
activities.hint: It is a soft plant that grows in fields and gardens.
activities.explanation: The male baya weaver uses grass to build its lovely hanging nest.

activities.prompt: What shape is the weaverbird's nest?
options: Like a pouch
Like a box
Like a cup
Like a ball
activities.explanation: The nest is shaped like a pouch. A cosy hanging home!

activities.prompt: Put the weaverbird's building steps in order.
items: Pick up strands of grass
Weave the strands over and under
The nest takes a pouch shape
The strong nest hangs from a branch
activities.explanation: First the bird gathers grass, then weaves it over and under. This makes the nest strong and pouch-shaped as it hangs.

activities.prompt: Match each weaverbird fact to its partner.
activities.explanation: Experts weave fine nests, while young learners start with rough ones. Practise makes perfect!

activities.prompt: A baya weaver puts grass strands over and under many times. Why is its nest strong?
options: Because the strands hold each other tightly.
Because the bird glues every strand down.
Because the nest hangs from a thin branch.
Because the grass is very thick and heavy.

why.Because the bird glues every strand down: Wrong: the bird weaves with grass, it does not use glue.
why.Because the nest hangs from a thin branc: Wrong: hanging does not make the woven part strong.
why.Because the grass is very thick and heav: Wrong: strength comes from the weaving, not thick grass.

activities.explanation: Right: weaving over and under makes the strands grip each other.

activities.prompt: One nest is fine and one nest is rough. Rina wants a fair test to see why. What should she do?
options: Watch one expert bird and one young bird with the same grass.
Watch one expert bird and give it different grass.
Watch one young bird and give it different grass.
Watch one young bird and count the trees nearby.

why.Watch one expert bird and give it differ: Wrong: changing the grass too makes the test unfair.
why.Watch one young bird and give it differe: Wrong: both birds are young, so skill never changes.
why.Watch one young bird and count the trees: Wrong: counting trees cannot show why nests differ.

activities.explanation: Right: only the birds' skill changes, so the test is fair.

activities.prompt: A friend says the baya weaver glues its nest together like a glue artist. The nest is made of woven grass strands. What is the flaw in the friend's claim?
options: The bird weaves strands over and under, so no glue is used.
The bird uses glue, but only a very small amount.
The bird uses glue only when the nest is a pouch.
The bird uses glue only when the grass is wet.

why.The bird uses glue, but only a very smal: Wrong: the friend is still keeping glue in the claim.
why.The bird uses glue only when the nest is: Wrong: the pouch shape does not mean glue was used.
why.The bird uses glue only when the grass i: Wrong: wet grass does not change weaving into gluing.

activities.explanation: Right: weaving over and under holds the strands, so glue is not needed.

activities.prompt: A baya weaver weaves grass strands only over other strands. It never weaves them under. What will happen to its nest?
options: It will be loose and not very strong.
It will be strong because over is enough.
It will be a fine pouch like an expert's.
It will be strong because glue holds it.

why.It will be strong because over is enough: Wrong: weaving only over cannot grip the strands tightly.
why.It will be a fine pouch like an expert's: Wrong: only expert weaving makes a very fine nest.
Wrong: the bird weaves grass, it does not use glue.

activities.explanation: Right: strands need over and under weaving to hold each other.

lessons.title: Weaving and Natural Materials

activities.prompt: How can grass and threads turn into cloth and baskets?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is weaving?
activities.body: Weaving joins strips or threads into patterned fabric like cloth. One set of thread is placed vertically, going up and down. The other set goes horizontally, side to side. The threads are crossed over and under each other. This crossing makes one unified fabric, like a mat or basket. People have long woven natural materials such as coconut fibre, bamboo, grass, jute, cotton and silk.
keyPoints: Weaving crosses threads over and under each other.
One set of thread is vertical, the other horizontal.
Natural materials include coconut fibre, bamboo, grass, jute, cotton and silk.
activities.explanation: Crossing threads is the secret that holds woven fabric together.

activities.prompt: Riya weaves paper strips in class and gets a flat mat. Her mother weaves with thin threads and gets cloth. Why are the two results different?
steps: Both Riya and her mother cross strips over and under each other, so both are weaving.
Paper strips are wide and stiff, so they stay flat like a mat.
Threads are thin and soft, so when they cross tightly they join into flexible cloth.
So the crossing is the same, but using threads instead of paper strips makes cloth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Indian muslin was so fine that people called it woven ______.
activities.hint: Think of the lightest, softest thing you cannot hold.
activities.explanation: Muslin was so fine and light that it was called 'woven air'.

activities.prompt: Indian muslin was so fine that it was called 'woven air'.
activities.explanation: Yes! Muslin was so light and fine that people called it 'woven air'.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Great matching! You remember the directions of thread and the famous muslin.

activities.prompt: How fine was Indian muslin? Choose the true sentence.
options: A whole basket could pass through a ring.
A whole saree could pass through a ring.
A whole mat could pass through a ring.
A whole tree could pass through a ring.
activities.explanation: Amazing! Muslin was so fine that a whole saree could slip through a ring.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of weaving in the correct order.
items: Place one set of thread vertically
Place the other set of thread horizontally
Cross the threads over and under each other
The crossing forms a unified fabric
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First the vertical threads, then the horizontal ones, then the crossing makes the fabric.

activities.prompt: What happens if the threads are NOT crossed over and under each other?
options: The threads will turn vertical by themselves.
The fabric will not hold together as one piece.
The fabric will become a basket instead.
The threads will change into natural materials.
activities.explanation: Good thinking! It is the crossing over and under that joins the threads into one fabric.

activities.prompt: In craft class you weave paper strips into a mat. At home you weave thin threads the same way, over and under. What will you make?
options: A mat, because the crossing is the same
A basket, because threads are soft
Cloth, because threads woven together make cloth
Nothing, because threads cannot be woven

why.A mat, because the crossing is the same: Wrong: the material matters, not just the crossing.
why.A basket, because threads are soft: Wrong: baskets come from stiff natural materials, not thin threads.
why.Nothing, because threads cannot be woven: Wrong: threads can be crossed over and under just like strips.

activities.explanation: Right: weaving with threads instead of paper strips makes cloth.

activities.prompt: A friend lays all her threads going up and down. She adds no threads going side to side. She tries to weave a mat. What will happen?
options: She can weave, because one set of threads is enough
She cannot weave, because there is no second set to cross
She can weave, because the threads will cross each other
She cannot weave, because the threads are too long

why.She can weave, because one set of thread: Wrong: weaving needs two sets of threads, not one.
why.She can weave, because the threads will: Wrong: threads going the same way cannot cross over and under.
why.She cannot weave, because the threads ar: Wrong: the length of the threads is not the problem.

activities.explanation: Right: one set goes up and down and the other goes side to side, so both are needed.

activities.prompt: A weaver makes every thread go over the threads below it. No thread ever goes under another. He says the mat will hold together. What is the flaw?
options: Threads must cross over and under to join into one fabric
The threads are too short to make a mat
The mat will hold, because all the threads touch
Threads must be tied in knots to make a mat

why.The threads are too short to make a mat: Wrong: the length of the threads is not the problem.
why.The mat will hold, because all the threa: Wrong: touching is not enough; the threads must hold each other.
why.Threads must be tied in knots to make a: Wrong: weaving does not need knots, only crossing.

activities.explanation: Right: the over-and-under crossing is what locks threads into one fabric.

activities.prompt: Dev says only cotton and silk can be woven. His grandmother weaves a basket from bamboo strips. What is wrong with Dev's claim?
options: Baskets are not weaving because they are not cloth
Bamboo strips are too thick to cross each other
Dev is wrong because natural materials like bamboo are woven too
Dev is right because cotton and silk are the only threads

why.Baskets are not weaving because they are: Wrong: mats and baskets are woven fabrics too.
why.Bamboo strips are too thick to cross eac: Wrong: bamboo strips can be crossed over and under.
why.Dev is right because cotton and silk are: Wrong: many natural materials, not only cotton and silk, can be woven.

activities.explanation: Right: people weave natural materials like bamboo into baskets.

activities.prompt: Meera says a grass mat is not a fabric because fabric must be cloth made from threads. Her friend shows her a woven grass mat. What is wrong with Meera's claim?
options: Grass mats are fabrics because the strips cross into one piece
Grass mats are fabrics only when they are coloured
Meera is right because grass is not a thread
Grass mats are fabrics because grass grows very fast

why.Grass mats are fabrics only when they ar: Wrong: colour does not decide if something is a fabric.
why.Meera is right because grass is not a th: Wrong: woven grass strips still join into one fabric.
why.Grass mats are fabrics because grass gro: Wrong: how fast grass grows does not matter here.

activities.explanation: Right: crossing over and under joins the grass into one unified fabric.

lessons.title: Traditions of Weaving

activities.prompt: How do threads turn into beautiful cloth? 🧵
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Weaving: Cloth Made by Hand
activities.body: People in India knew how to weave even 4,000 years ago! Weaving is done by hand on an instrument called a loom. Cloth made this way is called handloom fabric. India has some of the best handloom weavers in the world. Each region has its own special patterns and techniques, like Kanjeevaram, Pashmina and Ikat.
keyPoints: Weaving in India is at least 4,000 years old.
A loom is the instrument used for weaving by hand.
Cloth woven by hand is called handloom fabric.
India has many handloom traditions with unique techniques and patterns.
activities.explanation: Weaving is an old and proud skill that turns thread into beautiful cloth.

activities.prompt: Anu sees two cloths in a shop. One was made by hand on a loom. One was made by a machine. The shopkeeper only says, 'This one is handloom fabric.' How can Anu know which cloth was made by hand?
steps: The shopkeeper used the word 'handloom fabric' for one cloth.
Handloom fabric is the name for cloth made by hand on a loom.
So the cloth called handloom fabric is the one made by hand on a loom.
The other cloth was not made this way, so it is not handloom fabric.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the instrument called that is used for weaving by hand?
options: A loom
A spindle
A needle
A wheel
activities.explanation: Traditional weaving is done by hand on an instrument called a loom.

activities.prompt: India was the first country to grow and use cotton for clothes.
activities.explanation: Well done! India led the way with cotton, and this changed textiles all over the world.

activities.prompt: Cloth woven by hand on a loom is called ______ fabric.
activities.hint: It is one word made of two small words: hand and loom.
activities.explanation: Cloth made by hand on a loom is called handloom fabric.

activities.prompt: Match each handloom tradition to where it comes from.
activities.explanation: Each tradition grows in its own home, with its own special style.

activities.prompt: Pooja lives in Kashmir. Which handloom tradition is famous in her state?
options: Pashmina
Kanjeevaram
Ikat
None of these
activities.explanation: Pashmina comes from Kashmir, so Pooja lives near this famous tradition.

activities.prompt: Ikat comes only from Odisha.
activities.explanation: Ikat comes from two states: Odisha and Gujarat.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order, from oldest to newest.
items: People in India learned to weave 4,000 years ago.
India became the first country to grow and use cotton for clothes.
Cotton use revolutionised textiles worldwide.
Weaving today gives work to many families.
activities.explanation: Weaving came first, then cotton, then its worldwide effect, and weaving still gives work today.

activities.prompt: Why do handloom traditions matter to India today?
options: They give work and keep old skills alive
They are only used in museums
They are all exactly the same
They came from other countries
activities.explanation: Weaving provides work to many families and keeps traditional skills and designs alive.

activities.prompt: In a village, many families weave cloth every day. The village has less joblessness than nearby villages. Why does weaving help the village?
options: Weaving gives work to many families.
Weaving makes the weather warmer there.
Weaving stops children from going to school.
Weaving brings rain to the village fields.

Thinks weaving changes weather, but weaving only makes cloth.
why.Weaving stops children from going to sch: Mixes weaving with stopping school; weaving gives work, not this.
why.Weaving brings rain to the village field: Thinks weaving is magic for farms; it is work for families.

activities.explanation: Right. Weaving provides work to many families, so people can earn.

activities.prompt: Two weavers meet at a fair. One weaves in Tamil Nadu. One weaves in Odisha. Their cloths look very different from each other. Why?
options: Each tradition has its own unique techniques and patterns.
One weaver works at night and one works in the day.
Cloth always changes colour when it is carried far.
The weavers forgot how to weave the same cloth.

why.One weaver works at night and one works: Thinks time of work changes the cloth; the tradition does.
why.Cloth always changes colour when it is c: Thinks travel changes cloth; the patterns come from traditions.
why.The weavers forgot how to weave the same: Thinks weavers forget; the difference is their unique traditions.

activities.explanation: Right. Many handloom traditions have unique techniques and patterns.
