lessons.title: Thread and Spinning

activities.prompt: How does fluffy cotton turn into the thread that makes your clothes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where does cloth begin?
activities.body: Have you ever wondered where your shirt begins? It starts as tiny cotton fibres — thin, hair-like threads. When we twist many fibres together, we make a strong thread or yarn. This twisting is called spinning. A charkha, or spinning wheel, helps us spin thread from cotton. Threads can then be woven together to form cloth.
keyPoints: A fibre is a thin, hair-like thread from cotton.
Spinning means twisting fibres together to make thread or yarn.
A charkha is a spinning wheel that helps spin thread from cotton.
Threads woven together form cloth.
activities.explanation: Every piece of cloth starts with tiny fibres twisted into thread.

activities.prompt: Meera holds a cotton ball. She pulls it slowly. Soft fluffy bits come off. She pulls one bit. It is very thin, like hair. She asks: what is this thin thing called, and how can it become thread?
steps: The thin hair-like thing came from cotton, so it is a fibre.
One fibre alone is weak, so it cannot be thread by itself.
If Meera twists many fibres together, they hold each other tight.
So twisting fibres makes thread, and this twisting is called spinning.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spinning for freedom
activities.body: Long ago, Gandhi ji taught people to spin their own thread and weave their own cloth. He wanted everyone to become self-sufficient — able to make what they need. Making our own cloth became a symbol of the freedom struggle and a path to being atmanirbhar. Cloth made this way is known as khadi.
keyPoints: Gandhi ji showed that we should become self-sufficient.
Spinning and weaving our own cloth became a symbol of the freedom struggle.
Cloth made this way is called khadi.
activities.explanation: The humble charkha became a powerful sign of freedom.

activities.title: What is spinning?
activities.prompt: Twisting cotton fibres together to make thread or yarn is called ______. Which word fits?
options: Weaving
Spinning
Knitting
Dyeing
activities.explanation: Twisting fibres into thread is called spinning. Weaving comes later, when threads make cloth.

activities.title: Spot the fibre
activities.prompt: A fibre is a thick, strong rope made by twisting many threads together.
activities.explanation: A fibre is the opposite — a thin, hair-like thread from untwisting cotton. Good thinking!

activities.title: The spinning wheel
activities.prompt: Gandhi ji spun thread on a spinning wheel also known as the ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter 'c' and helps spin cotton.
activities.explanation: The charkha is a spinning wheel that helps spin thread from cotton.

activities.title: Match the pairs
activities.prompt: Match each word with what it means.
pairs: From the cocoon of the silk moth
Cloth spun and woven by hand
activities.explanation: Each word has its own special meaning. You matched them all!

activities.title: Where does silk come from?
activities.prompt: Silk is a fibre too, but not from cotton. Where does silk come from?
options: The cocoon of the silk moth
The leaves of the cotton plant
The wool of a mountain goat
The roots of a banyan tree
activities.explanation: Silk comes from the cocoon of a small insect called the silk moth. Cotton is not the only source of fibres!

activities.title: Khadi and the freedom struggle
activities.prompt: Making our own cloth by spinning and weaving became a symbol of the freedom struggle.
activities.explanation: Yes! Spinning and weaving our own cloth showed we could be self-sufficient. That is why khadi is so special.

activities.prompt: Ravi holds cotton fibres loosely without twisting. They pull apart easily. Then he twists them tightly into thread. The thread does not pull apart. Why does twisting help?
options: Twisting makes the fibres hold each other tightly.
Twisting makes the fibres become longer and longer.
Twisting makes the fibres turn into khadi cloth.
Twisting makes the fibres change into silk.

why.Twisting makes the fibres become longer: He thinks length is the reason, but the fibres do not grow longer.
why.Twisting makes the fibres turn into khad: He mixes up spinning with weaving, which makes cloth.
why.Twisting makes the fibres change into si: He confuses cotton with silk, which comes from a cocoon.

activities.explanation: Right. Twisting grips the fibres together, so spinning makes strong thread.

activities.prompt: Two children test cotton. Sana twists her cotton into thread. Dev does not twist his cotton at all. Both pull their cotton gently. Whose test fairly shows that spinning makes thread strong?
options: Sana's, because she twisted hers and Dev did not.
Dev's, because he kept his cotton soft and natural.
Both, because both children pulled their cotton gently.
Neither, because cotton always breaks when pulled.

why.Dev's, because he kept his cotton soft a: He thinks natural cotton is the test, but untwisted cotton is not spun.
why.Both, because both children pulled their: He forgets the two samples must differ in twisting to compare.
why.Neither, because cotton always breaks wh: He gives up too soon; twisted thread can be strong.

activities.explanation: Right. Only one thing is different, twisting, so the test is fair.

activities.prompt: A boy says his shirt is khadi because it came from a silk moth cocoon. His friend checks how khadi is made. What is the flaw in the boy's claim?
options: Khadi is made by spinning and weaving, not from cocoons.
Khadi is made only from silk, never from cotton.
Khadi needs a charkha, and cocoons need a charkha too.
Khadi comes from loose fibres, not from twisted thread.

why.Khadi is made only from silk, never from: He thinks khadi must be silk, but khadi can be cotton cloth.
why.Khadi needs a charkha, and cocoons need: He knows the charkha word but misses how khadi is really made.
why.Khadi comes from loose fibres, not from: He forgets that spinning twists fibres into thread first.

activities.explanation: Right. Khadi is cloth made by spinning and weaving, so cocoons are not the source.

activities.prompt: Long ago, people spun thread and wove their own cloth. This became a symbol of the freedom struggle. Why did making our own cloth matter so much?
options: It showed we could be self-sufficient and atmanirbhar.
It showed our cloth was softer than all other cloth.
It showed the charkha was faster than machines.
It showed silk moths could live near our homes.

why.It showed our cloth was softer than all: He thinks about comfort, but the real reason was self-reliance.
why.It showed the charkha was faster than ma: He focuses on speed, but the lesson is about self-sufficiency.
why.It showed silk moths could live near our: He connects the wrong idea; moths are not the point here.

activities.explanation: Right. Gandhi ji taught self-sufficiency, so own cloth meant being atmanirbhar.

lessons.title: Natural and Synthetic Fibres

activities.prompt: How does a tiny caterpillar help make the soft silk scarf you wear?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where do our clothes come from?
activities.body: Some fibres come from nature, like silk from silkworms and jute from plants. Synthetic fibres are made by humans using artificial materials. We all use things made from both kinds every day. India grows more jute than any other country in the world!
keyPoints: Natural fibres come from plants and animals.
Synthetic fibres are made by humans using artificial materials.
We use things made from both natural and synthetic fibres.
India is the largest producer of jute in the world.
activities.explanation: Fibres around you come from two places: nature and factories.

activities.prompt: A farmer finds a cocoon on his mulberry plant. He wants silk thread from it. What should he do first, and why?
steps: The silk thread is inside the cocoon, so the farmer must get it out without breaking it.
Cocoons are put in hot water first, so the thread can be pulled out gently and not torn.
Then the thread is gently pulled out and made into thread for silk fabric, so the farmer gets his silk.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Put the story of the silk moth in order.
items: Silk moth lays eggs
Eggs hatch into tiny caterpillars
Caterpillars eat mulberry leaves and grow big
Caterpillars spin cocoons around themselves
Adult moth comes out of the cocoon
activities.explanation: The moth lays eggs, caterpillars hatch and grow, spin cocoons, then a new moth comes out. Then the cycle begins again!

activities.prompt: To get the silk thread out, the cocoons are put in ______ water.
activities.hint: Think of water that is not cold.
activities.explanation: The cocoons are put in hot water before the thread is pulled out.

activities.prompt: What do the tiny caterpillars eat to grow big?
options: Jute leaves
Silk thread
Mulberry leaves
Cocoon pieces
activities.explanation: The caterpillars eat mulberry leaves and grow big.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what you learned about it.
activities.explanation: Great matching! You remembered the silk story, jute and synthetic fibres.

activities.prompt: Riya's school bag has a jute part and a synthetic part. What does this show?
options: Only synthetic fibres are useful
We use things made from both kinds of fibres
Jute comes from silkworms
Bags are never made from natural fibres
activities.explanation: We all use things made from both natural and synthetic fibres, often in one item.

activities.prompt: A caterpillar lives in a small box. The box has no mulberry leaves. Caterpillars eat mulberry leaves and grow big. What will happen to this caterpillar?
options: It will grow big anyway.
It will stay small.
It will spin a cocoon at once.
It will lay many eggs.

Thinks spinning a cocoon does not need growing first.
Thinks caterpillars lay eggs, but the moth lays eggs.

activities.explanation: Right: it cannot grow big without eating mulberry leaves.

activities.prompt: A worker has a cocoon. She does not put it in hot water. Now she wants to pull out the silk thread gently. What will happen?
options: The thread will come out gently.
The thread will be hard to pull out gently.
The cocoon will make more thread.
The thread will turn into silk fabric at once.

Thinks the hot water step does nothing.
Thinks cocoons make thread by themselves.
why.The thread will turn into silk fabric at: Threads do not turn into fabric by themselves.

activities.explanation: Right: the hot water step is there so the thread can be pulled out gently.

activities.prompt: A factory makes a school bag. Humans make it from artificial materials. Riya says the bag is made of natural fibre. Why is she wrong?
options: Because the bag is made by humans from artificial materials.
Because school bags are never made of fibre.
Because she uses the bag every day.
Because the bag is not strong.

why.Because school bags are never made of fi: Thinks bags cannot be made of fibre at all.
Thinks using a thing often makes it natural.
Thinks strength decides the kind of fibre.

activities.explanation: Right: synthetic fibres are made by humans using artificial materials.

activities.prompt: Ravi wears a shirt made from natural fibre. He carries a bag made from synthetic fibre. What does this show about the things we use?
options: We use things made from both kinds of fibre.
We use things made from only natural fibre.
We use things made from only synthetic fibre.
We use things made without any fibre.

why.We use things made from only natural fib: Thinks one natural thing means we use only natural things.
why.We use things made from only synthetic f: Thinks one synthetic thing means we use only synthetic things.
Thinks his things have no fibre, but both are made of fibre.

activities.explanation: Right: Ravi uses one natural thing and one synthetic thing on the same day.

lessons.title: Stitching, Embroidery and Recycling

activities.prompt: Can a tiny bird really sew its own nest?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Stitches all around us
activities.body: Stitching means joining cloth with a needle and thread. Even birds do it! The tailorbird is a tiny green bird that stitches its own nest. It uses plant fibres or spider silk as thread. People stitch too. The simple running stitch goes up, down, up, down in a straight line.
keyPoints: Stitching joins fabric with a needle and thread.
The tailorbird stitches its nest with plant fibres or spider silk.
A running stitch goes up, down, up, down in a line.
activities.explanation: Stitching is a skill shared by people and one clever little bird.

activities.prompt: Meera sees a tiny green bird. The nest looks sewn together. She wonders how a bird can stitch without hands.
steps: A bird has no hands, so it cannot hold a needle like we do.
The tailorbird is a tiny green bird that stitches its own nest.
It uses plant fibres or spider silk as thread, so it does not need a needle.
So the bird pushes the thread through leaves using its beak instead of hands.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Cloth traditions of India
activities.body: Different parts of India use many different kinds of stitches. Bandhani is a type of tie-dye. In Patan, Gujarat, weavers make the Patola saree, which is very complex. There is also an old tradition of making quilts by joining small pieces of cloth.
keyPoints: Different parts of India use different stitches.
Bandhani is a type of tie-dye.
The Patola saree from Patan, Gujarat, is very complex.
Quilts are made by joining small pieces of cloth.
activities.explanation: Every region has its own beautiful way of working with cloth.

activities.prompt: The tailorbird stitches its nest. What does it use as thread?
options: Plant fibres or spider silk
Wool from a goat
Long green leaves only
activities.explanation: The tailorbird is a tiny green bird that uses plant fibres or spider silk as its thread.

activities.prompt: To stitch fabric together, you need a needle and ______.
activities.hint: It is a long, thin string that goes through the needle.
activities.explanation: A needle and thread work together to join pieces of fabric.

activities.prompt: Pashmina wool comes from a special goat called the Changthangi.
activities.explanation: Well done! This special goat gives us the wool for very soft shawls.

activities.prompt: You are learning the running stitch. How does the needle move?
options: Round and round in a circle
Up, down, up, down in a straight line
Side to side in a zigzag
activities.explanation: The running stitch is made by going up, down, up, down in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what you learned about it.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each one has its own special story.

activities.prompt: Put the moves of a running stitch in the right order.
items: Needle goes up through the cloth
Needle goes down into the cloth
Needle goes up again
Needle goes down again
activities.explanation: Up, down, up, down — that is how a running stitch travels in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Ravi is learning the running stitch. He pushes the needle up, down, up, down. What will his fabric look like after this?
options: Two fabrics joined by small stitches in a straight line
Two fabrics joined by one very long single stitch
Two fabrics glued together with no thread at all
Two fabrics with a big hole where the needle went

why.Two fabrics joined by one very long sing: Wrong. A running stitch has many small moves, not one long stitch.
why.Two fabrics glued together with no threa: Wrong. Stitching needs a needle and thread, not glue.
why.Two fabrics with a big hole where the ne: Wrong. The needle makes small holes for thread, not a big hole.

activities.explanation: Right. Going up, down, up, down in a line makes a running stitch that joins fabric.

activities.prompt: A shop says its shawl is very soft Pashmina. A weaver says she spun the wool by hand. Which shawl matches the old way of making Pashmina?
options: A soft shawl hand-spun and hand-woven from goat wool
A rough shawl made from sheep wool by a machine
A soft shawl made from cotton picked from plants
A shiny shawl woven from silk taken from worms

why.A rough shawl made from sheep wool by a: Wrong. Pashmina comes from a special goat, not a sheep, and it is made by hand.
why.A soft shawl made from cotton picked fro: Wrong. Pashmina is wool from a goat, not cotton from plants.
why.A shiny shawl woven from silk taken from: Wrong. Pashmina is wool, not silk from worms.

activities.explanation: Right. Pashmina comes from a goat, and people hand-spin and weave it into soft shawls.

activities.prompt: A village weaver makes cloth on a handloom. The power goes off for two days. What will happen to her work?
options: She can keep weaving because a handloom uses no electricity
She must stop because a handloom needs electricity to move
She will weave faster because power cuts make looms strong
She will start stitching with a needle instead of weaving

why.She must stop because a handloom needs e: Wrong. A handloom works by hand, so it does not need electricity.
why.She will weave faster because power cuts: Wrong. A power cut does not change how fast a handloom works.
why.She will start stitching with a needle i: Wrong. She is a weaver, and a power cut does not change her work.

activities.explanation: Right. Handloom weaving uses no electricity, so a power cut does not stop it.

activities.context: Meera is helping her grandmother weave a mat for the courtyard. They have collected palm reeds and grass, and also some coconut fibre. Grandmother places one set of strips going up and down, and Meera weaves another set going side to side, taking each strip over and under the ones held straight. Later, Meera's aunt shows them fine cotton threads she is using to weave cloth on a loom.
activities.prompt: Why does the mat stay in one piece instead of falling apart?
options: The strips grip each other where they cross over and under, locking into one piece.
The strips are stuck together with glue made from coconut fibre.
Only the strips going up and down do all the work of holding the mat.
The mat holds together because the strips are all woven in the same direction.

why.The strips are stuck together with glue: Wrong: glue is not part of weaving; the joining comes from the crossing itself.
why.Only the strips going up and down do all: Wrong: both sets of strips are needed; one set alone cannot form fabric.
why.The mat holds together because the strip: Wrong: if all strips went one way they could not cross, so nothing would hold.

activities.explanation: Correct: the over-and-under crossing is what joins the two sets into one unified fabric.

activities.context: Meera is helping her grandmother weave a mat for the courtyard. They have collected palm reeds and grass, and also some coconut fibre. Grandmother places one set of strips going up and down, and Meera weaves another set going side to side, taking each strip over and under the ones held straight. Later, Meera's aunt shows them fine cotton threads she is using to weave cloth on a loom.
activities.prompt: Meera tries to weave a mat, but she lays every strip going only up and down and never adds the side-to-side set. What will happen?
options: She will not get a mat, because the strips cannot cross and hold each other.
She will get a mat, but it will be weaker than one made of jute.
She will get a mat with a pattern, but the colours will not match.
She will get a mat that is as fine as woven air.

why.She will get a mat, but it will be weake: Wrong: the problem is not the material; no amount of jute fixes missing strips.
why.She will get a mat with a pattern, but t: Wrong: a pattern needs both sets crossing; with one set there is no pattern at all.
why.She will get a mat that is as fine as wo: Wrong: 'woven air' describes very fine muslin cloth, not a mat made this way.

activities.explanation: Correct: without the horizontal set, there is no crossing, so no unified fabric forms.

activities.prompt: Explain why Indian muslin was given the name 'woven air'.
activities.answer: Indian muslin was woven so finely that the cloth was extremely light and delicate. It was so fine that a whole saree made from it could pass through a ring. Because the fabric seemed as light and thin as air, people called it 'woven air'.
points: Says the muslin was woven very finely.
Mentions that a whole saree could pass through a ring.
Links the great fineness/lightness to the name 'woven air'.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera's grandmother weaves cloth by hand on a loom, just as people in India have done for thousands of years. She makes Kanjeevaram cloth with special patterns found only in her family's village. Last year, a machine in the city made similar cloth faster and cheaper, and fewer customers came to buy grandmother's fabric.
activities.prompt: If fewer people buy grandmother's handloom cloth, what is the most likely effect on her village?
options: Families who earn money from weaving may lose that work
The loom will automatically start weaving faster
The village will begin growing more cotton than before
The patterns will change on their own

why.The loom will automatically start weavin: Wrong: a loom is a hand tool and does not speed up by itself
why.The village will begin growing more cott: Wrong: growing cotton is not connected to people buying her cloth
why.The patterns will change on their own: Wrong: patterns are kept alive by weavers, they do not change by themselves

activities.explanation: Correct: weaving gives work to many families, so fewer sales means less work

activities.context: Meera's grandmother weaves cloth by hand on a loom, just as people in India have done for thousands of years. She makes Kanjeevaram cloth with special patterns found only in her family's village. Last year, a machine in the city made similar cloth faster and cheaper, and fewer customers came to buy grandmother's fabric.
activities.prompt: Why can grandmother make patterns that the city machine cannot copy exactly?
options: Because her family uses unique techniques passed down through tradition
Because her loom is newer than the city machine
Because she weaves only at night
Because the machine cannot hold any thread

why.Because her loom is newer than the city: Wrong: the loom is an old hand tool, not newer than a machine
why.Because she weaves only at night: Wrong: the time of day she weaves does not matter
why.Because the machine cannot hold any thre: Wrong: a machine can hold thread; the difference is the special technique

activities.explanation: Correct: unique techniques and patterns are part of handloom traditions

activities.context: Meera's grandmother weaves cloth by hand on a loom, just as people in India have done for thousands of years. She makes Kanjeevaram cloth with special patterns found only in her family's village. Last year, a machine in the city made similar cloth faster and cheaper, and fewer customers came to buy grandmother's fabric.
activities.prompt: What should Meera do to help keep her grandmother's weaving tradition alive?
options: Learn the special weaving techniques and patterns from her
Ask her to stop weaving and rest all day
Tell her to buy cloth from the city instead
Hide the loom so no one else can use it

why.Ask her to stop weaving and rest all day: Wrong: stopping weaving would end the tradition, not save it
why.Tell her to buy cloth from the city inst: Wrong: buying city cloth would reduce demand for her handloom fabric
why.Hide the loom so no one else can use it: Wrong: hiding the loom stops weaving altogether

activities.explanation: Correct: learning the skills keeps traditional techniques and designs alive

activities.prompt: What is the difference between handloom fabric and cloth made by a machine?
activities.answer: Handloom fabric is woven by hand on an instrument called a loom, so it needs the skill of a weaver and can have unique techniques and patterns. Machine-made cloth does not use a handloom, so it may be faster and cheaper but lacks these traditional skills and special designs.
points: Handloom fabric is made by hand on a loom
Handloom traditions have unique techniques and patterns
Machine cloth lacks the traditional skill and special designs
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In Meera's village, the elders have started a small centre where cotton is turned into thread on charkhas and then woven into cloth. Meera's grandmother spins there every evening. The cloth they make is sold in the village market, and the elders say that by making their own cloth, the village does not have to depend on anyone else for it.
activities.prompt: One afternoon, Meera tries to use cotton straight from the plant without twisting it. What is she most likely to find?
options: The cotton will turn into cloth on its own
The cotton will not hold together as a long, usable thread
The cotton will become silk
The cotton will change into a cocoon

why.The cotton will turn into cloth on its o: Cotton never becomes cloth without first being made into thread, so this cannot happen.
why.The cotton will become silk: Silk comes from a different source altogether, not from cotton.
why.The cotton will change into a cocoon: A cocoon belongs to the silk moth, not to cotton.

activities.explanation: Correct. Without twisting, loose fibres stay separate and cannot form a strong thread.

activities.context: In Meera's village, the elders have started a small centre where cotton is turned into thread on charkhas and then woven into cloth. Meera's grandmother spins there every evening. The cloth they make is sold in the village market, and the elders say that by making their own cloth, the village does not have to depend on anyone else for it.
activities.prompt: Meera finds a soft, shiny fibre at the centre and thinks it also came from cotton. Her grandmother smiles and says it came from a living creature. What should Meera conclude?
options: The fibre came from the cocoon of a small insect
The fibre came from twisting cotton more tightly
The fibre came from weaving two threads together
The fibre came from a charkha spinning faster

why.The fibre came from twisting cotton more: Twisting cotton makes thread, but it cannot make a shiny fibre from a different source.
why.The fibre came from weaving two threads: Weaving joins threads into cloth; it does not create a new kind of fibre.
why.The fibre came from a charkha spinning f: A charkha spins cotton into thread; spinning speed does not change the source of a fibre.

activities.explanation: Correct. Silk is a natural fibre that comes from the cocoon of the silk moth, a small insect.

activities.prompt: Explain why making our own cloth by spinning and weaving became important during the freedom struggle.
activities.answer: Gandhi ji taught that we should become self-sufficient, meaning we should make the things we need ourselves. Spinning thread on the charkha and weaving it into khadi cloth showed this idea, so making our own cloth became a symbol of the freedom struggle and a path to being atmanirbhar.
points: Mentions Gandhi ji's message of becoming self-sufficient
Links spinning and weaving to making our own cloth
Says it became a symbol of the freedom struggle
Uses the idea of being atmanirbhar
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera's grandfather keeps silk moths on his farm. One morning, Meera sees a moth laying tiny eggs on a leaf. Her grandfather explains that the eggs will hatch into tiny caterpillars, which will eat mulberry leaves and grow big. Soon, each caterpillar will spin a cocoon around itself. Grandfather then collects the cocoons and puts them in hot water so the silk thread can be gently pulled out and made into thread for silk fabric.
activities.prompt: After the adult moth comes out of a cocoon, what will most likely happen on the farm next?
options: The moth will lay eggs and the cycle will begin again
The caterpillars will immediately spin new cocoons
The mulberry leaves will turn into silk thread
The cocoons will be woven into silk fabric directly

why.The caterpillars will immediately spin n: Cocoons come from caterpillars, which must hatch and grow first.
why.The mulberry leaves will turn into silk: Leaves are only food for caterpillars; they do not become thread.
why.The cocoons will be woven into silk fabr: Fabric is made from thread pulled out of cocoons, not from whole cocoons.

activities.explanation: Correct: the adult moth lays eggs, restarting the whole cycle.

activities.context: Meera's grandfather keeps silk moths on his farm. One morning, Meera sees a moth laying tiny eggs on a leaf. Her grandfather explains that the eggs will hatch into tiny caterpillars, which will eat mulberry leaves and grow big. Soon, each caterpillar will spin a cocoon around itself. Grandfather then collects the cocoons and puts them in hot water so the silk thread can be gently pulled out and made into thread for silk fabric.
activities.prompt: If the caterpillars on the farm could not get mulberry leaves, what would happen?
options: They would not grow big enough to spin proper cocoons
They would spin cocoons straight away without eating
They would turn into moths as soon as they hatched
They would make silk thread directly from their bodies

why.They would spin cocoons straight away wi: Cocoons are spun only after the caterpillars have grown big.
why.They would turn into moths as soon as th: Hatching gives caterpillars, not moths; growing must happen first.
why.They would make silk thread directly fro: Silk thread comes from cocoons after processing, not directly from bodies.

activities.explanation: Correct: caterpillars need mulberry leaves to eat and grow big before spinning cocoons.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between natural and synthetic fibres? Use jute and silk in your answer.
activities.answer: Natural fibres come from plants and animals, like jute, of which India is the largest producer in the world, and silk from moth cocoons. Synthetic fibres are made by humans using artificial materials. We all use things made from both natural and synthetic fibres in daily life.
points: Says synthetic fibres are made by humans using artificial materials
Gives jute as a natural fibre example
Mentions India is the largest producer of jute
States that we use things made from both kinds of fibres
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During her holidays in Gujarat, Anaya watches a weaver making a Patola saree on a handloom. The weaver says no electricity is used, and many families in the town depend on this work. Later, Anaya sees a tailorbird building a nest in the garden, stitching leaves with silk. At home, she learns the running stitch to join two cloth pieces.
activities.prompt: If the weaver's handloom were replaced by a machine that needs electricity, what would most likely happen to the families who depend on this work?
options: They would lose some work because the handloom supported them without electricity
They would earn more because Patola sarees would become simpler to make
They would start weaving Pashmina shawls instead of sarees
They would stop needing thread and needles for their work

why.They would earn more because Patola sare: Wrong: complexity of the Patola saree is not about machines, and no fact says earnings would rise
why.They would start weaving Pashmina shawls: Wrong: Pashmina comes from the Changthangi goat and is woven into shawls, not a swap for saree weaving
why.They would stop needing thread and needl: Wrong: stitching needs a needle and thread; a power change does not remove this need

activities.explanation: Correct: the passage says handloom weaving supports thousands of families and uses no electricity, so replacing it affects their livelihood

activities.context: During her holidays in Gujarat, Anaya watches a weaver making a Patola saree on a handloom. The weaver says no electricity is used, and many families in the town depend on this work. Later, Anaya sees a tailorbird building a nest in the garden, stitching leaves with silk. At home, she learns the running stitch to join two cloth pieces.
activities.prompt: The tailorbird in the garden cannot find spider silk. What will it most likely do to finish its nest?
options: Use plant fibres as thread instead
Ask the weaver for leftover saree thread
Weave its nest on the handloom like a Patola saree
Tie-dye the leaves using Bandhani before stitching

why.Ask the weaver for leftover saree thread: Wrong: the bird uses natural threads like silk or plant fibres, not saree thread from people
why.Weave its nest on the handloom like a Pa: Wrong: the bird stitches its own nest; a handloom is used by people for weaving fabric
why.Tie-dye the leaves using Bandhani before: Wrong: Bandhani is a tie-dye done by people on fabric, not something a bird does to leaves

activities.explanation: Correct: the tailorbird uses plant fibres OR spider silk, so it can switch to the other thread

activities.context: During her holidays in Gujarat, Anaya watches a weaver making a Patola saree on a handloom. The weaver says no electricity is used, and many families in the town depend on this work. Later, Anaya sees a tailorbird building a nest in the garden, stitching leaves with silk. At home, she learns the running stitch to join two cloth pieces.
activities.prompt: Anaya's first attempt at the running stitch looks messy because her needle goes up and down in a zigzag, not in a line. What should she change?
options: Keep the up, down, up, down movement in a straight line
Spin and weave the cloth herself before stitching
Join small pieces like a quilt instead of two pieces
Use wool from the Changthangi goat as her thread

why.Spin and weave the cloth herself before: Wrong: hand-spinning and weaving is how Pashmina shawls are made, not how to fix a stitch
why.Join small pieces like a quilt instead o: Wrong: quilt-making is about joining small pieces, not about the direction of the stitch
why.Use wool from the Changthangi goat as he: Wrong: Pashmina wool is for soft shawls; ordinary stitching uses normal thread

activities.explanation: Correct: the running stitch is made by going up, down, up, down in a straight line, so the line is what she must fix

activities.prompt: Explain why handloom weaving is helpful for families in villages and towns.
activities.answer: Handloom weaving gives work to thousands of families, so they can earn a living from it. It also uses no electricity, which means weavers do not have to spend money on power and can keep weaving even where electricity is not available.
points: Says it supports/gives work to thousands of families
Says it uses no electricity
Links no electricity to saving money or working anywhere
Answer written in the student's own words
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Clothes — How Things are Made

activities.prompt: The male baya weaverbird builds a hanging nest from grass. What shape is the nest?
options: Shaped like a pouch
Shaped like a cup
Shaped like a ball
activities.explanation: The weaverbird hangs its pouch-shaped nest from a branch. Weaving strands over and under makes it strong.

activities.prompt: The tailorbird uses plant fibres or spider silk as thread to stitch its nest.
activities.explanation: Well done! This tiny green bird stitches its own nest just like a tailor.

activities.prompt: Twisting cotton fibres together to make thread or yarn is called ______.
activities.hint: Think of what a spinning wheel helps us do.
activities.explanation: Spinning twists soft cotton fibres into one strong thread. A charkha helps to spin thread from cotton.

activities.prompt: Match each weaving tradition to its home.
activities.explanation: India has many handloom traditions, each with its own special techniques and patterns.

activities.prompt: Put the story of the silk moth in the right order.
items: Silk moth lays eggs
Eggs hatch into tiny caterpillars
Caterpillars eat mulberry leaves and grow big
Caterpillars spin cocoons around themselves
Adult moth comes out of the cocoon
activities.explanation: The silk moth's life moves in a circle, and the cycle begins again.

activities.prompt: Jute is a natural material used for weaving. What is India's place in the world for jute?
options: Largest producer
Smallest producer
Second largest producer
activities.explanation: India is the largest producer of jute in the world. Jute is one of the natural materials people weave.

activities.prompt: Handloom weaving needs a lot of electricity to run.
activities.explanation: Handloom weaving uses no electricity at all. It still supports thousands of families.

activities.prompt: Indian muslin was woven so finely that people called it 'woven ______'.
activities.hint: It was so light and fine, it felt like nothing at all.
activities.explanation: Muslin was so fine that a whole saree could pass through a ring. What amazing skill!

activities.prompt: You are stitching fabric with a running stitch. How do you move your needle?
options: Up, down, up, down in a straight line
Round and round in a circle
Side to side across the fabric
activities.explanation: A running stitch goes up, down, up, down in a straight line. Different parts of India use many different stitches.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of weaving in the right order, from start to finished fabric.
items: One set of thread is placed vertically
The other set of thread goes horizontally
Threads are crossed over and under each other
The crossing forms a unified fabric
activities.explanation: Weaving combines strips or threads into patterned fabric like cloth, a mat or a basket.

chapters.title: Rhythms of Nature
chapters.summary: In this chapter: changes around us; day and night; the globe and seasons' journal; seasons' chart.

lessons.title: Changes Around Us

activities.prompt: What things around you change every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Everything Changes!
activities.body: Saba and Aparna met after a long time. Aparna had grown taller and cut her hair short. Saba had started learning the guitar. Changes happen to us and to the world all the time. Some changes take years, like growing taller. Some happen in days or minutes, like the sky changing colour. Day turns into night, and night becomes day again.
keyPoints: Changes happen to us and the world all the time.
Some changes take years, some take days or minutes.
Day changes into night, and night becomes day.
activities.explanation: Look around you: people, trees, flowers and the sky are always changing.

activities.prompt: Saba met Aparna after a long time. Saba almost did not know her friend. Why did Aparna look so different?
steps: The two friends met after a long time, so many days and years passed.
Aparna had become taller, and her long hair was now short.
Changes happen to us all the time, so her body and hair slowly changed.
So Aparna looked different because many small changes added up over the years.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: When Saba and Aparna met after a long time, what did they do?
options: They embraced each other
They waved and walked away
They played a board game
They read a book together
activities.explanation: The two friends were happy to meet, so they embraced each other warmly.

activities.prompt: Saba had started learning to play the ______.
activities.hint: It is a musical instrument with strings.
activities.explanation: Saba had picked up a new skill, learning the guitar. That is a change too!

activities.prompt: Some changes take years. What kind of change is this?
options: You grow taller each year
The sky changes colour
The sun appears to set
Flowers bloom in the morning
activities.explanation: Growing taller happens slowly, over years. The other changes happen much faster.

activities.prompt: Match each change with what happens.
pairs: Fall off trees and grow again
Bloom, dry up and bloom again
activities.explanation: Nature is full of changes that happen again and again.

activities.prompt: Put these in order, starting with the day.
items: The day shines bright
The day changes into night
The night grows dark
Night becomes day again
activities.explanation: Day and night follow each other in a circle that never stops.

activities.prompt: Saba and Aparna talked about their old classroom, favourite games and new trees. What does this show about their school?
options: Many things there had changed
Nothing there had changed
The school had closed down
They had never studied there
activities.explanation: They remembered old things and saw new trees, so their school had changed over time.

activities.prompt: Ravi sees his cousin after two years. The cousin looks taller now. Why did the cousin look taller?
options: The cousin grew a little taller each year.
The cousin wore shoes with tall heels.
Ravi became shorter in those two years.
The cousin's hair grew longer and thicker.

Wrong: thinks clothes or shoes, not the body, cause the change.
Wrong: thinks the other person changed instead of the one who grew.
why.The cousin's hair grew longer and thicke: Wrong: mixes up hair growing with the body growing taller.

activities.explanation: Right: you grow taller each year, so two years of growing added up.

activities.prompt: Some changes are fast and some are slow. Leaves fall off trees and grow again. You grow taller each year. Which change takes years to happen?
options: Leaves falling off a tree outside.
The sky changing its colour in a day.
You growing taller than last year.
A flower drying up on a plant.

Wrong: thinks falling leaves are slow, but it happens in days.
Wrong: thinks the sky changes slowly, but it can change in minutes.
Wrong: thinks drying up is slow, but it happens in days.

activities.explanation: Right: growing taller happens little by little over each whole year.

activities.prompt: A boy says the sky stays one colour all day. He looks at the sky in the morning, noon and evening. What will he most likely see?
options: The sky looks the same at all three times.
The sky changes its colour by the evening.
The sky turns dark right at noon.
The sky disappears when the sun sets.

why.The sky looks the same at all three time: Wrong: believes his claim is right and does not expect a change.
Wrong: thinks the sky changes at the wrong time of day.
Wrong: thinks the sky vanishes instead of changing colour.

activities.explanation: Right: the sky changes colour, so evening will look different.

activities.prompt: Anu says nothing changes around her. Her house looks the same every day. What is the flaw in her thinking?
options: She forgot that she herself is growing taller.
She forgot that only houses can change.
She forgot that changes stop when it is night.
She forgot that changes happen only in school.

Wrong: thinks change belongs to one thing only, not everything.
why.She forgot that changes stop when it is: Wrong: thinks changes take a break at night, but they never stop.
why.She forgot that changes happen only in s: Wrong: thinks changes happen only in one place, not everywhere.

activities.explanation: Right: changes happen to us all the time, and she is growing too.

activities.prompt: It is evening. The sun looks like it is going down. What will happen next?
options: Night will come, and day will come after it.
The sun will stop moving in the sky.
The day will stay bright for many more hours.
Morning will come right away without night.

Wrong: thinks the sun can stop, but it appears to set every day.
why.The day will stay bright for many more h: Wrong: thinks the day will not end, but day always changes into night.
why.Morning will come right away without nig: Wrong: skips the night, but night must become day first.

activities.explanation: Right: the sun appears to set, then day changes into night and night becomes day.

activities.prompt: A girl sees a dry flower on a plant. She says the plant will never have flowers again. What is the flaw in her thinking?
options: She forgot that flowers can bloom again later.
She forgot that flowers never dry up at all.
She forgot that the plant can walk away.
She forgot that only new plants make flowers.

why.She forgot that flowers never dry up at: Wrong: thinks drying up never happens, but it is a normal change.
Wrong: thinks the plant must move, which plants cannot do.
why.She forgot that only new plants make flo: Wrong: thinks only brand new plants can bloom, not the same plant.

activities.explanation: Right: flowers bloom, dry up and bloom again, so new flowers will come.

lessons.title: Day and Night

activities.prompt: Why does the sun seem to go away every night?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why do we have day and night?
activities.body: Imagine a game where one friend is the Sun and another is the Earth. The Sun stands still at the centre. The Earth stays in one spot but slowly turns around. When the Earth faces the Sun, it is day. When the Earth turns away and cannot see the Sun, it is night. So day and night happen because the Earth rotates, not because the Sun moves.
keyPoints: The Sun stays in one place.
The Earth rotates, or turns around slowly.
The side of the Earth facing the Sun has day.
The side of the Earth away from the Sun has night.
activities.explanation: Day and night come from the Earth turning, while the Sun stays still.

activities.title: Spin the Earth

tasks.then: Your place has turned away from the Sun.
At sunrise your place is turning into the sunlight.

activities.takeaway: The Earth spins once a day, so each place turns into the sunlight and out of it again.
activities.explanation: The Earth spins once a day, so each place turns into the sunlight and out of it again.

activities.prompt: Meera shines a torch on a globe. She turns the globe slowly. Her friend says the torch must walk around the globe to make night. Is her friend right?
steps: The torch light is like the Sun, so it must stay still.
The globe is like the Earth, so the globe is the thing that turns.
When a side turns away from the light, that side gets night.
So the friend is wrong; the globe turns, not the torch.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In the game, which friend stays in one place at the centre?
options: The Sun
The Earth
The Moon
The torch
activities.explanation: The Sun stands at the centre and does not move. It is the Earth that turns.

activities.prompt: When the Earth can see the Sun, the children in the game say ______.
activities.hint: It is the bright time, not the dark time.
activities.explanation: Seeing the Sun means it is day for that side of the Earth.

activities.prompt: In the game, when do the children say 'night'?
options: When the Earth stops seeing the Sun
When the Earth sees the Sun
When the Sun starts moving
When the Earth stands still
activities.explanation: Night is when the Earth has turned away and can no longer see the Sun.

activities.prompt: Match each thing in the model to what it stands for.
activities.explanation: A torch and globe can show day and night. Light means day, and darkness means night.

activities.prompt: A place on the globe has no torchlight falling on it. Is it day or night there, and why?
options: Night, because no light falls there
Day, because the globe is turning
Night, because the torch has moved away
Day, because the globe is bright
activities.explanation: The side with no light has night. Light falling on a side makes it day.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the day and night game in the right order.
items: One student acts as the Sun and stands at the centre
Another student acts as the Earth and stands in one place
The Earth student slowly turns around
The Earth sees the Sun and says day
The Earth stops seeing the Sun and says night
activities.explanation: First set up the Sun and Earth, then turn the Earth. Facing the Sun gives day, and turning away gives night.

activities.prompt: A torch shines on a globe. The light side has day. The dark side has night. You turn the globe slowly. What happens to the night side?
options: It gets day when it turns to face the torch.
It stays night because the torch never moves.
It gets day only when the torch moves to it.
It gets brighter but never gets day.

why.It stays night because the torch never m: Thinks the globe stops mattering once it is dark.
why.It gets day only when the torch moves to: Thinks the torch must move, but the torch stays steady.
Confuses getting brighter with getting day from the light.

activities.explanation: Right: when the turning side faces the light, that side gets day.

activities.prompt: A torch and globe can show day and night. The torchlight is the Sun. Two friends try it. Who shows day and night the right way?
options: Anu keeps the torch steady and turns the globe slowly.
Bala moves the torch around and keeps the globe still.
Chotu turns the globe fast and moves the torch too.
Diya turns off the torch and spins the globe quickly.

why.Bala moves the torch around and keeps th: Moves the torch instead of the globe, so it is done wrongly.
why.Chotu turns the globe fast and moves the: Moves both, but the torch must stay steady and the turn is slow.
why.Diya turns off the torch and spins the g: No light means no day side to see at all.

activities.explanation: Right: the torch stays steady and the globe is slowly rotated.

activities.prompt: Ravi says the Sun moves around the Earth. He says that is why we get night. What is wrong with Ravi's claim?
options: Night comes when the Earth stops seeing the Sun.
Night comes only when the Sun hides behind clouds.
The Sun stays in one place; the Earth rotates instead.
Night comes when the torch light gets very weak.

why.Night comes when the Earth stops seeing: Right: night is when the turning Earth no longer sees the Sun.
why.Night comes only when the Sun hides behi: Thinks clouds make night, but night is about seeing the Sun.
why.Night comes when the torch light gets ve: Mixes up the torch game with the real Sun and Earth.

activities.explanation: Right: the Sun stays in one place; it is the Earth that rotates.

activities.prompt: In the game, the Earth student cannot see the Sun student. She says night. She keeps standing in one place. What should she do to say day again?
options: Walk over to stand in front of the Sun student.
Ask the Sun student to come and face her.
Keep turning slowly until she sees the Sun again.
Stop turning and wait for the Sun to come to her.

why.Walk over to stand in front of the Sun s: The Earth student must stay in one place and turn.
why.Ask the Sun student to come and face her: The Sun student stands still at the centre.
why.Stop turning and wait for the Sun to com: Waiting will not help; she must turn to see the Sun.

activities.explanation: Right: she says day when she sees the Sun while turning.

lessons.title: The Globe and Seasons' Journal

activities.prompt: Why do farmers in Odisha listen to the koel's song for rain?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a globe?
activities.body: A globe is a model of the Earth. It is shaped like a ball, just like the real Earth. On the globe, the blue parts are seas and oceans. Seas and oceans cover about three-fourths of the Earth. The remaining parts are land masses. Countries are on the land masses. Seas are usually smaller than oceans and partly enclosed by land. Oceans are vast and open water bodies.
keyPoints: A globe is a model shaped like a ball, just like the Earth.
Blue parts are seas and oceans; they cover about three-fourths of the Earth.
The remaining parts are land masses, and countries are on them.
activities.explanation: The globe is a small ball-shaped copy of our big Earth.

activities.title: Go round the Sun

tasks.then: Now the southern half leans toward the Sun: summer there, winter in India.

activities.takeaway: The tilted Earth leans each half toward the Sun in turn, which makes the seasons.
activities.explanation: The tilted Earth leans each half toward the Sun in turn, which makes the seasons.

activities.prompt: Anu looks at her school globe. She sees much more blue than any other colour. She asks why the globe has so much blue on it.
steps: The blue parts of a globe show seas and oceans.
Seas and oceans cover about three-fourths of the Earth.
So water takes up much more space than the land masses.
That is why the globe shows much more blue than land colours.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The seasons' journal
activities.body: Saba and Aparna sit in the school garden, looking at their seasons' journal. All year, they have looked closely at the world around them. They record what they see in their journal. In Odisha, when the koel sings, farmers know rains are coming. Watching nature helps us learn!
keyPoints: Saba and Aparna keep a seasons' journal.
They look closely at the world and record their observations.
In Odisha, the koel's song tells farmers that rains are coming.
activities.explanation: Careful watching, like Saba and Aparna's, helps us understand nature.

activities.prompt: Seas and oceans cover about ______ of the Earth.
activities.hint: Think of a chapati cut into four pieces, and how much is water.
activities.explanation: Water covers about three-fourths of the Earth. That is why the globe looks mostly blue!

activities.prompt: The globe is shaped like a ball, just like the real Earth.
activities.explanation: Yes! Both the globe and the Earth are ball-shaped.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it is like.
pairs: Smaller and partly enclosed by land
activities.explanation: Great matching! You know the water parts and land parts of the globe.

activities.prompt: Ravi says a sea and an ocean are the same size. What does the lesson tell you?
options: Seas are usually smaller than oceans
Oceans are usually smaller than seas
Seas and oceans are always the same size
Globes do not show seas or oceans
activities.explanation: Seas are usually smaller than oceans and partly enclosed by land. Oceans are vast and open.

activities.prompt: Put the children's journal work in order, from first to last.
items: Look closely at the world around them over the year
Record their observations in the journal
Sit in the garden and look back at the journal
activities.explanation: First you watch, then you write it down, then you can look back at your notes. Lovely work!

activities.prompt: A globe has blue paint and other colours. Blue paint shows seas and oceans. Oceans cover most of the Earth. Meera sees more blue than any other colour. Why is there more blue on the globe?
options: Because seas and oceans cover most of the Earth.
Because children like the colour blue the most.
Because the land masses are painted blue also.
Because the globe maker had only blue paint.

why.Because children like the colour blue th: Thinks the globe is painted to look pretty, not to show real water.
why.Because the land masses are painted blue: Thinks all parts of a globe can be any colour, so land may be blue too.
why.Because the globe maker had only blue pa: Thinks the globe shows the maker's choice, not the real Earth.

activities.explanation: Right. Water covers three-fourths of the Earth, so blue covers most of the globe.

activities.prompt: Look at two water bodies on a map. One is small. Land is around much of it. One is very big and open. Which one is the ocean?
options: The big and open water body.
The small one with land around it.
The small one, because land makes water big.
The big one, because land is around it.

Confuses sea and ocean; a partly enclosed water body is a sea.
why.The small one, because land makes water: Thinks land around water makes it an ocean, which is backwards.
Mixes up the two; land around water points to a sea, not an ocean.

activities.explanation: Right. Oceans are vast and open water bodies.

activities.prompt: In Odisha, the koel sings a sweet song. Farmers hear the koel and smile. Rains will come soon. Why do the farmers smile?
options: The koel's song tells them rains are coming.
The koel's song tells them the rains are over.
The koel's song tells them the cold days came.
The koel's song tells them the harvest is done.

why.The koel's song tells them the rains are: Gets the time wrong; the song comes before the rains, not after.
why.The koel's song tells them the cold days: Mixes up seasons; the koel's song is about rains, not cold days.
why.The koel's song tells them the harvest i: Thinks the song is about the end of farming, not rain coming.

activities.explanation: Right. When the koel sings, farmers know rains are coming.

activities.prompt: Saba and Aparna watch the world all year. They write what they see in a journal. Anu says, 'Do not write. Just remember everything.' What is wrong with Anu's idea?
options: Writing helps them look back at what they saw.
A journal is only for marks at school.
Remembering is easy, so writing wastes time.
Only the teacher should write in a journal.

Thinks a journal is for marks, not for recording what children observe.
why.Remembering is easy, so writing wastes t: Thinks memory is enough, but a journal keeps observations safe.
why.Only the teacher should write in a journ: Thinks journals belong to teachers, not to children who observe.

activities.explanation: Right. The journal records observations, so children can look back over the year.

lessons.title: Seasons' Chart

activities.prompt: How can we see all the changes in our seasons on one big chart?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Our Big Seasons' Chart
activities.body: Your class makes a big wall-sized chart of the seasons. Time periods go in columns, and themes like water and water bodies go in rows. For each box, one student asks the class for observations. Everyone shares what they wrote in their journals. Together you discuss and write the main observations on the chart. This helps you see patterns of change in nature.
keyPoints: A large wall-sized chart is prepared in the classroom.
Time periods are in columns and themes are in rows.
Students share journal observations, discuss, and write them on the chart.
activities.explanation: The chart brings everyone's learning together in one big picture.

activities.title: Go round the Sun

tasks.then: Now the southern half leans toward the Sun: summer there, winter in India.

activities.takeaway: The tilted Earth leans each half toward the Sun in turn, which makes the seasons.
activities.explanation: The tilted Earth leans each half toward the Sun in turn, which makes the seasons.

activities.prompt: Meera's class wants to show how the pond changed over the whole year. But there are many observations and only one wall. How can they show everything clearly?
steps: The class has many journals, so they need one big place to put all the observations together, because learning from many children is stronger than one child's notes alone.
A large wall-sized chart can hold everything, because it is big enough for the whole class to see and use together.
The year has different time periods, so putting time in columns lets them compare the same thing across the year.
They watch water, plants, animals, sunlight and people, so listing these themes in rows keeps each kind of observation in its own line.
So a chart with time in columns and themes in rows lets the whole class see the patterns of change clearly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: On the seasons' chart, what is written in the columns?
options: The names of students
The themes
The time periods
The page numbers
activities.explanation: Well done! The chart has time periods in columns, so you can follow the changes across the year.

activities.prompt: The chart notes the observations that students have written in their ______.
activities.hint: Think of the little notebook you write your observations in.
activities.explanation: Yes! Your journal observations are what go onto the big chart.

activities.prompt: Which of these is one of the themes on the seasons' chart?
options: Water and water bodies
Famous cricket players
Names of colours
Types of school bags
activities.explanation: Correct! Water and water bodies is one of the themes listed in the rows.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it means on the seasons' chart.
pairs: One student asks the class for observations
activities.explanation: Great matching! You know how the chart is set out.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for filling a box on the chart in the right order.
items: One student asks the class for observations
Students share observations from their journals
Everyone discusses the observations
The main observations are written on the chart
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First you ask, then you share, then you discuss, and finally you write.

activities.prompt: Why do children observe nature and make a seasons' chart like this?
options: To understand patterns of change
To keep the classroom walls busy
To have a test every single day
To make the journals look pretty
activities.explanation: Exactly! By bringing your learning together, you can see the patterns of change in nature.

activities.prompt: Ravi wrote in his journal: 'The pond was full in July.' The class is filling the chart box for July under the water row. What should Ravi do?
options: Keep his journal closed and let others talk only
Share his pond observation from his journal with the class
Write his observation on the chart without telling anyone
Wait for the teacher to read his journal to the class

why.Keep his journal closed and let others t: Hiding his notes wastes his own careful work and helps no one.
why.Write his observation on the chart witho: Writing alone skips the discussion where the class picks the main observations.
why.Wait for the teacher to read his journal: Waiting makes the teacher do the sharing that students should do.

activities.explanation: Right. Students share observations from their journals when a box is being filled.

activities.prompt: Two students give different observations for the same box. Anya says the stream was wide. Dev says it was narrow. What should the class do before writing on the chart?
options: Write both observations in the box without talking
Write Anya's words, because she spoke first
Discuss both observations and write the main one
Leave the box empty, because the class cannot agree

why.Write both observations in the box witho: Writing both without talking fills the box but skips the thinking step.
why.Write Anya's words, because she spoke fi: Speaking first does not make an observation the main one.
why.Leave the box empty, because the class c: An empty box throws away good observations instead of sorting them.

activities.explanation: Right. They discuss and write main observations on the chart.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'We can skip the chart and just keep our journals shut in our bags.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Journals in bags get lost more easily than charts
The chart is bigger, so it needs less writing
Shut journals cannot be shared, so the class cannot see patterns together
The chart is only for the teacher, not for students

why.Journals in bags get lost more easily th: Losing journals is a worry, but it is not the main flaw in the claim.
why.The chart is bigger, so it needs less wr: Size is not the reason; the chart's job is bringing observations together.
why.The chart is only for the teacher, not f: Students ask for and write observations, so the chart is for everyone.

activities.explanation: Right. The chart brings everyone's learning together to see patterns of change.

activities.prompt: The chart is finished. A student says: 'The water row shows the pond was full in the rainy time and low in the hot time.' What does this show about the chart?
options: The chart shows patterns of change across time periods
The chart shows which student wrote the best journal
The chart shows that water stays the same all year
The chart shows that only water themes can be listed

why.The chart shows which student wrote the: The chart is about observations, not a contest between students.
why.The chart shows that water stays the sam: The row shows water changing, so it does not stay the same.
why.The chart shows that only water themes c: Water is one theme; other themes like plants and animals are rows too.

activities.explanation: Right. Reading across time periods shows how things change, which is the chart's purpose.

lessons.title: Discovering Seasons and Six Seasons

activities.prompt: Why does the same sky change its mood every few months?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Are Seasons?
activities.body: Nature changes slowly over the year. The weather warms up, gets hot and then it rains. These changes follow a pattern that repeats every year. This repeating pattern is called seasons. India has six seasons, based on how nature changes.
keyPoints: Nature changes slowly through the year.
The repeating pattern of change is called seasons.
India has six seasons.
activities.explanation: Seasons are nature's yearly pattern of change.

activities.prompt: Meera's grandmother says, 'The days are getting very hot. Rain will come soon.' Why is grandmother right?
steps: Nature changes slowly, so hot days do not come all of a sudden.
The weather warms up, then gets hot, and then it rains.
This order happens again and again every year, so grandmother has seen it many times.
So the hot days are a sign that rain is coming next.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The repeating pattern of change in nature is called what?
options: Seasons
Monsoon
Desert
activities.explanation: Well done! The yearly repeating pattern in nature is called seasons.

activities.prompt: Mawsynram, the wettest place on Earth, is in ______.
activities.hint: It is a state in north-east India.
activities.explanation: Great! Mawsynram is in Meghalaya.

activities.prompt: Nature changes slowly over the year.
activities.explanation: Yes! Nature changes slowly, not all at once.

activities.prompt: Which shows the correct order of how the weather changes?
options: Hot, then warms up, then rains
Warms up, then gets hot, then rains
Rains, then gets hot, then warms up
activities.explanation: Correct! The weather warms up, gets hot and then it rains.

activities.prompt: Put the weather changes in the correct order.
items: The weather warms up
The weather gets hot
Then it rains
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Warm, then hot, then rain.

activities.prompt: Why do snakes come out of their burrows during monsoon?
options: Their burrows get flooded
They want to find the sun
They come out to celebrate
activities.explanation: Yes! Flooded burrows make snakes come out during monsoon.

activities.prompt: Ravi waters his garden every morning. For many days the weather gets hotter and hotter. What will most likely happen next?
options: It will keep getting hotter forever
Rain will come after the hot days
Snow will fall on his garden
The weather will become cold at once

why.It will keep getting hotter forever: Thinks the pattern stops, but the pattern repeats every year.
why.Snow will fall on his garden: Thinks hot weather brings snow, but snow is not part of this pattern.
why.The weather will become cold at once: Thinks weather jumps to cold, but changes come slowly in order.

activities.explanation: Right: the weather warms up, gets hot, and then it rains.

activities.prompt: One day it rained heavily in the Thar Desert. Suresh says, 'The Thar Desert is the wettest place on Earth.' What is wrong with his claim?
options: Nothing is wrong, one rainy day proves it
One rainy day does not make a place the wettest
Rain in a desert is not real rain at all
The wettest place is the one with the most sand

why.Nothing is wrong, one rainy day proves i: Thinks one day of rain decides everything, but it does not.
why.Rain in a desert is not real rain at all: Thinks desert rain is not real, but rain is rain anywhere.
why.The wettest place is the one with the mo: Thinks sand makes a place wet, which makes no sense.

activities.explanation: Right: Mawsynram is the wettest place, and the Thar is one of the driest.

activities.prompt: Every monsoon, snakes leave their flooded burrows. Around this time people celebrate Nag Panchami. Why did this festival grow near this time?
options: Because snakes are asleep and cannot be seen then
Because snakes come out more, so people show respect
Because the festival makes the rain stop falling
Because snakes like to dance during the festival

why.Because snakes are asleep and cannot be: Thinks snakes are hidden then, but floods bring them out.
why.Because the festival makes the rain stop: Thinks the festival controls rain, but it shows respect instead.
why.Because snakes like to dance during the: Thinks snakes dance, which is not why the festival came.

activities.explanation: Right: snakes come out of flooded burrows, and Nag Panchami shows respect to nature and reptiles.

lessons.sceneCaption: Dunes in the Thar Desert, one of the driest places in India.

lessons.title: Celebrating Seasons and Seasons Shape Life

activities.prompt: Why do our festivals and favourite foods change with the seasons?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Seasons Shape Our Lives
activities.body: Seasons are not just changes in weather. They shape everything around us. Farmers grow different crops in different seasons. Many of our festivals are connected with seasons too. Holi comes in spring, and Diwali comes in autumn. Every season brings something special and has its own magic.
keyPoints: Seasons shape everything around us.
Farmers grow different crops in different seasons.
Many festivals are connected with seasons.
Every season has its own magic.
activities.explanation: Seasons touch our food, our festivals and our songs.

activities.prompt: A farmer has seeds that need lots of water. The sky is dry and hot. His friend says, 'Wait for the rains.' Why is his friend right?
steps: The seeds need more water to grow, so dry soil cannot feed them.
The rainy season brings lots of water, so the soil stays wet.
If he plants in the heat, the little water will dry up fast.
So waiting for the rains gives the seeds the water they need.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Holi is celebrated when flowers bloom. In which season is Holi?
options: Winter
Spring
Autumn
activities.explanation: Holi is celebrated in spring, when flowers bloom. A colourful time for a colourful festival!

activities.prompt: Pongal and Makar Sankranti are new year and ______ festivals.
activities.hint: Think of the time when crops are gathered from the fields.
activities.explanation: Pongal and Makar Sankranti celebrate the new year and the harvest.

activities.prompt: Some crops are planted in the rainy season. Why?
options: They need more water to grow.
They need less light to grow.
They need cooler nights to grow.
activities.explanation: These crops need more water, so the rainy season suits them best.

activities.prompt: Match each festival to its season.
activities.explanation: Holi comes in spring, Diwali in autumn, and Pongal celebrates the harvest.

activities.prompt: Why do farmers grow different crops in different seasons?
options: Because each crop grows best in its own season.
Because farmers like to keep changing crops.
Because markets close in some seasons.
activities.explanation: Each crop has its own season. Some like winter, some like summer heat, some need rain.

activities.prompt: The lesson says seasons are not just changes in weather. What else do they do?
options: They shape everything around us.
They only change the temperature.
They happen only in some places.
activities.explanation: Seasons shape everything around us, from crops to festivals. Every season has its own magic!

activities.prompt: A farmer has seeds that need lots of water to grow. It has not rained for many days. When should he plant the seeds?
options: Right after rain, so the soil has plenty of water
On the hottest day, so the strong sun helps them
In the driest week, so the seeds do not get wet
Any day he likes, because water does not matter

why.On the hottest day, so the strong sun he: This confuses heat helping some crops with water helping these seeds.
why.In the driest week, so the seeds do not: This thinks dry soil is good, but these seeds need more water.
why.Any day he likes, because water does not: This forgets that some crops are planted in the rainy season.

activities.explanation: Right. Rainy season crops need more water, so planting after rain helps.

activities.prompt: Meena plants a crop that grows best in winter. She plants it in the hot summer. What will happen and why?
options: It will grow well, because all crops love strong sunshine
It will grow badly, because it likes the cold best
It will grow the same, because seeds do not care about seasons
It will grow faster, because heat makes every plant grow tall

why.It will grow well, because all crops lov: This thinks sun is always good, but this crop likes winter best.
why.It will grow the same, because seeds do: This forgets that farmers grow different crops in different seasons.
why.It will grow faster, because heat makes: This thinks heat is always good, but this crop likes the cold.

activities.explanation: Right. Some crops grow best in winter, so summer heat is wrong for them.

activities.prompt: Dev says, 'Seasons only change the weather and nothing else.' What is wrong with his claim?
options: He is right, because weather is the only thing that changes
Seasons also shape crops and festivals, not just weather
He is wrong, because seasons change nothing at all around us
He is wrong, because weather and seasons are the same thing

why.He is right, because weather is the only: This agrees with the claim, but seasons shape more than weather.
why.He is wrong, because seasons change noth: This goes too far; seasons do change the weather too.
why.He is wrong, because weather and seasons: This confuses two ideas instead of finding the real mistake.

activities.explanation: Right. Seasons shape crops, festivals and songs, not just weather.
