activities.context: Saba and Aparna met after a long time and embraced happily. Aparna had become taller, and her hair was short. Saba had started learning to play the guitar. The friends talked about their old classroom, their favourite games, and the new trees near school. They noticed that changes happen to us and the world all the time — some take years, while some happen in days or minutes.
activities.prompt: If Saba and Aparna meet again after one more year, what will most likely have happened?
options: Aparna will have grown even taller than she is now
Aparna will have become shorter than she was
Saba will have completely forgotten how to play the guitar
The new trees near the school will have stopped growing

why.Aparna will have become shorter than she: Wrong — the lesson says you grow taller each year, never shorter
why.Saba will have completely forgotten how: Wrong — nothing in the case suggests Saba would forget; she had only just started learning
why.The new trees near the school will have: Wrong — trees are like leaves and flowers; they grow and change, they do not stop

activities.explanation: Correct — a person grows taller each year, so another year means more growth

activities.context: Saba and Aparna met after a long time and embraced happily. Aparna had become taller, and her hair was short. Saba had started learning to play the guitar. The friends talked about their old classroom, their favourite games, and the new trees near school. They noticed that changes happen to us and the world all the time — some take years, while some happen in days or minutes.
activities.prompt: Why did the two friends notice so many changes when they met again?
options: Because things around them had kept changing ever since they last met
Because changes only begin when two friends meet after a long time
Because Saba's guitar playing stopped everything else from changing
Because the old classroom and the games had stayed exactly the same

why.Because changes only begin when two frie: Wrong — changes happen all the time, not only when friends meet
why.Because Saba's guitar playing stopped ev: Wrong — learning the guitar is one change in Saba; it does not control other changes
why.Because the old classroom and the games: Wrong — they talked about the classroom and games because they remembered them, not because nothing had changed

activities.explanation: Correct — changes happen to us and the world all the time, so much had changed since they last met

activities.context: Saba and Aparna met after a long time and embraced happily. Aparna had become taller, and her hair was short. Saba had started learning to play the guitar. The friends talked about their old classroom, their favourite games, and the new trees near school. They noticed that changes happen to us and the world all the time — some take years, while some happen in days or minutes.
activities.prompt: Aparna wants to see for herself that the sky keeps changing. What should she do?
options: Look at the sky at different times, from morning until night
Look at the sky only once, at exactly noon
Look at the sky only on one day of the year
Keep her eyes on the ground all day instead of the sky

why.Look at the sky only once, at exactly no: Wrong — one look at noon would show only one moment, not the changes
why.Look at the sky only on one day of the y: Wrong — the sun appears to rise and set every day, so one day a year would miss the daily changes
why.Keep her eyes on the ground all day inst: Wrong — she cannot observe the sky by looking away from it

activities.explanation: Correct — the sky changes colour and day becomes night, so watching through the whole day shows the changes

activities.prompt: How does day change into night and then become day again?
activities.answer: The sun appears to rise every day and then appears to set. When the sun sets, the day changes into night. When the sun appears to rise again the next morning, the night becomes day. This happens every day, so the change keeps repeating.
points: Mentions the sun appearing to rise
Mentions the sun appearing to set
Says day changes into night after the sun sets
Says night becomes day when the sun rises again
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a dark classroom, Riya holds a torch steady while Aarav slowly turns a globe in front of it. Riya keeps the torch pointed at the globe the whole time and does not walk around it. Aarav notices that only the half of the globe facing the torch is lit, while the other half stays dark. He sticks a small paper dot on one side of the globe and keeps turning it slowly.
activities.prompt: What will Aarav see happen to the paper dot as he keeps turning the globe?
options: It will stay in the light the whole time because the torch is steady
It will move into the dark part and later come back into the light
It will fall off because the globe is turning too fast
It will glow on its own once the torch has touched it

why.It will stay in the light the whole time: Wrong: as the globe turns, the dot cannot stay facing the torch forever
why.It will fall off because the globe is tu: Wrong: nothing in the case says the globe is turned fast or that the dot comes loose
why.It will glow on its own once the torch h: Wrong: the dot is just paper; only the side facing the torch is lit

activities.explanation: Correct: the turning globe carries the dot from the lit side into the dark side and back again

activities.context: In a dark classroom, Riya holds a torch steady while Aarav slowly turns a globe in front of it. Riya keeps the torch pointed at the globe the whole time and does not walk around it. Aarav notices that only the half of the globe facing the torch is lit, while the other half stays dark. He sticks a small paper dot on one side of the globe and keeps turning it slowly.
activities.prompt: Aarav asks why he can never see the whole globe lit at the same time. What is the best answer?
options: Because the globe is too big for the classroom torch
Because the torch battery is getting weaker
Because the light reaches only the side turned towards the torch
Because the globe must be turned much more slowly

why.Because the globe is too big for the cla: Wrong: the size of the globe is not the reason one half stays dark
why.Because the torch battery is getting wea: Wrong: the case does not say the battery is weak, and a weak torch would not light exactly half
why.Because the globe must be turned much mo: Wrong: turning speed does not change how much of the globe is lit at one moment

activities.explanation: Correct: the torchlight falls only on the side facing it, so that side has day and the other side has night

activities.prompt: Explain why the student playing the Earth says 'day' when facing the Sun and 'night' when facing away.
activities.answer: The Sun stands at the centre and does not move. The Earth student stands in one place and slowly turns around. When the Earth student turns towards the Sun and sees it, that position shows day. When the turning takes the Sun out of view, that position shows night.
points: Sun stays at the centre in one place
Earth student turns around slowly in one spot
Seeing the Sun means day
Not seeing the Sun means night
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Saba and Aparna are sitting in the school garden with their seasons' journal. All year they have looked closely at the world around them and recorded what they noticed. Today they are spinning a globe, the model of the Earth shaped like a ball. Saba points at the blue parts, and Aparna traces the land masses where countries lie.
activities.prompt: Saba says the globe should be painted mostly green instead of blue. What would this wrongly show about the Earth?
options: That land covers most of the Earth
That there are no countries on the land masses
That seas are bigger than oceans
That oceans are partly enclosed by land

why.That there are no countries on the land: Countries are on the land masses, so painting it green would not remove countries.
why.That seas are bigger than oceans: Size of seas compared to oceans is about their area, not the globe's colour.
why.That oceans are partly enclosed by land: Enclosure by land describes seas, not what the globe's colour would show.

activities.explanation: Correct: seas and oceans cover about three-fourths of the Earth, so blue must cover most of the globe.

activities.context: Saba and Aparna are sitting in the school garden with their seasons' journal. All year they have looked closely at the world around them and recorded what they noticed. Today they are spinning a globe, the model of the Earth shaped like a ball. Saba points at the blue parts, and Aparna traces the land masses where countries lie.
activities.prompt: Aparna marks a water body on the globe that is small and almost surrounded by land. What should she label it, and why?
options: A sea, because seas are usually smaller and partly enclosed by land
An ocean, because oceans are the water bodies near land
A land mass, because land surrounds it
A country, because countries are marked on the globe

why.An ocean, because oceans are the water b: Oceans are vast and open, not small and partly enclosed.
why.A land mass, because land surrounds it: The water body is water, not land, so it cannot be a land mass.
why.A country, because countries are marked: Countries lie on land masses, not on water bodies.

activities.explanation: Correct: small size and being partly enclosed by land are the clues for a sea.

activities.context: Saba and Aparna are sitting in the school garden with their seasons' journal. All year they have looked closely at the world around them and recorded what they noticed. Today they are spinning a globe, the model of the Earth shaped like a ball. Saba points at the blue parts, and Aparna traces the land masses where countries lie.
activities.prompt: In their journal, the children once recorded that in Odisha farmers listen for the koel's song. A farmer hears the koel singing this morning. What is he most likely to expect, and what should he do?
options: Expect rains soon and get his farm ready for them
Expect dry days and store extra water for irrigation
Expect the koel to stop singing and wait for another sign
Expect the seas and oceans to swell and stay away from the shore

why.Expect dry days and store extra water fo: Dry days are the opposite of what the koel's song signals.
why.Expect the koel to stop singing and wait: Waiting for another sign ignores the signal the children recorded.
why.Expect the seas and oceans to swell and: The koel's song says nothing about seas and oceans changing.

activities.explanation: Correct: the koel's song is the natural sign that tells farmers rains are coming.

activities.prompt: Explain why most of the globe is coloured blue.
activities.answer: The blue parts of a globe show seas and oceans. Since seas and oceans cover about three-fourths of the Earth, most of the globe's surface must be blue. Only the remaining parts are land masses, where countries are, so those parts take up less space on the globe.
points: Blue parts represent seas and oceans
Seas and oceans cover about three-fourths of the Earth
Remaining parts are land masses where countries are
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera's class has been curious explorers of nature all term. They observed plants, animals, sunlight, water and human activities, and recorded everything in their journals. Now they want to bring their learning together to understand patterns of change. Their teacher hangs a large wall-sized chart in the classroom. Time periods fill the columns, and themes are listed in the rows. One of the themes is water and water bodies.
activities.prompt: Rahul asks why the chart has time periods in columns and themes in rows instead of being filled randomly. What is the best reason?
options: It lets the class see how each theme changed from one time period to the next
It makes the chart look colourful and decorative on the wall
It allows the teacher to give marks for neat handwriting in each box
It hides which observations came from which student's journal

why.It makes the chart look colourful and de: Decoration is not the purpose; the chart is a tool for understanding change
why.It allows the teacher to give marks for: Marks for handwriting are not part of how the chart is used
why.It hides which observations came from wh: The chart collects shared class observations, so hiding sources is not its aim

activities.explanation: Correct: arranging time against theme helps them bring learning together and see patterns of change

activities.context: Meera's class has been curious explorers of nature all term. They observed plants, animals, sunlight, water and human activities, and recorded everything in their journals. Now they want to bring their learning together to understand patterns of change. Their teacher hangs a large wall-sized chart in the classroom. Time periods fill the columns, and themes are listed in the rows. One of the themes is water and water bodies.
activities.prompt: Ananya wants to copy every single detail from her journal into one box of the chart. What should the class do instead, and why?
options: Discuss the shared observations and write only the main ones, so the box stays useful
Write every detail, because more writing always makes a chart better
Leave the box empty until the teacher fills it for them
Write only Ananya's journal entries, since she observed the most

why.Write every detail, because more writing: Copying every detail would crowd the box and hide the main pattern of change
why.Leave the box empty until the teacher fi: The chart is made by the students from their own shared observations
why.Write only Ananya's journal entries, sin: One student's entries alone would not represent the whole class's observations

activities.explanation: Correct: the class discusses and writes the main observations, which keeps each box clear

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the students' journals and the wall-sized chart?
activities.answer: Journals hold each student's own recorded observations of plants, animals, sunlight, water and human activities. The chart brings all this learning together in one place, arranged by time periods and themes, showing only the main observations the class agrees on.
points: Journals are individual records of observations
The chart combines the whole class's learning
The chart is organised with time periods in columns and themes in rows
Only main observations, chosen after discussion, go on the chart
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why India has places with very different amounts of rainfall. Give examples in your answer.
activities.answer: Rainfall is not the same everywhere in India. Some places get very heavy rain while others stay almost dry. Mawsynram in Meghalaya is the wettest place on Earth, while the Thar Desert is one of the driest places. So India has both very wet and very dry areas.
points: Says rainfall is not the same everywhere in India
Names Mawsynram in Meghalaya as the wettest place on Earth
Names the Thar Desert as one of the driest places
Shows the contrast between very wet and very dry places
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a small village, a girl watches the fields change with the seasons. Her uncle plants one crop when the rains arrive because it needs more water to grow. Another crop grows best in the cool of winter, and one more loves the heat of summer. When flowers bloom in spring, the village celebrates Holi, and after the harvest in autumn, Diwali is celebrated.
activities.prompt: One year the rains fail and the fields stay dry. What is most likely to happen to the crop the uncle planted when the rains usually arrive?
options: It will grow poorly, because it will not get the extra water it needs.
It will grow even better, because crops planted in the rains prefer dry fields.
It will do fine, because every crop grows best in the heat of summer.
It will be ready to harvest earlier than the winter crop.

why.It will grow even better, because crops: Wrong: crops planted in the rains need water, not dry weather.
why.It will do fine, because every crop grow: Wrong: it is a different crop that grows best in the heat of summer, not this water-loving one.
why.It will be ready to harvest earlier than: Wrong: nothing in the lesson says a dry field makes a crop ready sooner.

activities.explanation: Correct: this crop was planted in the rainy season because it needs more water to grow, so without rain it will suffer.

activities.context: In a small village, a girl watches the fields change with the seasons. Her uncle plants one crop when the rains arrive because it needs more water to grow. Another crop grows best in the cool of winter, and one more loves the heat of summer. When flowers bloom in spring, the village celebrates Holi, and after the harvest in autumn, Diwali is celebrated.
activities.prompt: On a walk in spring, the girl sees flowers blooming everywhere and people preparing for a festival. Which festival is the village most likely getting ready for?
options: Holi
Diwali
Pongal
Makar Sankranti

why.Diwali: Wrong: Diwali comes in autumn, after crops are harvested, not when flowers bloom.
why.Pongal: Wrong: Pongal is a new year and harvest festival, not the festival of blooming flowers.
why.Makar Sankranti: Wrong: Makar Sankranti is a new year and harvest festival, not linked to flowers blooming.

activities.explanation: Correct: Holi is celebrated in spring, when flowers bloom.

activities.context: In a small village, a girl watches the fields change with the seasons. Her uncle plants one crop when the rains arrive because it needs more water to grow. Another crop grows best in the cool of winter, and one more loves the heat of summer. When flowers bloom in spring, the village celebrates Holi, and after the harvest in autumn, Diwali is celebrated.
activities.prompt: The uncle has seeds of a crop that needs a lot of water. What should he do?
options: Plant it in the rainy season, when there is plenty of water for it.
Plant it in winter, since some crops grow best in that season.
Plant it in the heat of summer, since some crops grow best then.
Plant it right after the harvest festival, since festivals show when to sow.

why.Plant it in winter, since some crops gro: Wrong: winter suits crops that like the cool, not crops needing extra water.
why.Plant it in the heat of summer, since so: Wrong: summer heat suits some crops, but this one needs more water instead.
why.Plant it right after the harvest festiva: Wrong: festivals celebrate seasons and harvests; they are not a guide for when to plant a thirsty crop.

activities.explanation: Correct: crops that need more water are planted in the rainy season.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Rhythms of Nature

activities.prompt: A torch shines on a globe. The side of the globe facing the torch shows day. What does the dark side show?
options: Morning
Night
Evening
Rain
activities.explanation: The side where light falls has day, and the side with no light has night. You spotted the pattern!

activities.prompt: The Sun moves around the Earth to make day and night.
activities.explanation: It is actually the Earth that rotates. The Sun stays in one place.

activities.prompt: The repeating pattern of changes in nature is called ______.
activities.hint: It comes again and again every year.
activities.explanation: Nature follows a pattern that repeats every year. This pattern is called seasons.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the globe with what it shows.
activities.explanation: The globe is a model of the Earth. Blue shows water, and countries sit on the land masses.

activities.prompt: Holi is celebrated in autumn after crops are harvested.
activities.explanation: Holi is celebrated in spring when flowers bloom. Diwali comes in autumn after the harvest.

activities.prompt: Seas and oceans cover about ______ of the Earth.
activities.hint: Think of cutting the Earth into four equal parts.
activities.explanation: Water covers about three-fourths of the Earth. The remaining parts are land masses.

activities.prompt: Put the changes in the weather in the order they happen over the year.
items: The weather warms up
It gets hot
Then it rains
activities.explanation: Nature changes slowly over the year: it warms up, gets hot, and then it rains. This pattern repeats every year.

activities.prompt: Match each festival with its season or reason.
activities.explanation: Many festivals are connected with seasons. Each one marks something special in nature.

chapters.title: Earth — Our Shared Home
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the blue planet; nature has no boundaries; the travelling birds and yoga; chilli and sugar.

lessons.title: The Blue Planet

activities.prompt: What does our home look like from way up in space?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One Home in Space
activities.body: From high up in space, the Earth looks tiny. You cannot see your city or your village from there. You only see broad shapes of land and sea on our blue planet. No border can be seen from outside. It seems that no border, no state and no countries exist. The Earth looks completely one. That is why we say the Earth is our one home, and we all are part of humanity.
keyPoints: From space, the Earth looks tiny and completely one.
No border, state or country can be seen from outside.
We only see broad shapes of land and sea.
The Earth is our one home, and we all are part of humanity.
activities.explanation: From far away, our planet looks like one single home for everyone.

activities.prompt: Meera sees a photo of Earth taken from space. It is a round blue ball. She asks, 'Where is India? Where is my city? Why can I not see them?'
steps: The astronaut took the photo very far away, so Earth looks tiny.
Because Earth looks tiny, small things like houses and cities are too small to see.
Borders are lines people draw on maps, so they are not painted on the ground.
So Meera can only see broad shapes of land and sea, not her city or any borders.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Two Brave Indians in Space
activities.body: Two Indians have seen our planet from space. Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian to see the Earth from space. When asked how India looked from above, he said "Saare Jahaan Se Achcha". Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla was the first Indian to reach the International Space Station. He shared inspiring words with the then Prime Minister of India.
keyPoints: Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian to see the Earth from space.
He said "Saare Jahaan Se Achcha" about India.
Shubhanshu Shukla was the first Indian to reach the International Space Station.
Shukla shared inspiring words with the then Prime Minister of India.
activities.explanation: Two brave Indians looked at our home from space and shared their joy.

activities.prompt: You are high up in space and you look at the Earth. How does it look?
options: Very big and shiny
Tiny
Flat like a plate
Covered with clouds only
activities.explanation: From high up in space, the Earth looks tiny. Well done!

activities.prompt: When asked how India looked from above, Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma said "Saare Jahaan Se ______".
activities.hint: It means the best of all.
activities.explanation: Rakesh Sharma said "Saare Jahaan Se Achcha". It means India looked the best of all.

activities.prompt: From outside in space, you can see the borders between countries on the Earth.
activities.explanation: No border can be seen from outside. The Earth looks completely one.

activities.prompt: Match each one with what it is known for.
pairs: First Indian to see the Earth from space
First Indian to reach the International Space Station
Words about how India looked from above
activities.explanation: Each astronaut and each word tells us something special about our blue planet.

activities.prompt: From space, small details like your city or village cannot be seen. So what CAN you see from there?
options: Broad shapes of land masses and the sea
The names of countries written on the ground
People walking in the market
The lights inside your house
activities.explanation: From space we only see broad shapes of land masses and the sea on our blue planet.

activities.prompt: A camera moves from space down towards your village. Put these views in order, from highest up to closest.
items: The whole Earth looking tiny
Broad shapes of land masses and the sea
Your city or village with its small details
activities.explanation: From high up the Earth looks tiny, then broad shapes appear, and small details are seen only when you come close.

activities.prompt: A boy says he will fly in a spaceship. He says he will point to his own house from space. What is wrong with his claim?
options: His house will be hiding behind thick clouds
His house will be too tiny to see from space
His house will look the same as all others
His house will be turned away from the ship

why.His house will be hiding behind thick cl: This child blames clouds, but the real reason is the size of the house.
why.His house will look the same as all othe: This child thinks the problem is many houses, but even one house is too small to see.
why.His house will be turned away from the s: This child thinks the direction of the house matters, but size is the real problem.

activities.explanation: Right. Earth looks tiny from space, so small details like a house cannot be seen.

activities.prompt: Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian to see Earth from space. He was asked how India looked. He said, 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha'. Why did Earth look so special to him?
options: He saw India's border lines shining below him
He saw our one beautiful home for all people
He saw his own city looking very pretty below
He saw India looking bigger than other lands

why.He saw India's border lines shining belo: This child thinks borders can be seen, but no border can be seen from outside.
why.He saw his own city looking very pretty: This child thinks small details can be seen, but cities cannot be seen from space.
why.He saw India looking bigger than other l: This child thinks he compared countries, but Earth looks completely one from outside.

activities.explanation: Right. Earth looks like one whole home, and we all are part of humanity.

activities.prompt: Shubhanshu Shukla was the first Indian to reach the space station. He shared inspiring words with the Prime Minister. Seeing Earth from space most likely made him feel that...
options: India is a bigger country than all others
space trips are easy and fun to do
Earth is our one home for all people
maps of the world are often wrong

why.India is a bigger country than all other: This child thinks space makes countries seem to compete, but Earth looks completely one.
why.space trips are easy and fun to do: This child thinks about the fun of the trip, not the view of Earth.
why.maps of the world are often wrong: This child thinks the view proved maps wrong, but maps are drawings, not the view.

activities.explanation: Right. From outside, Earth looks one, so it feels like our one shared home.

activities.prompt: A photo of Earth from space is mostly blue. Some broad shapes of land are also seen. Why does our planet look blue?
options: Because the blue sky paints the whole Earth
Because the sea covers broad shapes of Earth
Because blue clouds float all around the Earth
Because blue lights shine on Earth from the sun

why.Because the blue sky paints the whole Ea: This child thinks the sky above paints Earth, but the sea itself looks blue.
why.Because blue clouds float all around the: This child thinks clouds are blue, but clouds are white, not blue.
why.Because blue lights shine on Earth from: This child thinks sunlight is blue, but the blue comes from the sea.

activities.explanation: Right. From space we see broad shapes of land and sea, and the sea is blue.

lessons.title: Nature Has No Boundaries

activities.prompt: If a bird flies across the sky, can anyone stop it at a border?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nature Knows No Lines
activities.body: If you flew far above the Earth, you would not see any borders or lines between countries. Nature has no boundaries. Air, water, clouds, seeds and animals all move freely across the world. A bird does not stop at a fence in the sky, and a cloud does not ask permission to drift. The whole Earth is one big, connected home.
keyPoints: From far above, we do not see borders or lines between countries.
Nature has no boundaries.
Air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world.
activities.explanation: Nature moves freely everywhere, even though people draw lines on maps.

activities.prompt: Meera sees a bird fly over her house and fly over the next town. She asks: does the bird cross a border line in the sky?
steps: The bird flies high above the ground, so it is like looking from far above, where we do not see borders or lines between countries.
Nature has no boundaries, so the sky does not stop the bird at any line.
Air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world, so the bird can fly anywhere it needs.
So the bird crosses no real line, because nature has no boundaries.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: We Are All Connected
activities.body: People around the world are connected in many ways. We share ideas, food, music, stories and inventions. Your clothes, food and toys may have come from different parts of the world. Everything is linked through nature, trade, travel, and caring for our planet together. Earth is our shared home, so we look after it as one big family.
keyPoints: People around the world are connected in many ways.
Ideas, food, music, stories and inventions are shared.
Earth is our shared home.
activities.explanation: Sharing and caring link people everywhere, just like nature links the land and sky.

activities.prompt: You are far above the Earth, looking down like a bird. What do you see?
options: Thick walls between every country
Bright painted lines on the ground
No borders or lines between countries
Big signboards naming each country
activities.explanation: Well done! From far above, borders and lines between countries cannot be seen.

activities.prompt: Air, water, clouds, seeds and ______ move freely across the world.
activities.hint: Think of creatures that fly, swim or walk across lands.
activities.explanation: Yes! Animals, like clouds and seeds, are part of nature and move freely across the world.

activities.prompt: Nature has strong boundaries that stop clouds and seeds from crossing them.
activities.explanation: Nature has no boundaries. Clouds and seeds travel freely wherever wind and water take them.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with how it travels between people.
activities.explanation: Great matching! People share things near and far, and we all share one planet.

activities.prompt: Why do people around the world feel connected to each other?
options: Because they share ideas, food and music
Because they all speak the same language
Because they all live in the same country
Because clouds carry their letters
activities.explanation: Yes! Ideas, food, music, stories and inventions are shared, and that connects people.

activities.prompt: Earth is our shared home. So what is the best thing for people everywhere to do?
options: Each country should guard only its own air
Care for our planet together
Wait for someone else to fix things
Build higher walls around each country
activities.explanation: Well thought out! Everything is linked, so we care for our planet together.

activities.prompt: A boy looks at Earth from a rocket, very far above. He looks for the line between two countries. What will he see?
options: A thick black line drawn on the land
No line, because nature has no boundaries
A red line only around his own country
A line that moves when the wind blows

why.A thick black line drawn on the land: He thinks borders are drawn like lines on paper, but borders are not painted on the land.
why.A red line only around his own country: He thinks only his country has no line, but no country shows a line from above.
why.A line that moves when the wind blows: He thinks borders are real things that can move, but there is no line at all.

activities.explanation: Right. From far above we do not see borders or lines between countries.

activities.prompt: A cloud forms over one town. Wind blows it for many days. Where can the cloud go?
options: It stops at the edge of the town
It turns back because clouds are scared
It moves freely across the world
It falls down as rain at once

why.It stops at the edge of the town: He thinks clouds obey town borders, but nature has no boundaries.
why.It turns back because clouds are scared: He gives clouds feelings they do not have; clouds just move with the wind.
why.It falls down as rain at once: He confuses moving with raining; a cloud can travel before it rains.

activities.explanation: Right. Clouds move freely across the world like air and water.

activities.prompt: Ravi wears a shirt, eats rice, and plays with a toy. Each thing may have come from a different part of the world. What does this show?
options: People around the world are connected in many ways
Ravi is the only child with such things
Things from far away are always better
Ravi's family travels to buy every single thing

why.Ravi is the only child with such things: He thinks only he has such things, but this is true for many people.
why.Things from far away are always better: He judges far things as better, but the fact is about being connected, not quality.
why.Ravi's family travels to buy every singl: He thinks his family must travel, but things come to us through trade.

activities.explanation: Right. Our clothes, food and toys may come from different parts of the world, so people are connected.

activities.prompt: A girl says: 'My river is only mine. It stops at my village wall.' Her friend drops a leaf in the river upstream. What happens?
options: The leaf stops at the village wall
The leaf floats on to other places
The leaf sinks because it left home
The leaf flies up into the sky

why.The leaf stops at the village wall: She thinks walls can stop water, but water moves freely across the world.
why.The leaf sinks because it left home: She thinks leaving home makes things sink; water carries leaves along.
why.The leaf flies up into the sky: She confuses a leaf with a bird; leaves float on water.

activities.explanation: Right. Water moves freely across the world, so the leaf travels on.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'Earth belongs only to my country, so I need not care for other lands.' What is the flaw in his claim?
options: Earth is our shared home, so all lands matter
He is right, because his country is the biggest
He is right, because caring is only for adults
He is wrong, because other lands are not real

why.He is right, because his country is the: He thinks size decides who owns Earth, but Earth belongs to all of us.
why.He is right, because caring is only for: He thinks children cannot care, but everyone shares the job of caring.
why.He is wrong, because other lands are not: He agrees Earth is not shared but says other lands are not real, which is silly.

activities.explanation: Right. Earth is our shared home, so we care for our planet together.

lessons.title: The Travelling Birds and Yoga

activities.prompt: How do birds and yoga both travel across the whole world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Birds on a Long Journey, and an Old Indian Gift
activities.body: Rosy starlings are pink and black birds that fly in big groups. Every winter, they travel thousands of kilometres to India from southern Russia, Mongolia and nearby countries. They eat locusts and grasshoppers, so they help farmers. India also gave the world yoga, a practise over 3,000 years old for a healthy body and a peaceful mind.
keyPoints: Rosy starlings fly to India every winter from southern Russia and Mongolia.
They eat locusts and grasshoppers, which helps farmers.
Yoga began in India and is now practised in almost every country.
activities.explanation: Birds connect lands far apart, and yoga connects India to the world.

activities.prompt: A farmer sees many pink and black birds on his crop. He gets angry. Should he chase them away?
steps: The birds are rosy starlings, so look closely first.
They eat locusts and grasshoppers, which are pests on crops.
So the birds are eating the pests, not the crop.
Chasing them away would help the pests, so the farmer should let them stay.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Yoga: India's Gift to the World
activities.body: Since ancient times, people in India practised yoga for healthy bodies and peaceful minds. It was a way to live in harmony with oneself and nature. Travellers, scholars and teachers from India shared yoga with the world. Today, it is practised in almost every country. The United Nations declared 21 June as International Day of Yoga in 2014.
keyPoints: Yoga has been practised in India for more than 3,000 years.
Travellers, scholars and teachers carried yoga to other lands.
21 June is International Day of Yoga, declared by the United Nations in 2014.
activities.explanation: A practise born in India now helps people all over the world.

activities.prompt: Where do rosy starlings come from before they reach India?
options: Southern Russia, Mongolia and nearby countries
Africa and its nearby islands
Australia and New Zealand
activities.explanation: Well done! These birds travel from southern Russia, Mongolia and nearby countries.

activities.prompt: Every winter, rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres to ______.
activities.hint: Think of the country the birds visit when it is cold at home.
activities.explanation: Great job! India is their warm winter home.

activities.prompt: Rosy starlings are pink and black birds that fly in big groups.
activities.explanation: Yes! Their pink and black feathers make them easy to spot in a big flock.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does or is.
pairs: Are helped when pests are eaten
Keeps the body healthy and the mind peaceful
activities.explanation: Birds help crops grow, and yoga helps people stay well. Both are gifts of nature and India.

activities.prompt: Why are rosy starlings good news for farmers?
options: They build nests that protect crops
They eat locusts and grasshoppers that harm crops
They carry water to the fields
activities.explanation: Right! By eating pests on crops, these birds help farmers.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order, from earliest to latest.
items: People in India practise yoga for more than 3,000 years
Travellers, scholars and teachers share yoga with the world
Yoga is practised in almost every country
The United Nations declares 21 June as International Day of Yoga in 2014
activities.explanation: Yoga grew in India first, then spread across the world, and finally got its own special day.

activities.prompt: A farmer sprays strong poison. All the grasshoppers in his fields die. What will most likely happen to the rosy starlings that visit his fields?
options: Fewer starlings will come, because their food is gone.
More starlings will come, because the fields are clean.
The same starlings will come, because they eat crops.
The starlings will come and eat the poison instead.

why.More starlings will come, because the fi: This thinks clean fields attract birds, but the birds come for the pests.
why.The same starlings will come, because th: This thinks starlings eat crops, but they eat insects, not the crop.
why.The starlings will come and eat the pois: This confuses the birds with the pests; the poison kills insects, not birds.

activities.explanation: Right. Starlings feed on locusts and grasshoppers, so no pests means no food.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'Yoga cannot be very old. My cousin started yoga only last year.' What is wrong with his claim?
options: One person starting late does not tell when yoga began.
His cousin is too young to do yoga at all.
Yoga is old only in countries far away from India.
Yoga is old only if every child in India does it.

why.His cousin is too young to do yoga at al: This attacks the cousin, but the cousin's age is not the problem.
why.Yoga is old only in countries far away f: This adds a wrong rule; yoga began in India long ago.
why.Yoga is old only if every child in India: This adds a wrong rule; a practice can be old without everyone doing it.

activities.explanation: Right. Yoga has been practised for more than 3,000 years, so one late start proves nothing.

activities.prompt: A big fence is built across the starlings' flying path, so the birds cannot move safely. What does this show about nature?
options: Nature is deeply connected, so blocking one part harms many parts.
Nature is made of separate parts that never touch each other.
Nature works better when animals cannot move around freely.
Nature only needs birds in summer, not in winter.

why.Nature is made of separate parts that ne: This is the opposite of the truth; the birds' journey links faraway places.
why.Nature works better when animals cannot: Free and safe movement is what keeps nature connected and healthy.
why.Nature only needs birds in summer, not i: The birds travel in winter, so winter matters to them.

activities.explanation: Right. When animals move freely and safely, it shows nature is deeply connected, so blocking them breaks that link.

activities.prompt: The United Nations made 21 June the International Day of Yoga in 2014. Why did the world need such a day?
options: Because yoga spread from India and is now practised almost everywhere.
Because yoga was a secret that no country had heard about.
Because yoga is practised in only one country in the world.
Because yoga was invented by the United Nations in 2014.

why.Because yoga was a secret that no countr: This is the opposite; yoga spread widely, so many countries know it.
why.Because yoga is practised in only one co: This is the opposite; yoga is practised in almost every country today.
why.Because yoga was invented by the United: This confuses the day with the practice; yoga began in India long ago.

activities.explanation: Right. Travellers, scholars and teachers shared yoga, so it is now practised in almost every country.

lessons.title: Chilli and Sugar

activities.prompt: How did a spicy pepper travel across the world to reach your plate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Chilli's Long Journey
activities.body: Long ago, chilli plants grew only in South America. About 400 to 500 years ago, travellers from Portugal carried them to India. The chillies liked the new soil and the new climate. Soon they entered Indian kitchens. People loved them so much that today we cannot imagine Indian food without chillies!
keyPoints: Chilli plants were first found only in South America.
Travellers from Portugal brought chillies to India 400 to 500 years ago.
Today, Indian food feels incomplete without chillies.
activities.explanation: Chilli is not Indian by birth, but India gave it a loving home.

activities.prompt: Meera loves very spicy food. Her friend says, 'Chilli is an Indian plant, so of course our food is spicy.' Is her friend right?
steps: Chilli plants grew only in South America long ago, so they were not Indian plants at first.
Travellers from Portugal brought chillies to India 400 to 500 years ago, so chilli came from somewhere else.
Once chilli entered Indian kitchens, people loved it so much that food without it feels strange today.
So the friend is wrong: chilli came from outside India, but India made it its own because people loved it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sugar's Indian Story
activities.body: Sugar has a wonderful Indian story too. Long ago, people in other lands did not know about sugar at all. In India, people discovered how to make jaggery from sugarcane juice. This clever method spread to other parts of the world through trade and travel. Rice, mangoes and bananas from India also reached other lands.
keyPoints: Long ago, people across the world did not know about sugar.
Making jaggery from sugarcane juice was first discovered in India.
Trade and travel carried this knowledge to other lands.
activities.explanation: Just like chilli travelled to India, sugar travelled from India to the world.

activities.prompt: Long ago, where were chilli plants found?
options: Only in India
Only in Africa
Only in South America
Only in Portugal
activities.explanation: Chilli plants grew only in South America long ago. They came to India much later.

activities.prompt: Travellers from ______ brought chilli plants to India about 400 to 500 years ago.
activities.hint: Think of the country whose sailors carried the chilli plants.
activities.explanation: Portuguese travellers brought chillies to India, and the plants found a new home here.

activities.prompt: Travellers from Portugal brought chillies to India.
activities.explanation: Well done! Portuguese travellers carried chillies from South America to India 400 to 500 years ago.

activities.prompt: Before chillies arrived in India, which spice did people use to make food tasty?
options: Black pepper
Sugar
Jaggery
Salt from the sea
activities.explanation: Black pepper was the spice people used before chillies reached India.

activities.prompt: Match each food fact with its partner.
activities.explanation: Chilli came to India from South America, while sugar and jaggery travelled out from India.

activities.prompt: Put the chilli's journey in the correct order, from first to last.
items: Chilli plants grew only in South America.
Travellers from Portugal brought chillies to India.
The chillies found new soil and a new climate.
Chillies entered Indian kitchens.
People loved chillies, and now food feels incomplete without them.
activities.explanation: The chilli travelled from South America to India, settled in, and won every kitchen!

activities.prompt: A new spice comes to a town. People love it and put it in every dish. Before this, they used an old spice every day. What will most likely happen to the old spice?
options: People will use the old spice much less.
People will use the old spice much more.
The old spice will vanish from the whole world.
Nothing will change for the old spice.

This gets it backwards; a loved new spice does not make the old one more used.
why.The old spice will vanish from the whole: Too strong; the old spice may still be used a little, just not much.
This ignores how people change when they love something new.

activities.explanation: Right, because when people love a new spice, they use it instead of the old one.

activities.prompt: Long ago, a child in a faraway land never tasted sugar. Sugar was first known in India. Why did that child not know sugar?
options: Because the child did not like sweet things.
Because sugar had not travelled to that land yet.
Because sugar was only for grown-ups then.
Because the child never wanted to taste it.

why.Because the child did not like sweet thi: This blames the child's taste, but the child simply had never tried sugar.
why.Because sugar was only for grown-ups the: This invents a rule about grown-ups that the facts do not say.
why.Because the child never wanted to taste: Same mistake as the first; the child could not want what was never known.

activities.explanation: Right, because long ago people across the world did not know about sugar.

activities.prompt: Ravi plants chilli seeds in two pots. Pot A gets soil and weather like India. Pot B gets very cold weather. Both pots get water and sun. Which pot will grow better, and why?
options: Pot B, because cold weather makes plants grow faster.
Pot A, because the plant needs the right soil and climate.
Both pots the same, because water and sun are all a plant needs.
Pot B, because Ravi watered it more than Pot A.

why.Pot B, because cold weather makes plants: This thinks cold helps plants, but cold is not the climate chillies need.
why.Both pots the same, because water and su: This forgets that soil and climate also matter, not just water and sun.
why.Pot B, because Ravi watered it more than: The question says both pots got the same water, so this cannot be it.

activities.explanation: Right, because chillies grew well in India when they found new soil and a new climate.

activities.prompt: A trader sails from India to a far land. There he learns how to make jaggery from sugarcane juice. What will most likely happen next?
options: He will keep the method secret for ever.
He will forget the method on the way home.
He will share the method with people in the far land.
He will make the far land stop using sugarcane.

This thinks traders hide things, but knowledge usually travels with them.
why.He will forget the method on the way hom: This thinks travel makes people forget, but traders carry knowledge home and onward.
why.He will make the far land stop using sug: This makes no sense; sharing a method does not stop a crop.

activities.explanation: Right, because knowledge of making jaggery spread through trade and travel.

activities.prompt: A child in a far country eats a sweet mango. Long ago, mango plants grew only in India. How did the mango reach that far country?
options: It grew there on its own long ago.
People carried it there from India.
The child only dreamed about the mango.
Birds flew the mango tree there.

This forgets that the plant first grew only in India.
This runs away from the question instead of answering it.
This is a silly story, not how plants travel to new lands.

activities.explanation: Right, because rice, mangoes and bananas from India found their way to other lands.

lessons.title: The Mexican Marigold and The Cows that Went to Brazil

activities.prompt: How did our flowers and cows travel all the way across the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Flower and Some Cows Travel the World
activities.body: The bright marigold flower first grew in Mexico. In Mexico, people use it in festivals. Long ago, it travelled across the world and reached India. Its orange and yellow colours reminded us of warmth and celebration. Today you see marigolds in temples, homes, weddings and Diwali. Indian cows also travelled! Portuguese traders took them to Brazil. There, the cows grew in number and now give Brazil most of its milk.
keyPoints: The marigold came from Mexico and is now loved all over India.
Marigolds are used in temples, homes, weddings and festivals like Diwali.
Portuguese traders took Indian cows to Brazil long ago.
Three Indian cow breeds give Brazil most of its milk.
activities.explanation: Flowers and cows can travel far, and both made India and other lands happier!

activities.prompt: Meera sees orange marigolds at a temple, at a wedding, and at Diwali. She thinks marigolds started in India. Is she right?
steps: Meera sees marigolds everywhere in India today, so she feels sure they began here.
But seeing a plant in many places only shows people love using it now.
The marigold flower actually came from Mexico, far across the sea.
So Meera's feeling is wrong; the flower travelled to India later.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where does the marigold flower come from?
options: India
Mexico
Brazil
Portugal
activities.explanation: The marigold is from Mexico. Later it travelled all the way to India.

activities.prompt: The marigold's bright orange and yellow colours reminded people of...
options: rain and winter
warmth and celebration
rivers and boats
mountains and snow
activities.explanation: The happy colours reminded people of warmth, celebration and spirituality.

activities.prompt: Long ago, ______ traders took some Indian cows to Brazil.
activities.hint: Think of the country whose traders sailed to India long ago.
activities.explanation: Portuguese traders took Indian cows across the sea to Brazil.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to where it belongs.
activities.explanation: The flower came from Mexico to India. The cows went from India to Brazil!

activities.prompt: More than three-fourths of Brazil's milk comes from three Indian cow breeds. Which three?
options: Gir, Kankrej and Ongole
Gir, Sahiwal and Tharparkar
Ongole, Red Sindhi and Gir
Kankrej, Ongole and Hallikar
activities.explanation: The three breeds are Gir, Kankrej and Ongole. They give Brazil most of its milk.

activities.prompt: Put the marigold's journey in the correct order.
items: The marigold grew in Mexico.
It travelled across the world.
It reached India.
Its colours reminded people of warmth and celebration.
Today it is seen everywhere in India.
activities.explanation: The marigold started in Mexico, travelled the world, reached India, and now blooms everywhere here!

activities.prompt: Ravi lives in Mexico. His family is getting ready for a big festival. They want flowers that show celebration and warmth. Which flowers should they pick?
options: Bright orange and yellow marigold flowers
Plain brown dry leaves from the garden
Pale grey stones from the river side
Dark black seeds from the store shop

why.Plain brown dry leaves from the garden: Wrong: he thinks any dry thing from home can be a festival flower.
why.Pale grey stones from the river side: Wrong: he thinks anything pale can show warmth and celebration.
why.Dark black seeds from the store shop: Wrong: he thinks dark things can show warm, happy feelings.

activities.explanation: Right: marigolds are special festival flowers, and their bright colours mean warmth and celebration.

activities.prompt: Anita says, 'Marigolds began in India. I see them everywhere here.' What is wrong with Anita's thinking?
options: Seeing them now does not show where they began
She should count the flowers to find the answer
Flowers that grow in many places have no home
Only flowers in gardens can tell us their home

why.She should count the flowers to find the: Wrong: she thinks counting flowers now tells where they first grew.
why.Flowers that grow in many places have no: Wrong: she thinks a flower with no home is the answer here.
why.Only flowers in gardens can tell us thei: Wrong: she thinks only garden flowers can show where they began.

activities.explanation: Right: marigolds came from Mexico and only later travelled to India.

activities.prompt: Brazil put pictures of Gir, Kankrej and Ongole cows on stamps and coins. Why did Brazil honour these cows this way?
options: These Indian cows make most of Brazil's milk
These cows were born inside Brazil long ago
These cows can jump higher than other cows
These cows are the fastest cows in Brazil

why.These cows were born inside Brazil long: Wrong: he forgets the cows came from India, not Brazil.
why.These cows can jump higher than other co: Wrong: he thinks jumping made the cows special to Brazil.
why.These cows are the fastest cows in Brazi: Wrong: he thinks speed made the cows special to Brazil.

activities.explanation: Right: more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk comes from these three breeds.

activities.prompt: A farmer in Brazil wants a cow that gives good milk and stays healthy in Brazil's weather. Which cows should he choose?
options: Gir, Kankrej or Ongole cows from India
Any cow he finds walking on the road
The smallest cow he can buy at the fair
The cow with the loudest moo in the shed

why.Any cow he finds walking on the road: Wrong: he thinks any random cow will give good milk anywhere.
why.The smallest cow he can buy at the fair: Wrong: he thinks small size means good milk and strong health.
why.The cow with the loudest moo in the shed: Wrong: he thinks a loud moo means a good milk cow.

activities.explanation: Right: these breeds give good milk and do not mind Brazil's weather.

activities.prompt: Sam says, 'Gir cows must be from Brazil. Their pictures are on Brazilian stamps.' What is the flaw in Sam's claim?
options: Stamps can show animals that came from elsewhere
Stamps only show animals born in that country
Gir cows cannot be drawn on stamps or coins
A country puts only flowers on its own stamps

why.Stamps only show animals born in that co: Wrong: he thinks stamps must show only locally born animals.
why.Gir cows cannot be drawn on stamps or co: Wrong: he thinks the pictures on stamps cannot be real cows.
why.A country puts only flowers on its own s: Wrong: he thinks stamps can show only flowers, not cows.

activities.explanation: Right: Gir cows came from India; Brazil only honoured them on stamps.

lessons.title: Web of Life and One Earth, One Family

activities.prompt: Could the whole wide world really be one big family?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth: One Big Web of Life
activities.body: Earth is a living web of life. People, animals, plants and ideas travel, mix and grow together. A bird flying far away, a seed growing in a new land, or yoga reaching every corner reminds us we are all connected. Ancient India gave us a saying: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'. It means the world is one family.
keyPoints: Earth is a living web of life where everything travels, mixes and grows together.
A bird, a seed or yoga travelling far reminds us we are all connected.
'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' means the world is one family.
activities.explanation: We are all part of one big, living family on Earth.

activities.prompt: A crow flies over Meera's house every day. One day it does not come. Meera wonders: does the crow leaving change anything in her garden?
steps: The crow eats insects and small snails in the garden, so the garden depends on the crow.
If the crow stops coming, the insects may grow more, because no bird is eating them.
More insects may eat the leaves of Meera's plants, so the plants can get weaker.
So one bird leaving can change the whole garden, because living things in a place depend on each other.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Belongs to This Family?
activities.body: All people, animals, trees, rivers, air and sky belong to Earth's family. We live together, depend on each other, and share the same home. When we see the world as one family, we learn to live with respect, care and love. Earth has supported people, animals and plants for thousands of years.
keyPoints: People, animals, trees, rivers, air and sky all belong to the family.
We live together, depend on each other and share the same home.
Seeing the world as one family teaches us respect, care and love.
activities.explanation: One family means everyone and everything belongs, and we look after each other.

activities.prompt: What does the saying 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' mean?
options: The sky is one roof
The world is one family
Rivers all flow one way
Games have one winner
activities.explanation: This saying from ancient India tells us the whole world is one family.

activities.prompt: Earth is a living ______ of life where people, animals, plants and ideas grow together.
activities.hint: Think of threads joined together, like a spider makes.
activities.explanation: A web joins many threads, just as Earth joins many lives.

activities.prompt: Earth is the only planet we know that has life.
activities.explanation: Yes! That is why caring for Earth matters so much.

activities.prompt: Match each traveller with where it goes.
activities.explanation: Birds, seeds and ideas like yoga all travel. They remind us we are all connected.

activities.prompt: When we see the world as one family, what do we learn to live with?
options: Money, gold and silver
Respect, care and love
Maps, clocks and rules
Speed, power and prizes
activities.explanation: Seeing everyone as family helps us live with respect, care and love.

activities.prompt: Meera waters the young tree near her home every day. When she cares for Earth, who else is she caring for?
options: Only the tree she waters
Only her own family
Each other, all of us
Nobody else at all
activities.explanation: When we care for Earth, we care for each other, because we all share one home.

activities.prompt: Ravi's family moves to a new town. The children there play a game Ravi never saw before. Ravi teaches them a game from his old town. After some weeks, what will most likely happen?
options: The children will play both games and mix new ideas into them.
The children will forget their own game and play only Ravi's game.
Ravi will stop playing games because his game is different.
The children will not learn anything from a new person.

why.The children will forget their own game: Wrong: mixing does not mean one side loses everything; cultures blend, not replace.
why.Ravi will stop playing games because his: Wrong: being different does not stop sharing; difference is what makes sharing useful.
why.The children will not learn anything fro: Wrong: we learn from and inspire one another, even from someone new.

activities.explanation: Right: people share and blend ideas when they meet, so both games grow together.

activities.prompt: A seed from one country grows into a plant in a faraway land. A bird carries the idea of a song to a new place too. What do the seed and the song both show?
options: Things can only stay safe if they never leave their home.
Living things and ideas can travel, mix and grow in new places.
Only birds can carry things from one place to another place.
New places are always better than the old home place.

why.Things can only stay safe if they never: Wrong: the lesson shows travel and mixing, not staying closed in one place.
why.Only birds can carry things from one pla: Wrong: seeds and songs can travel in many ways; birds are only one example.
why.New places are always better than the ol: Wrong: the lesson never says one place is better; it says places connect.

activities.explanation: Right: a seed and a song both travel, mix with new things and grow somewhere new.

activities.prompt: A girl says: 'My family is only my mother, father and brother. The river near my house is not family.' Her friend smiles and remembers an old Indian saying. What should the friend say?
options: The river is family too, because the whole world is one family.
The girl is right, because only people can be in a family.
The river is family only when we drink its water every day.
The saying is only about people who live in the same house.

why.The girl is right, because only people c: Wrong: the saying includes animals, trees, rivers, air and sky, not only people.
why.The river is family only when we drink i: Wrong: belonging does not depend on using something every day.
why.The saying is only about people who live: Wrong: the saying is about the whole world, not one house.

activities.explanation: Right: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' means the world is one family, and rivers belong to it.

activities.prompt: Two children argue. Ali says: 'We depend on each other, so I must care for the trees.' Neha says: 'Trees grow alone in forests, so trees need nothing from me.' Who is thinking like the lesson, and why?
options: Neha, because trees in forests live far away from people.
Neha, because trees can make their own food from sunlight.
Ali, because we all live together and depend on each other.
Ali, because trees give more shade than any other plant.

why.Neha, because trees in forests live far: Wrong: living far away does not end the web that connects all living things.
why.Neha, because trees can make their own f: Wrong: even if trees make food, the lesson is about depending on each other, not food only.
why.Ali, because trees give more shade than: Wrong: comparing shade misses the real reason, which is depending on each other.

activities.explanation: Right: the lesson says we live together, depend on each other and share one home.

activities.prompt: A boy throws rubbish into the park pond. He says: 'It is only one pond. It cannot matter to anyone.' What is the flaw in his claim?
options: He is right, because small ponds are not important places.
He forgot that caring for Earth means caring for each other.
He is right, because rubbish always sinks and disappears fast.
He forgot that only grown-ups should care about ponds.

why.He is right, because small ponds are not: Wrong: every pond is part of the living web, so no pond is unimportant.
why.He is right, because rubbish always sink: Wrong: rubbish does not just vanish; it harms the living things in the pond.
why.He forgot that only grown-ups should car: Wrong: caring for Earth is for everyone, not only grown-ups.

activities.explanation: Right: when we care for Earth, we care for each other, so one pond matters.

activities.prompt: A class makes a poster of Earth as one big family. Sam draws only people holding hands. Meera says something is missing. What should Meera say, and why?
options: Add more people, because a family poster needs many faces.
Add a border, because posters always look better with borders.
Add animals, trees, rivers, air and sky, because they belong to the family too.
Add only houses, because a family needs a house to live in.

why.Add more people, because a family poster: Wrong: the problem is not the number of people; the family is bigger than people.
why.Add a border, because posters always loo: Wrong: decoration is not the point; the poster must show who belongs to the family.
why.Add only houses, because a family needs: Wrong: the family in the lesson is about living things and nature, not houses.

activities.explanation: Right: all people, animals, trees, rivers, air and sky belong to this one family.

lessons.sceneAlt: The whole Earth seen as one blue and white sphere from space, photographed by the Apollo 17 spacecraft.
